parts.problemMd:
The graph shows the variation with length *l *of resistance *R* for two wires X and Y made from the same material.

![cie-ial-images513png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/041-cie-ial-images513png.png)

What does the graph show?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- Electrical power is given by $P=VI$
- Using Ohm's Law we can combine these to get

  - $P = ( I R ) I = I^{ } 2 R$
- We can see from the graph, when *l* is 0.6 m:

  - The resistance of X is 20 Ω
  - The resistance of Y is 10 Ω
- Therefore, the resistance of X is double that of Y
- Since $P=I^{2}R$, power and resistance are directly proportional to each other

  - The ratio of power in X to power in Y is $\frac{P_{X}}{P_{Y}}=\frac{20I^{2}}{10I^{2}}=2$
- Therefore, when equal lengths of X and Y are connected in series to a battery, the power in X is double the power in Y

**A **is incorrect because from $R = ( \frac{rho}{A} ) l$  , we can see the gradient of the line is $\frac{ρ}{A}$ , since the resistivity is the same for both wires, the cross-sectional area in Y will be double that of X

**B **is incorrect because the wires are made from the same material; hence, they both have the same resistivity

**D **is incorrect because from $R=\frac{V}{I}$ , we can see resistance and current are inversely proportional, so the current in Y will be double the current in X

**Exam Tip: **Sometimes, in physics questions, you can use common sense to work out whether or not your answer makes logical sense. In this question, for example, as the resistance in wire X is double that of wire Y, it makes sense that the cross-sectional area, and hence, the current will be lower in wire X. Think about water flowing through a pipe - a smaller cross-sectional area means a thinner pipe, and hence water will travel at a slower rate than in a wider pipe (one with a larger cross-sectional area)

parts.problemMd:
A light-dependent resistor *R* has a resistance of about 1 MΩ in the dark and about 1 kΩ when illuminated. It is connected in series with a 5 kΩ resistor to a 1.5 V cell of negligible internal resistance.

![cie-ial-images514png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/009-cie-ial-images514png.png)

The light-dependent resistor is illuminated (in an otherwise dark room) by a flashing light.

Which graph best shows the variation with time *t* of potential difference *V* across *R *?

![cie-ial-physics-images-9-3-m-q6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/010-cie-ial-physics-images-9-3-m-q6.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- The LDR and the 5 kΩ resistor form a potential divider
- The potential divider equation is given by $V_{e} m f \times ( \frac{R_{1}}{R_{1} + R_{2}} )$ , where:

  - *V *<sub>*emf*</sub> is the e. m .f. of the supply = 1.5 V
  - *R*<sub>*1*</sub> is the resistance across the LDR = *R*
  - *R*<sub>*2*</sub> is the resistance of the fixed resistor = 5 kΩ
- So, the p. d. across the LDR is equal to $\frac{1.5 R}{ ( R + 5000 ) }$
- When *R* is 1000 kΩ, the p. d. is very close to 1.5 V:

  - $V = 1.5 \times ( \frac{ ( 1 \times 10^{6} ) }{ ( 1 \times 10^{6} ) + 5000} ) = 1.492 \approx 1.5 \mathrm{V}$
- When *R* is 1 kΩ, then the p. d. is about $\frac{1.5}{6}$  :

  - $V = 1.5 \times ( \frac{1000}{1000 + 5000} ) = 0.25 \mathrm{V}$
- So, the graph must show a peak value of very close to 1.5 and a minimum value that is more than zero

**A **is incorrect because this graph shows the minimum to be only slightly less than 1.5 V

**C **is incorrect because this graph shows the minimum to be zero

**D **is incorrect because the maximum is far below 1.5 V

parts.problemMd:
Tensile strain may be measured by the change in electrical resistance of a strain gauge.

A strain gauge consists of folded fine metal wire mounted on a flexible insulating backing sheet.

The strain gauge is firmly attached to the specimen, so that the strain in the metal wire is always identical to that in the specimen.

![cie-ial-images519png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/016-cie-ial-images519png.png)

When the strain in the specimen is increased, what happens to the resistance of the wire?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- As the strain in the specimen is increased, the wire is extended meaning its length increases
- Resistance and wire length are directly proportional, so an increase in length results in an increase in resistance
- At the same time, the strain causes the cross-sectional area of the wire to become smaller (as the overall volume does not change)
- Resistance and cross-sectional area are inversely proportional, so, a decrease in cross-sectional area also results in an increase in the resistance
- So, as the strain in the specimen increases, the resistance of the wire increases, because the length increases and the cross-sectional area decreases

parts.problemMd:
A researcher has two pieces of copper of the same volume. All of the first piece is made into a cylindrical resistor P of length *x*.

![cie-ial-images520png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/001-cie-ial-images520png.png)

All of the second piece is made into uniform wires each of the same length *x* which he connects between two bars of negligible resistance to form a resistor Q.

![cie-ial-images521png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/002-cie-ial-images521png.png)

How do the electrical resistances of P and Q compare ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Let's compare each of these quantities

  - The wires are all made of the same material, so the resistivity *ρ* is the same for both
  - Both wires have the same length *x*
  - The only difference between the two resistors is the number of wires in each configuration
- Both resistors contain the same amount (volume) of material, so the cross-sectional area *A* of resistor P will equal to collective cross-sectional areas of all the wires in resistor Q
- Therefore, since none of the quantities in  $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$are different, P and Q both have the same resistance

parts.problemMd:
Two wires have the same length and the same resistance. Wire X is made of a metal of resistivity 1.7 × 10<sup>–8</sup> Ωm, and wire Y is made of a metal of resistivity 5.6 × 10<sup>–8</sup> Ωm.

The diameter of wire X is 0.315 mm.

What is the diameter of wire Y?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Cross-sectional area is equal to $A = \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{r}^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } ( \frac{\mathrm{d}}{2} )^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{4}$

  - So, $R = \frac{\rho L}{A} = \rho L ( \frac{4}{\mathrm{\pi }} \mathrm{d}^{2} )$
- The two wires have the same resistance and same length

  - Resistance in wire X$= \frac{4 ( 1.7 \\times 10^{- 8} ) L}{ \mathrm{\pi } ( 0.315 )^{2}}$
  - Resistance in wire Y$= \frac{4 ( 5.6 \\times 10^{- 8} ) L}{ \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{d}^{2}}$
- Resistance in wire X = Resistance in wire Y

  - $\frac{4 ( 1.7 \\times 10^{- 8} ) L}{ \mathrm{\pi } ( 0.315 )^{2}} = \frac{4 ( 5.6 \\times 10^{- 8} ) L}{ \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{d}^{2}}$
- Cancelling the common terms $( \frac{4 L}{ \mathrm{\pi } } )$  , we have

  - $\frac{1.7 \times 10^{ - } 8}{ ( 0.315 ) ^{2} } = \frac{5.6 \times 10^{ - } 8}{d ^{2} }$
- Rearranging for *d*<sup>*2*</sup>

  - $d^{ } 2 = \frac{ ( 5.6 \times 10^{ - } 8 ) ( 0.315 ) ^{2} }{1.7 \times 10^{ - } 8} = 0.327$
- Therefore, the diameter of wire Y is

  - $d=\sqrt{0.327}=0.57\mathrm{mm}$

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows an electric pump for a garden fountain connected by an 18 m cable to a 230 V mains electrical supply.

![cie-ial-images467png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/033-cie-ial-images467png.png)

The performance of the pump is acceptable if the potential difference (p.d.) across it is at least 218 V. The current through it is then 0.83 A.

What is the maximum resistance per meter of each of the two wires in the cable if the pump is to perform acceptably?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- Ohm's Law states $V=IR$
- For the pump to perform acceptably, we are told the potential difference across it should be at least 218 V

  - So, the potential difference across the cables is 230 -218 = 12 V
- The current through the electric pump is 0.83 A
- The same current flows through the cable since it is in series with the pump. So, the cable has a total resistance of $R=\frac{230-218}{0.83}=14.5$Ω
- From the diagram, it can be seen that the cable is made up of two wires

  - So, the total length of wire in the cable is 2 × 18 = 36 m
- The wires are not connected to each other - so, they are not in parallel. Instead, one wire connects one terminal of the mains to one terminal of the pump, and the other wire connected the other terminal of the mains to the other terminal of the pump
- This total length of wire corresponds to a total resistance of 14.5 Ω

  - Therefore, the resistance per meter is equal to $=\frac{14.5}{36}=0.4$Ω $m^{-1}$

- In the second test, where only S<sub>1</sub> is closed, we can see that lamp A is not faulty

parts.problemMd:
A copper wire is to be replaced by an aluminium alloy wire of the same length and resistance.

Copper has half the resistivity of the alloy.

What is the ratio  $\frac{diameterofalloywire}{diameterofcopperwire}$?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B because:**

- Copper has half the resistivity of the alloy $ρ_{c}=\frac{1}{2}ρ_{a}$
- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Both wires have the same resistance, $R$ and length, $L$, so

  - $ρ_{c}\frac{L}{A_{c}}=ρ_{a}\frac{L}{A_{a}}$
  - $\frac{ρ_{c}}{A_{c}}=\frac{ρ_{a}}{A_{a}}$
- Substitute $p_{c}=\frac{1}{2}ρ_{a}$

  - $\frac{1}{2A_{c}}=\frac{1}{A_{a}}$
  - $A_{a}=2A_{c}$
- The alloy wire must have twice the cross-sectional area
- Since area is proportional to diameter squared

  - $\frac{A_{a}}{A_{c}}=\frac{d_{a}^{2}}{d_{c}^{2}}=2$
  - $\frac{d_{a}}{d_{c}}=\sqrt{2}$
- This is answer **B**

parts.problemMd:
The current in a block of semiconductor is 30.0 mA when there is a potential difference (p.d.) of 10.0 V across it. The dimensions of the block and the direction of the current in it are as shown.

![cie-ial-images526png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/021-cie-ial-images526png.png)

The electrical meters used are accurate to ± 0.1 mA and ± 0.1 V. The dimensions of the block are accurate to ± 0.2 mm.

What is the resistivity of the semiconductor?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- So, resistivity is equal to $ρ=\frac{AR}{L}$
- From Ohm's law, resistance is equal to $R=\frac{V}{I}$
- So, combining this with the equation for resistivity, we get

  - $ρ=\frac{VA}{IL}$
- The cross-sectional area of the block is equal to the area of the grey rectangle through which the current flows

  - $A=lw$ , where *l* is the length and *w* is the width
- So, resistivity is equal to $ρ=\frac{Vlw}{IL}$

  - The p. d. is equal to* V* = 10.0 V
  - The current through the block is equal to* I* = 30 mA = 30 × 10<sup>–3</sup> A
- The dimensions of the block are equal to

  - *l* = 15 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m, *w* = 30 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m, *L* = 15 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- So, resistivity $\text{rho} = \frac{V l w}{I L} = \frac{10 \times ( 15 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times ( 30 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) }{ ( 30 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times ( 15 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) } = 10$ Ωm
- Next, we must consider the uncertainty in resistivity *ρ*

  - $\frac{\Delta rho}{rho} = ( \frac{\Delta V}{V} ) + ( \frac{\Delta l}{l} ) + ( \frac{\Delta w}{w} ) + ( \frac{\Delta I}{I} ) + ( \frac{\Delta L}{L} )$
  - $\Delta \text{rho} = [ ( \frac{\Delta v}{V} ) + ( \frac{\Delta l}{l} ) + ( \frac{\Delta w}{w} ) + ( \frac{\Delta I}{I} ) + ( \frac{\Delta L}{L} ) ] \times \text{rho}$
  - $\Delta \text{rho} = [ ( \frac{0.1}{10} ) + ( \frac{0.2}{15} ) + ( \frac{0.2}{30} ) + ( \frac{0.1}{30} ) + ( \frac{0.2}{15} ) ] \times 10$
  - Δ*ρ* = 0.467 = 0.5 Ωm
- Therefore, resistivity is equal to *ρ* = 10.0 ± 0.5 Ωm

parts.problemMd:
The resistance of a metal cube is measured by placing it between two parallel plates, as shown.

![cie-ial-images527png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/034-cie-ial-images527png.png)

The cube has volume *V* and is made of a material with resistivity *ρ*. The connections to the cube have negligible resistance.

Which expression gives the electrical resistance of the metal cube between X and Y?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Where *L* is the length of the wire and *A* is the cross-sectional area of the wire
- For a cube, all the sides are of equal lengths
- Let the length of a side be *L*

  - So, the volume of the cube is $V=L^{3}$
  - The cross-sectional area in contact with the plates is equal to $A=L^{2}$
- Resistance is therefore equal to $R=\frac{ρL}{L^{2}}=\frac{ρ}{L}$
- But since $V=L^{3}$  , length *L* is equal to $L = \sqrt[3]{V} = V^{1 \frac{1}{3}}$

  - So, resistance  $R=\frac{ρ}{V^{\frac{1}{3}}}$

**Exam Tip:** An alternative (and potentially quicker) method is to consider the units of the quantities involved, only choice **C** gives the unit of resistance (Ω):

- Unit of resistivity = Ωm
- Unit of volume *V* = m<sup>3</sup>
- Unit of    $\frac{\rho }{V^{1 \frac{1}{3}}} = [ \mathrm{\Omega } \mathrm{m} ] [ \mathrm{m}^{3} ]^{- 1 \frac{1}{3}} = [ \mathrm{\Omega } \mathrm{m} ] \mathrm{m}^{- 1} = \mathrm{\Omega }$

parts.problemMd:
A strain gauge consists of a length of wire with a uniform cross-sectional area. Its resistance is 2.50 kΩ. It is attached to a large pipe.

When the pipe expands, the strain gauge changes in dimensions, such that the length increases by 4% and the diameter reduced by 1%.

What is the new resistance of the strain gauge?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Cross-sectional area of a wire is equal to $A = \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{r}^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } ( \frac{\mathrm{d}}{2} )^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } ( \frac{\mathrm{d}}{2} )^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{4}$
- When the pipe expands

  - The new length is given by $L ' = ( 1 + 0.04 ) L = 1.04 L$
  - The new cross-sectional area is given by $A ' = ( 1 - 0.01 ) ^{2} A = ( 0.99 ) ^{2} A$  (squared because A is proportional to d<sup>2</sup>)
  - The resistivity ρ doesn't change since the material stays the same
- So, the new resistance is equal to

  - $R ' = \frac{ \rho L '}{A '} = \frac{1.04 \rho L}{ ( 0.99 ) ^{2} A} = \frac{1.04}{ ( 0.99 ) ^{2} } R = \frac{1.04}{ ( 0.99 ) ^{2} } \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \times 2.5 = 2.653 \mathrm{k}$Ω
- Therefore, the new resistance is 2.65 kΩ

- So, the cross-sectional area *A* is proportional to *y*

parts.problemMd:
The following strain gauge consists of a fine metal wire, so that an applied tension on the strain gauge results in changes in the length and cross-sectional area of the wire.

![cie-ial-images535png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/020-cie-ial-images535png.png)

When the length of the wire is stretched by 5%, what is the percentage change in the resistance of the wire? Assume that the volume of a wire remains constant when it is stretched.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Let's call the new length and cross-sectional area *L' *and *A'* respectively
- Since the volume remains constant

  - $V=AL=A'L'$
- When the wire expands

  - The new length is given by $L ' = ( 1 + 0.05 ) L = 1.05 L$
  - The new cross-sectional area is given by $V = A L = ( 1.05 L ) ( \frac{A}{1.05} )$
  - So, $A^{'}=\frac{A}{1.05}$
  - The resistivity *ρ* doesn't change since the material stays the same
- So, the new resistance is equal to

  - `R ' = \frac{ \text{rho} L '}{A '} = \text{rho} ( 1.05 ) ( \frac{1.05}{A} ) = ( 1.05 ) ^{2} ( \frac{ \text{rho} L}{A} ) = 1.10 R`
- Therefore, the percentage change in *R* is equal to

  - (1.10 – 1.00) × 100 % = 10 %

parts.problemMd:
Aluminum and copper rods are designed to have the same length and the same resistance.

The resistivity of copper is half that of aluminum, but its density is three times that of aluminum.

Determine the ratio of the mass of the aluminum rod to the mass of the copper rod.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- In this question we will refer to density by *d *and resistivity by *ρ*
- Density of a material is given by $d=\frac{m}{v}$

  - The mass of the aluminium rod is $m_{A}=d_{A}V_{A}$
  - The mass of the copper rod is $m_{c}=d_{c}V_{c}$
- The volume of a rod is given by $V=AL$

  - The volume of the aluminium rod is $V_{A}=A_{A}L$
  - The volume of the copper rod is $V_{c}=A_{c}L$
- The ratio of mass of aluminium to mass of copper is equal to

  - $\frac{m_{A}}{m_{c}}=\frac{d_{A}V_{A}}{d_{c}V_{c}}=\frac{d_{A}A_{A}L}{d_{c}A_{c}L}=\frac{d_{A}A_{A}}{d_{c}A_{c}}$
- Since $d_{c}=3d_{A}$  (the density of copper is three times that of aluminium)

  - `m _ A / m _ c = (d _ A A _ A)/(3 d _ A A _ c) = 1 third ( A _ A / A _ c )`
- The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\frac{ρL}{A}$
- Since the resistance and length of the rods are the same, $\frac{ρ}{A}$ is constant, so:

  - $\frac{ρ_{c}}{A_{c}}=\frac{ρ_{A}}{A_{A}}$
  - $\frac{A_{A}}{A_{c}}=\frac{ρ_{A}}{ρ_{c}}$
- The question states the resistivity of copper is half that of aluminium, therefore  $ρ_{A}=2ρ_{c}$
- Since *R* and* L* are identical for both rods, the ratio of their cross-sectional areas must match the ratio of their resistivities

  - $\frac{A_{A}}{A_{c}}=\frac{ρ_{A}}{ρ_{C}}=\frac{2}{1}$
- Therefore, the ratio `(m a s s o f a l u m i n i u m)/(m a s s o f c o p p e r) = m _ A / m _ c = 1 third ( A _ A / A _ c ) = 1 third x 2 / 1 = 2 / 3`

parts.problemMd:
A simple circuit is formed by connecting a resistor of resistance *R* between the terminals of a battery of electromotive force (e .m .f.) 9.0 V and constant internal resistance *r *.

![cie-ial-images551png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-1-practical-circuits/assets/001-cie-ial-images551png.png)

A charge of 6.0 C flows through the resistor in a time of 2.0 minutes, causing it to dissipate 48 J of thermal energy.

What is the internal resistance *r* of the battery ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- Current is equal to $I=\frac{Q}{t}$
- A charge of 6.0 C flows through the resistor in a time of 2.0 minutes
- So, the current through the resistor is $I=\frac{6.0}{2\times60}=0.05A$
- Power dissipated in a resistor is equal to $P=I^{2}R$
- Power is also equal to $\frac{energy}{time}$

  - So, energy dissipated $= P \times t = ( I^{ } 2 R ) \times t = 48 \text{thin J}$
  - $( 0.05 ) ^{2} = R \times ( 2 \times 60 ) = 48$
  - Therefore, resistance $R = \frac{48}{( 0.05 )^{2} \\times ( 2 \\times 60 )} = 160 \mathrm{\Omega }$
- The internal resistance of the battery and the resistor are in series, hence, the same current flows through them
- So, the sum of p. d. across these two resistors is equal to the e. m .f in the circuit

  - $E = I \times ( R + r ) = 9.0 \mathrm{V}$
  - $( R + r ) = \frac{9.0}{0.05} = 180 \mathrm{\Omega }$
  - $160+r=180$
- Therefore, the internal resistance is equal to *r* = 180 – 160 = 20 Ω

Given that the current through the circuit is 1.5 A, what is the value of the lost volts from the battery?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The known quantities are

  - E.m.f, ε = 15 V
  - Resistance of the resistor, *R* = 8.0 Ω
  - Current, *I* = 1.5 A
- The e.m.f of a circuit is equal to

  - *ε = I *(*R + r*)
- The internal resistance is

  - $\frac{ε}{I}=R+r$
  - $r=\frac{ε}{I}-R$
  - $r=\frac{15}{1.5}-8.0=2Ω$
- The lost volts from the battery is

  - *V* = *I r*
  - V = 1.5 × 2 V
- This is option **A**

parts.problemMd:
A resistor *R* is connected to the terminals of a battery of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance *r*.

![q11_electric-cells_ib-sl-physics-mcq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-1-practical-circuits/assets/013-q11-electric-cells-ib-sl-physics-mcq.png)

A charge of 240 C passes through the circuit in two minutes. During this time, 1440 J of energy is transferred to the external resistor. What is the internal resistance *r* of the battery?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- A charge of 240 C flows through the resistor in a time of 2 minutes = 120 s
- Calculating current:

  - $Q=It\rightarrowI=\frac{Q}{t}=\frac{240}{120}=2A$
- Power dissipated is $P=I^{2}R$  and $P=\frac{E}{t}$

  - $\frac{E}{t}=I^{2}R\rightarrowR=\frac{E}{I^{2}t}$
  - $R = \frac{ 1440}{( 2 )^{2} \\times 120} = 3 \mathrm{\Omega }$
- The emf of the circuit, $E = I ( R + r ) = 9.0 \mathrm{V}$

  - Therefore, the total resistance in the circuit, $( R + r ) = \frac{ E}{I} = \frac{ 9.0}{2} = 4.5 \mathrm{\Omega }$
- Therefore, since *R* = 3 Ω

  - $r = ( R + r ) - R = 4.5 - 3 = 1.5 \mathrm{\Omega }$

**A **is incorrect as this is the resistance of the resistor and not the internal resistance of the e.m.f

**B **is incorrect as this is the current in the circuit and not the internal resistance of the e.m.f.

**D **is incorrect as this is the total resistance in the circuit and not the internal resistance of the e.m.f.

parts.problemMd:
In the circuit below, a voltmeter of resistance *R*<sub>*V*</sub> and an ammeter of resistance *R*<sub>A</sub> are used to measure the resistance *R* of the fixed resistor.

![cie-ial-images598png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-1-practical-circuits/assets/008-cie-ial-images598png.png)

Which condition is necessary for an accurate value to be obtained for *R *?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- To obtain the resistance of resistor R from the set-up shown, the potential difference and current flowing through the resistor are measured

  - Ohm's law states $V=IR$ , so resistance $R=\frac{V}{I}$
- In this circuit the voltmeter is connected in parallel with *R* (reading the true potential difference across it), while the ammeter sits in the main line and reads the **total** current — the current through *R* plus the current diverted through the voltmeter
- Ideally, a voltmeter should have infinite resistance so that it draws negligible current; if its resistance is finite, some current bypasses the ammeter reading and the measured value of *R* is too low
- For the diverted current to be negligible, the voltmeter resistance must be much larger than *R*, so that *I*<sub>V</sub> ≪ *I*<sub>R</sub>
- Therefore, in order to obtain an accurate value of *R*, the necessary condition is that *R* should be much smaller than *R*<sub>V</sub>

**B** & **D** are incorrect because *R*<sub>A</sub> does not affect the result. The voltmeter reads the potential difference across *R* directly, and the ammeter sits in the main supply line, so its resistance *R*<sub>A</sub> only reduces the total current drawn from the supply — it does not change the ratio $\frac{V}{I}$, and so the measured value of *R* is unaffected by whether *R*<sub>A</sub> is small or large

**C** is incorrect because an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so *R* could not be higher than this

> *Note that the ammeter is not in series with resistor **R** alone — it is in series with the parallel combination of the voltmeter and the resistor. So the ammeter measures **I*<sub>*R*</sub>* + **I*<sub>*V*</sub>*, not the current through R*

parts.problemMd:
A power supply of electromotive force (e .m .f.) 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected in series with a load resistor. The value of the load resistor is varied from 0.5 Ω to 4 Ω.

Which graph shows how the power *P* dissipated in the load resistor varies with the resistance of the load resistor ?

![cie-ial-images557png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-1-practical-circuits/assets/006-cie-ial-images557png.png)

![cie-ial-images558png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-1-practical-circuits/assets/007-cie-ial-images558png.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- The internal resistance of the supply is *r* = 2 Ω
- The resistance of the load resistor, *R* varies from 0.5 Ω to 4 Ω
- Power *P* dissipated in the load resistor is equal to $I^{2}R$
- The power dissipated is maximum when the load resistance is equal to the internal resistance, *R* = *r* = 2 Ω
- Since 2 Ω lies within the range 0.5 Ω - 4 Ω, the graph peaks at 2 Ω, as illustrated in option **A**

**B** is incorrect because this graph shows that the power reaches a minimum value when the load resistance equals the internal resistance

**C & D** are incorrect because at a glance of the equation between power and resistance $P=I^{2}R$ , you might initially think the relationship is directly proportional. However, we have to consider the internal and external resistors as two resistors in series. Initially, the value of *R* is zero, so the power dissipated across it is also zero. Similarly, if the value of *R* is infinite, the power dissipated is also zero as the current will then also be zero. So, the power dissipated must increase and then decrease as *R* increases from zero. As the value of *R* increases, the current *I* decreases and hence the p. d. across the external resistor increases. The p .d. across the internal resistor *r* decreases and the power dissipated in *r* (given by $I^{2}r$  ) decreases. Therefore, the maximum power dissipated across R occurs when *R* = *r*

parts.problemMd:
A relay is required to operate 800 m from its power supply. The power supply has negligible internal resistance. The relay requires 16.0 V and a current of 0.60 A to operate.

A cable connects the relay to the power supply, and two of the wires in the cable are used to supply power to the relay.

The resistance of each of these wires is 0.0050 Ω per meter.

What is the minimum output e .m .f. of the power supply ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- In the cable, two of the wires are used to supply power to the relay
- So, the circuit is connected as follows:

  - One terminal of power supply — 1st wire — relay — 2nd wire — other terminal of power supply, therefore, it is a series connection
- The resistance of each of these wires is 0.0050 Ω per meter and each wire measures 800 m long

  - So, the total resistance of one wire $=800\times0.0050=4\text{Ω}$
  - Therefore, the total resistance due to both wires = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω
- There will be a p.d. across the wires and since this is a series connection, the same current flows through the whole circuit

  - So, the p.d. across the two wires $=IR=0.60\times8=4.8V$
- The sum of p.d. across the whole circuit should be equal to the minimum e.m.f

  - Therefore, the minimum output e.m.f. = 16.0 + 4.8 = 20.8 V

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- Kirchhoff's First Law (or current Law) states that current flowing into a junction must be equal to current flowing out of it

  - This is a consequence of charge conservation
  - It is well known in physics that charge will always be conserved. In the context of circuits this means that, since the current is the rate of flow of charge, the current flowing into a point must be the same as the current flowing out of that point
- Kirchhoff's Second Law (or voltage Law) states that the sum of all voltages around any closed loop in a circuit must equal the e.m.f. of the supply

  - This is a consequence of the principle of conservation of energy
  - This is due to the fact that work is done $( W = V Q )$  on charge carriers by the electric forces inside the circuit components meaning* *they either gain or lose electrical energy, depending upon the type of component

parts.problemMd:
In deriving a formula for the combined resistance of three different resistors in series, Kirchhoff's Laws are used.

Which physics principle is involved in this derivation ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- The physics principle involved in deriving Kirchhoff's Laws for 3 different resistors connected in series is the conservation of charge
- The shared e .m .f. source V causes a current I to flow through all three resistors, by the conservation of charge, this must be the same at all points in a series circuit
- From Ohm's Law $V=IR$
- The e. m .f. is split into V<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>2</sub> and V<sub>3</sub> between the three resistors

  - $V_{1}=IR_{1}$       $V_{2}=IR_{2}$      $V_{3}=IR_{3}$
- From Kirchoff's Second Law, we know that the voltages around a loop in a circuit add up to the e.m.f. of the supply

  - $V = V_{1} + V_{2} + V_{3} = I R_{1} + I R_{2} + I R_{3} = I ( R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3} )$
  - $\frac{V}{I}=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}$
- From Ohm's Law, we know $\frac{V}{I}$ = total resistance of the circuit

  - $R_{total}=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}$

parts.problemMd:
The combined resistance *R*<sub>T </sub>of two resistors of resistances *R*<sub>1</sub> and *R*<sub>2</sub> connected in parallel is given by the formula

$\frac{1}{R_{T}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}$

Which statement is used in the derivation of this formula?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- Each resistor in parallel has the same p .d. applied to it, but the total current is split amongst them
- Let the current through resistor R<sub>1</sub> be I<sub>1</sub> and the current through R<sub>2</sub> be I<sub>2</sub>
- The p. d. across both R<sub>1 </sub>and R<sub>2</sub> is equal to the supply voltage V
- Therefore from Ohm's Law

  - $I_{1}=\frac{V}{R_{1}}$ and $I_{2}=\frac{V}{R_{2}}$
- But from Kirchhoff's Current Law, we know the current entering a junction is equal to the current leaving the junction

  - Therefore, $I=I_{1}+I_{2}$
- Substituting the values derived for I<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> gives us'

  - $I = \frac{V}{R} _{1} + \frac{V}{R} _{2} = V ( \frac{1}{R} _{1} + \frac{1}{R} _{2} )$
- Rearranging gives us

  - $\frac{I}{V}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}$
- From Ohm's Law, we know $\frac{V}{I}=$ total resistance of the circuit

  - $\frac{1}{R_{total}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}$

A cell of e .m .f. 2.0 V and negligible internal resistance is connected to a network of resistors as shown.

![cie-ial-images541png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/006-cie-ial-images541png.png)

What is the current *I *?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- First, we must find the equivalent resistance of all the resistors combined
- We'll start with the two 4.0 Ω resistors, let's call these *R*<sub>*1*</sub>* *and *R*<sub>*2*</sub>
- For resistors in parallel : `1 / R = 1 / R _ 1 + 1 / R _ 2 + * * * + 1 / R _ n`

  - $\frac{1}{R_{1+2}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{2}$
  - So, $R_{1+2}=2.0$ Ω
- Next, we'll add the combined *R*<sub>*1*</sub> and *R*<sub>*2*</sub> in series with *R*<sub>*3*</sub>
- For resistors in series : $R = R_{1} + R_{2} + \times \times \times + R_{n}$

  - So, $R_{1+2+3}=2+2=4.0$ Ω
- And then, to get the total resistance, we'll add the combined 3 resistors in parallel with *R*<sub>*4*</sub>

  - So, $\frac{1}{R_{total}}=\frac{1}{R_{1+2+3}}+\frac{1}{R_{4}}=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{4}$
- Therefore, the total resistance is $R_{total}=\frac{4}{3}$ Ω
- Now, we must find the value of the current *I* through *R*<sub>*2*</sub>
- Ohm's Law states $I=\frac{V}{R}$

  - So, the current through the cell is equal to $I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{2.0V}{\frac{4}{3}Ω}=1.5A$
- If we consider there to be three resistors of 2.0 Ω each, the current through each resistor will be $\frac{2}{6}\times1.5=0.5A$
- Since the resistance is equal in both branches, the current will divide equally

  - So, $I=\frac{0.5}{2}=0.25A$

parts.problemMd:
Six resistors, each of resistance 5 Ω, are connected to a 2 V cell of negligible internal resistance.

![cie-ial-images560png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/011-cie-ial-images560png.png)

What is the potential difference between terminals X and Y ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because:**

- To obtain the potential difference between terminals X and Y, we first need to know the values of the potential at X and Y

  - The positive terminal of the cell can be taken to be at a potential of 2 V and the negative terminal to be at a potential of 0 V
- It can be seen that the circuit consists of 2 loops, with a junction at the top and one at the bottom

  - Since there are no components connected between the upper junction and the positive terminal of the cell, the upper junction must be at a potential of 2 V, and the lower junction must be at a potential of 0 V
- Therefore, in any loop, going from up to down, the potential decreases across each component until it is zero at the lower junction
- From Kirchhoff's Law, the sum of p .d. in any loop is equal to the e. m .f in the circuit
- Consider the first loop (where terminal X is connected):
- From the potential divider equation:

  - p. d. across the upper resistor $= ( \frac{R_{1}}{R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3}} ) \times E = ( \frac{5}{5 + 5 + 5} ) \times 2 = \frac{2}{3} V$
  - Note that this is the potential difference across the upper resistor. It is also the p. d. across each resistor since they all have the same resistance
- Since the upper junction is at a potential of 2 V, the p .d. at terminal X is equal to $=2-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}V$
- Consider the second loop (where terminal Y is connected):
- From the upper junction to terminal Y, there are 2 resistors and the p. d. across each is $\frac{2}{3}V$

  - So, the p. d. at terminal Y $= 2 - 2 ( \frac{2}{3} ) = \frac{2}{3} V$
- Therefore, the p .d. between X and Y$=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{2}{3}V$

parts.problemMd:
Four resistors of equal value are connected as shown.

![cie-ial-images561png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/003-cie-ial-images561png.png)

How will the powers to the resistors change when resistor W is removed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- Power dissipated in a resistor $=I^{2}R$
- Let's say the resistance of each resistor is *R*
- Two resistors in series causes the overall resistance to increase: *R* + *R* = 2*R*
- Two resistors in parallel causes the overall resistance to decrease : $[ \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{R} ] ^{ - } 1 = \frac{R}{2}$
- Since the 4 resistors have the same resistance in the connection shown, the p .d. across each parallel connection will be the same

  - Overall the resistance in the circuit is $=\frac{R}{2}+\frac{R}{2}=R$
- Let's say the e .m .f. in the circuit is *E,* so, the current in the circuit is $I=\frac{E}{R}$
- The total current splits at the parallel combination

  - Power dissipated in X $= ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{2} R = \frac{I^{ } 2 R}{4} = 0.25 I^{ } 2 R$
  - This is the power dissipated in all the resistors
- When W is removed, the overall resistance of the parallel combination of W and X changes from 0.5*R* to *R* as only X is left
- Total resistance in new circuit = *R* + 0.5*R* = 1.5*R*

  - Current in circuit $=\frac{E}{1.5R}=\frac{2}{3}I$
- The overall current in the circuit will also change — it decreases since the overall resistance in the complete circuit has increased. This current flows through X but is split into half at the combination of Y and Z, so, the current through Y and Z is half that through X, so:

  - Power dissipated in X $= ( \frac{2}{3} I ) ^{2} R = \frac{4}{9} I^{ } 2 R = 0.44 I^{ } 2 R$
- Half the current flows through Y and Z, and the same power is dissipated through both resistors, so:

  - Power dissipated in Y $= [ \frac{1}{2} ( \frac{2}{3} I ) ] ^{2} R = \frac{1}{9} I^{ } 2 R = 0.11 I^{ } 2 R$
- Therefore, the power in X increases and the power in Y and Z decreases

parts.problemMd:
A p. d. of 12 V is connected between P and Q.

![cie-ial-images564png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/010-cie-ial-images564png.png)

What is the p. d. between X and Y?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- The statement "p. *d. of 12 V is connected between P and Q *" means that the difference in potential between P and Q is 12 V
- So, any potential can be assigned to P and Q as long as the difference is 12 V

  - Let's assign a potential of 0 V at P and 12 V at Q
- So, when we go from P to Q, the potential should increase and point X would be at a potential between 0 and 12 V
- The same is true for point Y; hence, it can be concluded that points P, Q, X and Y are all at different potentials
- The circuit consists of a parallel combination of resistors

  - So, the total p. d. across the upper and lower parts of the circuit are both 12 V
- Now, both the upper and lower part of the circuit each consist of two resistors in series
- For series connection of two resistors R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>, the p. d. across R<sub>1</sub> is given by the potential divider equation

  - $V = ( \frac{R_{1}}{R_{1} + R_{2}} ) \times E$  where *E* is the e. m. f. of the supply
- The potential at point X = p. d. across 500 Ω in the upper part

  - Potential at point X$= ( \frac{500}{500 + 1000} ) \times 12 = 4 \mathrm{V}$
- Similarly, the potential at point Y = p. d. across 2000 Ω in the lower part

  - Potential at point Y$= ( \frac{2000}{2000 + 1000} ) \times 12 = 8 \mathrm{V}$
- So, the p .d. between X and Y is the difference in potential at point X and point Y

  - Therefore, p .d. between X and Y = 8 – 4 = 4 V** **

**Exam Tip:** Note that 0 V could be assigned at Q and 12 V at P, but the process discussed would have to be reversed

  - Where *R*<sub>*1*</sub> = 10 kΩ, *R*<sub>*2*</sub> = 15 kΩ and *V *<sub>*out *</sub>= 4.8 V
- $V_{i} n = V_{o} u t \div ( \frac{R_{1}}{R_{1} + R_{2}} ) = V_{o} u t \times ( \frac{R_{1} + R_{2}}{R_{1}} )$
- $V_{i} n = V_{o} u t ( \frac{R_{1} + R_{2}}{R_{1}} ) = \frac{4.8 ( 10 + 15 ) }{10} = 12 \mathrm{V}$
- Therefore, the input voltage is 12 V

parts.problemMd:
A battery with e.m.f. *E* and internal resistance *r* is connected in series with an external variable resistor.

![cie-ial-images5978png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/030-cie-ial-images5978png.png)

The value of the external resistance *R* is slowly increased from zero.

Which statement is correct ? (Ignore any temperature effects.)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- Ohm's law states $V=IR$ , so, as the resistance of a component increases the p. d. across it increases
- So, as the value of external resistance *R* is increased, the p. d. across it increases, while the p. d. across the internal resistance decreases
- The external resistance *R* and the internal resistance r form a potential divider
- Power dissipated in external resistor $=I^{2}R$

  - Initially, the value of *R* is zero, so the power dissipated across it is also zero
  - Similarly, if the value of *R* is infinite, the power dissipated is also zero as the current will then also be zero
- So, the power dissipated must increase and then decrease as *R* increases from zero

  - As the value of *R* increases, the current I decreases and hence the p. d. across the external resistor increases
  - The p. d. across the internal resistor *r* decreases and the power dissipated in *r* (given by $I^{2}R$ ) decreases
  - The maximum power dissipated across R occurs when *R* = *r*
- Overall, the only correct statement is that the power dissipated in R increases and then decreases

**A **&** B **are incorrect because the sum of p .d. in a circuit is equal to the e .m .f. in the circuit, so as the p .d. of one component rises, the other will fall

**C **is incorrect because as the value of *R* increases, the p d. across the external resistor increases, so the p. d. across the internal resistor decreases and the power dissipation across it also decreases

- The resistance of an LDR decreases when the light intensity on it increases, so, as the LDR is covered up, the light intensity decreases - this causes its resistance to increase
- Considering the resistor and the LDR in the middle section, an increase in the resistance of the LDR causes the p. d. across it to increase $( V = I R )$

- The left end of the wire is connected to the positive terminal of the supply and is at the maximum potential (equal to the e. m .f of the supply)

parts.problemMd:
A power supply and a solar cell are compared using the potentiometer circuit shown.

![cie-ial-images599png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/029-cie-ial-images599png.png)

The e.m.f. produced by the solar cell is measured on the potentiometer.

The potentiometer wire PQ is 100.0 cm long and has a resistance of 5.00 Ω. The power supply has an e. m .f. of 2.000 V, and the solar cell has an e .m. f. of 5.00 mV.

Which resistance *R* must be used so that the galvanometer reads zero when PS = 40.0 cm ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**

- The potentiometer wire PQ:

  - Length =100.0 cm
  - Resistance = 5.0 Ω
  - Emf supplied by battery =  2.000 V through resistor *R*
- Current through the wire

$I=\frac{2.000}{R+5.0}$

- Potential gradient along the wire

$k=\frac{I\times5.0}{100.0}$

- Balance point at PS = 40.0 cm requires:

$V_{solar}=k\times40.0$

- Solar cell e.m.f.

$V_{solar}=5.0\mathrm{mV}$

- Voltage across whole potentiometer wire

$V_{wire}=I\times5.0=\frac{2.0\times5.0}{R+5.0}$

- Potential gradient

$k = \frac{ V_{w} i r e}{100.0} = \frac{ 10}{100 ( R + 5 ) } = \frac{ 0.1}{R + 5}$

- Substitute 5.0 mV = 5.0 × 10<sup>-</sup>³ V

$5.0\times10^{-3}=\frac{0.1}{R+5}\times40$

$5.0\times10^{-3}=\frac{4.0}{R+5}$

- Solve

$R+5=\frac{4.0}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=800$

$R=795Ω$

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is not a standard potential-divider situation.
> 
> A potentiometer wire is not acting as a fixed resistor in series with R.
> 
> Instead:
> 
> - The potentiometer wire always carries a constant current from the supply.
> - The voltage along the wire varies linearly with distance.
> - The galvanometer reads zero when the p.d. per unit length × balancing length equals the emf of the solar cell.
> 
> The potential divider equation applies only when:
> 
> - both resistors are fixed
> - they are in series
> - the voltage is measured across one of the fixed resistors
> 
> A potentiometer wire is not a fixed resistor used as a divider. It is a uniform resistance wire supplying a linear potential scale.
> 
> This distinction is examined frequently in CIE papers.

parts.problemMd:
In the circuit shown, XY is a length *L* of uniform resistance wire. R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub> are unknown resistors. J is a sliding contact that joins the junction of R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub> to points on XY through a small signal lamp S.

![cie-ial-images602png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/014-cie-ial-images602png.png)

To determine the ratio  $\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}$  of the potential differences across R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>, a point is found on XY at which the lamp is off. This point is at a distance *x* from *X*.

What is the value of the ratio $\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}$   ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D ****because:**

- For the lamp to be off, the potential difference across it should be zero so that no current flows through it

  - This means, the potential at the junction of *R*<sub>*1*</sub> and *R*<sub>*2*</sub> should be equal to the potential at the sliding contact J
- The p. d. across *R*<sub>*1*</sub> is *V*<sub>*1*</sub> and the p .d. across *R*<sub>*2*</sub> is *V*<sub>*2*</sub>, so, *V*<sub>*1*</sub> should be equal to the p. d. across XJ and *V*<sub>*2*</sub> should be equal to the p .d. across JY
- Since point X is connected to the negative terminal of the supply, it can be considered to be at a potential of 0, while point Y is at the maximum potential, equal to the e .m. f. of the supply
- The wire XY, together with the sliding contact J, can be considered as a potential divider
- Resistance *R* of the wire $=\frac{ρL}{A}$ and from Ohm's Law$V=IR$ , so, the p. d. across the wire is proportional to the length of wire $VαL$
- A length of *L* corresponds to a p. d. equal to the e .m .f. *E* of the supply and a length of *x* corresponds to a p. d. equal of $( \frac{E}{L} ) \times x = ( \frac{x}{L} ) \times E$
- Since X is at a potential of zero, point J would be at a potential of:

  - $V_{1} = [ ( \frac{x}{L} ) \times E ] - 0 = ( \frac{x}{L} ) \times E$
- Now, the part JY of the wire corresponds to a length (*L* – *x*) of the wire. A length of (*L* – *x*) corresponds to a p.d. equal to

  - $V_{2} = ( \frac{E}{L} ) \times ( L - x ) = \frac{ ( L - x ) }{L} \times E$
- Therefore, the ratio $= \frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}} = ( \frac{x}{L} ) E \div \frac{ ( L - x ) }{L} E = \frac{x}{L - x}$

- Section B is made up of the variable resistor and another 1.5 kΩ fixed resistor

- From the graph, at 0730, the resistance of the thermistor = 1.5 kΩ

  - $R_{V}=\frac{4.5}{0.001}=4500Ω=4.5kΩ$

parts.problemMd:
The resistance *R* of an unknown resistor is compared with a fixed 100 Ω resistor using the circuit as shown in the diagram.

The balance length *l* is 30.0 cm and 48.3 cm when P is connected to Q and R, respectively.

![cie-ial-images608png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/028-cie-ial-images608png.png)

The length of the wire XY is 100 cm and has a resistance of 40 Ω. The two cells E<sub>1</sub> and E<sub>2,</sub> have negligible internal resistances.

What is the value of resistance *R *?
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- When P is connected to Q, the potential difference across the balance length is equal to the potential difference across the 100 Ω resistor

  - $\frac{l}{XY}\timesE_{1}=\frac{100}{100+R}\timesE_{2}\,$              **(1)**
- When P is connected to R, the potential difference across the balance length is equal to the potential difference across the 100 Ω resistor and the unknown resistor (which is the same as the e. m .f. as cell E)

  - $\frac{l'}{XY}\timesE_{1}=E_{2}$                                           **(2)**
- Substitute equation **(2)** into **(1)**

  - $\frac{l}{XY}\timesE_{1}=\frac{100}{100+R}\times\frac{l'}{XY}\timesE_{1}$
  - $\frac{30.0}{XY}\timesE_{1}=\frac{100}{100+R}\times\frac{48.3}{XY}\timesE_{1}$
- The E<sub>1</sub> and XY terms cancel out, so we have:

  - $30.0=\frac{100}{100+R}\times48.3$
  - $100+R=\frac{100\times48.3}{30.0}=161$
  - $R=161-100=61Ω$
- Therefore, the resistance *R* of the unknown resistor is 61 Ω

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

  - `X _ Z ^ A -> Y _ Z + 1 end _ ^ A end ^ + beta _ negative 1 end _ ^ 0 + top v _ e`

- An α-particle is made of two protons and two neutrons, ${}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{ \alpha }$

  - ${}_{Z}^{A}\mathrm{X}    \rightarrow    {}_{Z  -  2}^{A  -  4}\mathrm{Y}    +    {}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{ \alpha }$
- The nucleon number is reduced by 4, emitting two neutrons and 2 protons
- The difference in mass between

  - ${}_{86}^{222}\mathrm{R} n$ and ${}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b$ is 222 – 206 = 16

parts.problemMd:
A stationary decay ${}_{84}^{210}\mathrm{P} o$ of  by *α*-emission has a total kinetic energy of *E*<sub>*k*</sub>

${}_{84}^{210}\mathrm{P} o    \rightarrow    {}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b    +     \alpha $

What is the kinetic energy of the daughter nucleus ${}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b$ ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- By the Principle of Conservation of Momentum :
- Total momentum before *α*-emission = Total momentum after *α*-emission

  - Total momentum before *α*-emission = 0
  - Total momentum after *α*-emission$=MV-mv$
- Where *M* and *V* are the mass and velocity of ${}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b$ and *m* and *v* are the mass and velocity of the *α*-particle

  - $0=MV-mv$
  - $MV=mv$
  - $M^{2}V^{2}=m^{2}v^{2}$
  - $M ( \frac{1}{2} M V^{ } 2 ) = m ( \frac{1}{2} m v ^{2} )$
- Therefore, $\frac{KEofPb-206}{KEofα}=\frac{massofα}{massofPb-206}$

  - $\frac{K E ( P b ) }{K E ( \alpha ) } = \frac{4}{206} = 0.0194$
- From Conservation of Energy : $K E ( P b ) + K E ( \alpha ) = E_{k}$

  - $K E ( \alpha ) = \frac{K E ( P b ) }{0.0194}$
  - $K E ( P b ) + \frac{K E ( P b ) }{0.0194} = E_{k}$
  - $K E ( P b ) [ 1 + \frac{1}{0.0194} ] = E_{k}$
  
  - So, $K E ( P b ) = \frac{E_{k}}{ ( 1 + \frac{1}{0.0194} ) } = 0.0190 E_{k}$
- Therefore, the kinetic energy of ${}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b$ is between 0 and $\frac{E_{k}}{2}$

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

  - A helium ${}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{H} e$ particle is emitted
  - The atomic number decreases by two and the mass number by four
- When β<sup>− </sup>-decay occurs

  - A neutron transforms into a proton and an electron
  - The mass number remains the same but the atomic number increases by one
- When γ-decay occurs

  - A γ ray is emitted so there is no change in the mass or atomic number
- The end nuclide is Thorium-228

  - The isotope can be written as ${}_{90}^{228}\mathrm{T} h$
- The flow diagram for the decay of ${}_{\mathit{Z}}^{\mathit{A}}X$is $N_{93}^{236} p \xrightarrow{\gamma } N_{93}^{236} p \xrightarrow{\beta ^{^{-} } } P_{94}^{236} u \xrightarrow{\alpha } U_{92}^{232} \xrightarrow{\alpha } T_{90}^{228} h \xrightarrow{\gamma } T_{90}^{228} h$

- This is option **C  **

- In order to find the original unknown isotope, you will need to work backwards from ${}_{90}^{228}\mathrm{T} h$

  - For α-decay add four onto the mass number and two onto the atomic number
  - For β<sup>−</sup>-decay minus one from the atomic number and keep the mass number the same

a quark combination of up, strange, strange would give a charge of zero | |---|---| | **C **is incorrect because | $-\frac{1}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e=-1e$

a quark combination of down, strange, strange would be a Σ - baryon with a −1 charge | | **D **is incorrect because | $-\frac{1}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e=-1e$

parts.problemMd:
When high-speed hadrons collide in particle accelerators, a positive pion (π<sup>+</sup>) is an unstable particle produced. The π<sup>+</sup> particle has a charge of +*e*.

What is the quark combination of the π<sup>+</sup> particle?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **  The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- A meson contains one quark and one anti-quark bound by a gluon
- The 'up' quark has a charge of $\frac{2}{3}e$

  - Where *e* is the elementary charge + 1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C
- The anti-'down' quark has a charge of $\frac{1}{3}e$

  - $\frac{2}{3}e+\frac{1}{3}e=+1e$
- Therefore, the π<sup>+</sup> particle must have one up quark and one anti-down quark to have an overall charge of +1*e*

**A **is incorrect because  a meson with a  $u \vec{u}$ combination would be a π<sup>0</sup> particle

**C **is incorrect because a meson with a  $\text{size} 22px d \text{size} 22px \vec{s} \text{ize} 22px u \text{size} 22px$ combination would be a π<sup>−</sup> particle

**D **is incorrect because a meson with a  $d \vec{d}$ combination would be a π<sup>0</sup> particle

parts.problemMd:
A graph of nucleon number A against proton number Z is shown in the diagram below.

![cie-ial-images628png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/11-particle-physics/11-2-fundamental-particles/assets/007-cie-ial-images628png.png)

The graph shows a cross that represents a nucleus P.

Nucleus P decays by emitting an *α*-particle to form a nucleus Q.

Nucleus Q then decays by emitting a *β*<sup>*–*</sup> particle to form a nucleus R.

The quark composition of one nucleon in Q is changed during the emission of the *β*<sup>*–*</sup> particle.

What is the corresponding change in quark composition from nucleus Q to nucleus R ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Nucleus P has a nucleon number *A* = 214 and a proton number *Z* = 84
- It decays via *α*-emission to form nucleus Q:

  - ${}_{84}^{214}\mathrm{P}    \rightarrow    {}_{82}^{210}\mathrm{Q}    +    {}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{ \alpha }$
- Overall, the emission of an *α*-particle from a nucleus will cause the proton number to decrease by two and the nucleon number to decrease by four, as shown on the diagram

  - So, nucleus Q has a nucleon number *A* = 210 and a proton number *Z* = 82
- It then decays via *β*-emission to form nucleus R

  - ${}_{82}^{210}\mathrm{Q}    \rightarrow    {}_{83}^{210}\mathrm{R}    +    {}_{- 1}^{0}\mathrm{ \beta }$
- Overall, the emission of a *β*-particle from a nucleus will cause the proton number to increase by one and the nucleon number to stay the same, as shown on the diagram

  - So, nucleus R has a nucleon number *A* = 210 and a proton number *Z* = 83
- During the decay of Q into R, a neutron is changed into a proton

  - Quark composition of neutron$=udd$
  - Quark composition of proton$=uud$
- Therefore, a *d*-quark has changed into a *u*-quark

parts.problemMd:
The equation for β<sup>–</sup> decay is

$n \rightarrow p + e^{-} + \vec{v}_{e}$

Using your knowledge of antiparticles and the weak interaction, what is the equation for β<sup>+</sup> decay?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Protons and neutrons are not antiparticles of each other, instead the weak interaction between quarks gives rise to a change in quark composition

  - Quark composition of neutron$=udd$
  - Quark composition of proton$=uud$
- In β<sup>–</sup> decay, a neutron turns into a proton $( u d d \rightarrow u u d )$
- Whereas, in β<sup>+</sup> decay, a proton turns into a neutron $( u u d \rightarrow u d d )$
- Since electrons and neutrinos are both leptons, they are fundamental particles
- The a β<sup>–</sup> particle is simply an electron (e<sup>–</sup>), and a β<sup>+</sup> particle is its antiparticle – a positron (e<sup>+</sup>)
- In β<sup>–</sup> decay, an anti-electron neutrino is produced, so, in β<sup>+</sup> decay an electron neutrino is produced
- Therefore, the overall equation for β<sup>+</sup> decay is:

  - $p\rightarrown+e^{+}+v_{e}$

**A **is incorrect because in beta-minus and beta-plus decay, a neutron turns into a proton or a proton turns into a neutron due to the weak interaction, their antiparticles are not involved

**C **is incorrect because as it is a decay equation, the β<sup>+</sup> particle must be on the right hand side as a product of the reaction

**D **is incorrect because in β<sup>–</sup> decay, an anti-electron neutrino is produced, so, in β<sup>+</sup> decay an electron neutrino is produced, an antiparticle is represented by the line above the symbol

For the radius of the ramp in Fig 1.1, the skateboarder travels at a speed of 6.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

Show that the angle *θ *is 32°.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the angle *θ *is 32°

- Speed of the skateboarder, *v* = 6.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acceleration of free fall, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>–2</sup>

Determine an equation for the angle, *θ*:

- $W=F\mathrm{tan}θ$ (from part b)
- $W = m g$ and $F = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$
- $mg=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}\mathrm{tan}θ$

A ‘loop the loop’ is a vertical circular path. Fig. 1.1 shows a toy car of mass 70 g completing a ‘loop the loop’ which has a radius of 0.15 m.

![6-1-s-q--q1a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/12-motion-in-a-circle/12-2-centripetal-acceleration/assets/006-6-1-s-q-q1a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The car enters the loop with a speed of 2.0 m s<sup>–1</sup> and then undergoes a constant deceleration until it passes** **A** **with a speed of 1.21 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

After A, the car undergoes a constant acceleration before leaving the loop with a speed of 2.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate the time taken for a car to complete the ‘loop the loop’.

[3]

(ii) Sketch a speed-time graph for the journey through the loop. Mark the time to the nearest tenth of a second and indicate at which time the car passes position A.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) List the known quantities:

- Radius of the circle, *r *= 0.15 m
- Initial speed, $S_{1}$= 2.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Speed at A, $S_{A}$*= *1.21 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Final speed, $S_{2}$= 2.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>

Determine the average speed for the journey, *v*:

- The car undergoes constant deceleration to A at the halfway point and then an acceleration to the bottom of the loop
- Average speed , *v *= $\frac{2.0+1.21}{2}$ = 1.61 m s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Determine an expression for the time taken* *to A, , *t*<sub>*1/2*</sub>* *:

- Circumference of ½ circle = $1 half \times ( 2 pi r ) = pi r$
- Time taken to A, *t*<sub>*1/2*</sub>  = $\frac{distance}{averagespeed}$ = $\frac{\mathrm{πr}}{s}$ = $\frac{π\times0.15}{1.61}=0.29$ = 0.3 s **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total time taken, *t*:

- *t  *= 2 × *t*<sub>*1/2*</sub>
- *t  *= 2 × 0.29
- *t  *= 0.58 = 0.6 s **[1 mark]**

(ii) Sketch a speed-time graph of the journey through the loop:

![amended-ms-circular-motion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/12-motion-in-a-circle/12-2-centripetal-acceleration/assets/007-amended-ms-circular-motion.png)

- Straight lines drawn, values for speed and time labelled, and A marked halfway at the turning point for the line; **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A 'loop the loop' is a vertical circular path. Fig. 1.1 shows a toy car of mass 70 g completing a 'loop the loop' which has a radius of 0.15 m. The car enters the loop with a speed of 2.0 m s^–1^ and then undergoes a constant deceleration until it passes A with a speed of 1.21 m s^–1^. After A, the car undergoes a constant acceleration before leaving the loop with a speed of 2.0 m s^–1^

(i) Describe the origin of the centripetal force that keeps the car on the track throughout the loop.

[2]

(ii) Determine the minimum and maximum values of the reaction force experienced by the car as it makes its loop.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The origin of the centripetal force is:

- Always directed towards the centre of the circle
- In the bottom half of the loop the force is caused by the <u>normal reaction force</u> from the track <u>minus</u> the <u>weight</u> of the car; **[1 mark]**
- In the top half of the track the <u>weight</u>** **of the car <u>and</u> the <u>normal</u> reaction force provide the centripetal force; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the minimum and maximum values of the reaction force:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of car, *m  *= 70 g = 70 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg
- Radius of track, *r  *= 0.15 m
- Linear velocity of car at bottom, *v*<sub>*1*</sub>*  *= 2.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Linear velocity of car at top, *v*<sub>*2*</sub> = 1.21 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Acceleration due to free-fall, *g  *= 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

The minimum reaction force:

- Occurs at the <u>top</u> of the loop
- At the minimum speed of 1.21 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- When the weight supplies all the centripetal force
- To 2 s.f. $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=mg$
- So, reaction force = 0 N **[1 mark]**

The maximum reaction force:

- Occurs at the <u>bottom</u> of the loop
- When the normal reaction force = centripetal force + weight
- Maximum reaction force = $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}+mg$
- Maximum reaction force = $\frac{ ( 70 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times 2 ^{2} }{0.15} + ( 70 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times 9.81$ = 2.55 N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *The **origin **of the centripetal force will **change** throughout the loop, but it is always directed towards the **centre** of the loop. It can be difficult to determine the direction of each of the three forces in the different positions as the car travels around the track. There is a **constant downward force** caused by **gravity** but a **varying normal force**. It is important to recognise that upward forces ≠ downward forces on a conventional force diagram because the car is accelerating towards the centre of the loop. *

> *At the **top** where reaction force is minimum: **Centripetal force = reaction force + weight *

> *At the **bottom** where reaction force is maximum: **Centripetal force = reaction force - weight*

parts.problemMd:
A student is investigating the energy changes in a ‘loop the loop’, as shown in Fig. 1.2.

They want to determine the minimum height, *h,* required for a toy car of mass *m* to complete a loop the loop of radius *r*, when starting from rest.** **

![6-1-s-q--q1d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/12-motion-in-a-circle/12-2-centripetal-acceleration/assets/009-6-1-s-q-q1d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Show that the minimum height, *h* is:

$h=\frac{5}{2}r$
parts.solutionMd:
Determine an expression for minimum velocity:

- The minimum velocity of the car is at the <u>top</u> of the loop
- At the top of the loop, centripetal force = weight
- *mg* =$\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$
- *v* =$\sqrt{gr}$ **[1 mark]**

Deduce the change in gravitational potential energy, Δ*E*<sub>*p*</sub>*:*

- *E*<sub>*p*</sub> at start = *mgh*
- *E*<sub>*p*</sub> at top of loop = *mg2r*
- Δ*E*<sub>*p*</sub> = *mgh* – *mg2r ***[1 mark]**

Equate change in Δ*E*<sub>*p*</sub>  to *E*<sub>*k*</sub>:

- The kinetic energy of the car at the top of loop is equal to the gravitational potential energy lost when falling a distance *h*
- *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = $\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>*2*</sup> = *mgh* – *mg2r ***[1 mark]**

Substitute in the expression for minimum velocity into the kinetic energy expression:

- $\frac{1}{2} m v ^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m ( \sqrt{g r} ) ^{2} = m g h - m g 2 r$
- $\frac{1}{2}$*mgr*  = *mgh* – *mg2r*
- $\frac{5}{2}$*mgr*  = *mgh*
- *h *= $\frac{5}{2}$*r ***[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *Remember that on long ‘show that’ questions, it is important to structure your working out so that the examiner can see the steps you have gone through. You may be asked to apply equations from other areas of the course, but you will not be expected to derive those equations.*

parts.problemMd:
A satellite orbits the Earth, as shown in Fig. 1.1. It remains in orbit due to the gravitational field of the Earth.

![6-1-s-q--q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/12-motion-in-a-circle/12-2-centripetal-acceleration/assets/015-6-1-s-q-q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

It takes the satellite 200 minutes to complete one full revolution around the Earth. The mass of the Earth is 6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg and the radius of the Earth is 6400 km.

Show that the distance of the satellite from the surface of the Earth is approximately 5000 km.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Period, *T*  = 200 minutes  = 12 000 s
- Mass of Earth, $m_{E}$ *=  *6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg
- Radius of the Earth, $R_{E}$ *=*  6400 km
- Newton’s Gravitational constant, *G*  = 6.67 × 10<sup>-11 </sup>m<sup>3 </sup>kg<sup>-1 </sup>s<sup>-2</sup>

Equate Newton’s Law of Gravitation with centripetal force:

- Law of Gravitation: $F_{grav}$= *G *$\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}$
- Centripetal force: $F_{cent}$ = $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$
- Centripetal force = Gravitational force
- $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ = *G*$\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}$* ***[1 mark]**

Substitute in the equation for orbital velocity, *v *into the equation for centripetal force, *F*<sub>*cent*</sub>* *:

- Recall the equation for orbital velocity: $v=\frac{2πr}{T}$
- $F_{c} e n t = \frac{m ( \frac{2 pi r}{T} ) ^{2} }{r}$
- $F_{cent}=\frac{4mπ^{2}r^{2}}{T^{2}}\times\frac{1}{r}$ **[1 mark]**

Combine the equations for centripetal and gravitational force:

- $\frac{4mπ^{2}r^{2}}{rT^{2}}$ = *G *$\frac{m_{E}m}{r^{2}}$
- $\frac{4π^{2}r^{3}}{T^{2}}=Gm_{E}$
- $r^{3}=\frac{Gm_{E}T^{2}}{4π^{2}}$
- *r  =  *$\sqrt[3]{ \frac{G m_{E} T^{2}}{4 \mathrm{\pi }^{2}} }$**[1 mark]**
- *r  =  *$\sqrt[3]{ \frac{( 6.67 \\times 10^{- 11} ) \\times ( 6.0 \\times 10^{24} ) \\times ( 12 000 )^{2}}{4 \mathrm{\pi }^{2}} }$* *= 11 343 836 m **[1 mark]**

Determine the height of the orbit by subtracting the radius of Earth:

- *h*  = *r* – $R_{E}$ = 11 343 836 ­– 6 400 000 = 4 943 836 m = 5000 km **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 5 marks]**** **

> *Remember to show your work clearly throughout longer questions to pick up marks even if you don’t get to the correct answer. This will make it easier to see where you’ve gone wrong when looking back at it. Steps like the final subtraction here are easily forgotten, so make sure to check through your work afterwards. Substitute each equation step by step, don't rush. *

parts.problemMd:
Astronaut A travels from the Earth to the Moon.

Explain the effect on astronaut A's mass and weight.
parts.solutionMd:
To explain the effect on astronaut A's mass as they travel from Earth to the moon:

- The mass of the astronaut will not change;** [1 mark]**
- Because mass is not affected by gravitational field strength;** [1 mark]**

To explain the effect on astronaut A's weight as they travel from Earth to the moon:

- The weight of the astronaut will be less on the Moon than it is on Earth; **[1 mark]**
- Because weight = mass × gravitational field strength  **OR**  $W=mg$; **[1 mark]**
- And the gravitational field strength of the Moon is less (because the Moon is less massive than Earth);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Determine the gravitational field strength of the Moon using the following information about the astronaut.

- $F_{gEarth}=770N$
- $F_{gMoon}=128N$
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the gravitational field strength of the moon:

List the known quantities:

- Weight of astronaut on Earth, $F_{gEarth}$= 770 N
- Weight of astronaut on Moon, $F_{gMoon}$= 128 N
- Gravitational field strength on Earth, $g$= 9.81 N kg<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the mass of the astronaut:

- $g=\frac{F_{g}}{m}\rightarrowm=\frac{F_{g}}{g}$  **OR**  $W=mg\rightarrowm=\frac{W}{g}$
- $m=\frac{770}{9.81}$ **[1 mark]**
- $m=78.5\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the value of $g$ on the Moon:

- $g=\frac{128}{78.5}$ **[1 mark]**
- $g = 1.63 \mathrm{N} kg^{ - } 1 ( 3 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Astronaut A leaves the moon and visits the planet Mars. As they leave Mars, they notice that it takes less fuel to leave Mars' atmosphere than Earth's, but more fuel to leave Mars' atmosphere than the Moon's.

Suggest what this implies about the gravitational field strength on Mars.
parts.solutionMd:
Suggest what this implies about the gravitational field strength on Mars:

- The gravitational field strength / *g* on Mars is greater than the gravitational field strength / *g *on the Moon; **[1 mark]**
- Because more work is done to raise the spacecraft / an object through the gravitational field of Mars than the Moon; **[1 mark]**
- The gravitational field strength / *g* on Mars is less than the gravitational field strength / *g *on the Earth; **[1 mark]**
- Because less work is done to raise the spacecraft / an object through the gravitational field of Mars than Earth; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The spacecraft Centurion leaves Earth for Venus to identify potential mining locations based on fluctuations in the gravitational field strength on the surface of Venus.

The Centurion sends a landing party to the surface in a shuttle. The shuttle has a mass of 3.24×10<sup>7</sup> kg when launched from the Centurion, but loses 5% of its total mass in fuel combustion due to landing. The shuttle has a weight of 270 MN when it comes to rest on the surface of Venus.

Calculate the gravitational field strength on the surface of Venus.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Initial mass of shuttle, *m* = 3.24 × 10<sup>7</sup> kg
- Mass of shuttle upon surface of Venus = 0.95*m*
- Weight of shuttle upon surface of Venus, *W* = 270 MN = 270 × 10<sup>6</sup> N

To calculate the gravitational field strength on Venus:

- Gravitational field strength, $g=\frac{F_{g}}{m}=\frac{W}{m}$
- $g = \frac{270 \\times 10^{6} }{0.95 \\times ( 3.24 \\times 10^{7} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $g = 8.8 \mathrm{N} kg^{ - } 1 ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The spacecraft Centurion leaves Earth for Venus to identify potential mining locations based on fluctuations in the gravitational field strength on the surface of Venus. The Centurion sends a landing party to the surface in a shuttle. The shuttle has a mass of 3.24×10^7 kg when launched from the Centurion, but loses 5% of its total mass in fuel combustion due to landing. The shuttle has a weight of 270 MN when it comes to rest on the surface of Venus.

The landing crew collect rock samples from the landing site. When the landing crew has finished its mission, the shuttle launches to return to the Centurion. At an altitude of 250 km above the surface of Venus, the mass lost through fuel combustion is equal to the total mass of the rocks collected at the surface.

Gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between masses.

$F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$

Calculate the gravitational field strength of Venus at 250 km above the surface.

The radius of Venus is 6.3 × 10<sup>6</sup> m.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Radius of Venus, $R_{V}$= 6.3 × 10<sup>6</sup> m
- Altitude = 250 km = 250 × 10<sup>3</sup> m
- Force (weight) acting on shuttle at the surface of Venus, *F*<sub>s</sub> = 270 × 10<sup>6</sup> N (from part (b))
- Mass of shuttle at altitude is equal to mass of shuttle at surface, *m*<sub>A</sub> = *m*<sub>S</sub> = 0.95*m *(from part (b))
- Initial mass of shuttle, *m* = 3.24 × 10<sup>7</sup> kg

Construct an equation to find the gravitational force on the shuttle at altitude, *F*<sub>A</sub>:

- $F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$
- $\frac{F_{A}}{F_{S}}=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\div\frac{1}{R_{V}^{2}}=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\times\frac{R_{V}^{2}}{1}=\frac{R_{V}^{2}}{r^{2}}$
- $F_{A} = \frac{F_{S} ( R_{V} ) ^{2} }{r ^{2} }$** [1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate the force on the shuttle at altitude:

- $F_{A} = \frac{ ( 270 \times 10^{6} ) \times ( 6.3 \times 10^{6} ) ^{2} }{ ( ( 6.3 \times 10^{6} ) + ( 250 \times 10 ^{3} ) ) ^{2} }$ **[1 mark]**

  - The total *r* is the radius of Venus plus the altitude
- $F_{A}=2.49\times10^{8}N$ **OR** 249 MN **[1 mark]**

Use this value of force to calculate *g* at altitude:

- $g = \frac{ F_{g} }{m} = \frac{2.49 \\times 10^{8} }{0.95 \\times ( 3.24 \\times 10^{7} )}$
- $g = 8.1 \mathrm{N} kg^{ - } 1 ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]*** *

> *Remember to always do a quick sanity check on your answers. From part (c), **g** on the surface of Venus was calculated to be 8.8 N kg*<sup>*–1*</sup>*. Therefore, above its surface you would expect it to be slightly less. If you get an answer that is greater than 8.80 N kg*<sup>*–1*</sup>* or drastically less, something may have gone wrong in your calculation. *

> *A common mistake is to also use the altitude as **r** and forget to add on the radius of the planet. **r** is the total distance from the centre of Venus to the shuttle.*

parts.problemMd:
The gravitational force between the Earth and the Sun is 3.52 × 10<sup>22</sup> N.

Calculate the radius of the Earth's orbit around the Sun.

Mass of Earth = 6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg

Mass of Sun = 2.0 × 10<sup>30</sup> kg
parts.solutionMd:
The radius of the Earth's orbit around the Sun is:

List the known quantities:

- Gravitational force between Earth and Sun, *F* = 3.52 × 10<sup>22</sup> N
- Mass of Earth, *m*<sub>1</sub> = 6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg
- Mass of Sun, *m*<sub>2</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>30</sup> kg

Determine the equation for the radius of the Earth's orbit, *r*:

- $F=\frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\Rightarrowr=\sqrt{\frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{F}}$**[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $r = \sqrt{ \frac{( 6.67 \\times 10^{- 11} ) \\times ( 6.0 \\times 10^{24} ) \\times ( 2.0 \\times 10^{30} )}{3.52 \\times 10^{22} } }$**[1 mark]**
- $r=1.5\times10^{11}m$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *r** is always measured from the **centre** of the two masses that we are calculating the gravitational force for. The radius of orbit of the Earth around the Sun is also measured in this way. You must recognise different wording for the same thing!*

> *To help, look at what variables you have already been given. Although you could use a circular motion equation, we haven't been given the linear speed which could make this difficult. However, since we have been given the gravitational force, we can also use Newton's law of gravitation.*

parts.problemMd:
A satellite of mass *m* is in a circular orbit around a planet of mass *M *with linear speed *v*.

Show that *M* is given by the expression:

$M=\frac{v^{2}r}{G}$
parts.solutionMd:
*M* is given by $M=\frac{v^{2}r}{G}$ because:

Equate the centripetal and gravitational force:

- $F=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{GMm}{r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Cancel and rearrange for mass *M*:

- $\frac{ \cancel{m} v^{2}}{r} = \frac{ G M \cancel{m} }{r^{2}}$
- $v^{2}=\frac{GM}{r}$
- $M=\frac{v^{2}r}{G}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A satellite of mass m is in a circular orbit around a planet of mass M with linear speed v. Show that M is given by the expression: M = v²r/G

Show that the mass *M* can also be written in terms of the time period of the satellite *T* as

$M=\frac{4π^{2}r^{3}}{T^{2}G}$
parts.solutionMd:
*M* can also be written as $M=\frac{4π^{2}r^{3}}{T^{2}G}$ because:

Determine an equation for *v* in terms of *T*:

- $ω=\frac{\Deltaθ}{T}$
- So for 1 revolution $\Deltaθ=2π$
- $v=ωr=\frac{2πr}{T}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute this equation into the equation for *M* in terms of *v*:

- $M = \frac{ v^{2} r}{G} \Leftrightarrow M = \frac{ ( \frac{2 \pi r}{T} )^{2} r}{G}$
- $M=\frac{\frac{4π^{2}r^{2}}{T^{2}}r}{G}=\frac{4π^{2}r^{3}}{T^{2}G}$ **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Since satellites travel roughly in a circular path, you will need to be familiar with all the circular motion equations for this section of gravitational fields as well.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Show that the mass *M* can also be written in terms of the time period of the satellite *T* as M = 4π²r³/(T²G)

Calculate the radius of a geostationary orbit around Earth.

Mass of Earth = 6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg
parts.solutionMd:
The radius of a geostationary orbit around Earth is:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the Earth, *M* = 6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg
- Time period of a geostationary orbit, *T* = 24 hours
- gravitational constant, *G* = 6.67 × 10<sup>–11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>–2</sup>

Calculate the time period in seconds, *T*:

- *T* = 24 hours = 24 × 60 × 60
- *T* = 86 400 s **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the mass equation for the radius or orbit, *r*:

- $MT^{2}G=4π^{2}r^{3}$
- $\frac{MT^{2}G}{4π^{2}}=r^{3}$
- $r = \sqrt[3]{ \frac{ M T^{2} G}{4 \pi ^{2}} }$**[1 mark]**

Substitute values into the radius equation:

- $r = \sqrt[3]{ \frac{( 6.0 \\times 10^{24 ) \\times ( 86 400 )^{2} \\times ( 6.67 \\times 10^{-11} } ) }{4 \pi ^{2}} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $r=4.2\times10^{7}m$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**
