parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Four identical ice spheres are dropped into a thermally isolated cylinder containing water. The specific heat capacity of the ice is 1.9 kJ kg^−1^ K^−1^ and the specific heat capacity of water is 5.7 kJ kg^−1^ K^−1^.

The ice spheres have a radius of 20 mm and a density of 870 kg m<sup>−3</sup>. Their initial temperature is −7.2 °C. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 442 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup>. The water has an initial temperature of 22.2 °C and a mass of 0.75 kg.

Determine the final temperature of the water.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the final temperature of the water:

List the known quantities:

- Specific heat capacity of ice, *c*<sub>*i*</sub> = 1.9 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> = 1.9 × 10<sup>3</sup> J kg<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))
- Specific heat capacity of water, *c*<sub>*w*</sub> = 5.7 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> = 5.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> J kg<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))
- Radius of ice sphere, *r *= 20 mm = 20 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m
- Density of ice, *ρ* = 870 kg m<sup>−3</sup>
- Initial temperature of water, *T*<sub>*w*</sub> = 22.2 °C
- Initial temperature of ice, *T*<sub>*i*</sub> = −7.2 °C
- Mass of water, *m*<sub>*w*</sub> = 0.75 kg
- Specific latent heat of fusion, *L* = 442 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> = 442 × 10<sup>3</sup> J kg<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the volume of the 4 ice spheres, *V*:

- Volume of sphere = $\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$
- Volume of 4 spheres, *V *= $4\times\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$
- $V = 4 \times \frac{4}{3} pi ( 20 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) ^{3} = 4 \times ( 3.35 \times 10^{ - } 5 )$
- $V=1.34\times10^{-4}m^{3}$** [1 mark]**

Calculate the mass of the ice spheres, *m*<sub>*i*</sub>:

- Recall the equation for density: $ρ=\frac{m_{i}}{V}$ so $m_{i}=ρV$
- $m_{i} = 870 \times ( 1.34 \times 10^{ - } 4 )$
- $m_{i}=0.12\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the equation for the energy gained by the ice spheres, *Q*<sub>*i*</sub>:

- Energy gained by ice = energy required to heat ice + energy required to melt ice + energy required to heat water
- Energy gained by ice, $Q_{i} = ( m_{i} c_{i} \Delta T_{i} ) + ( m_{i} L ) + ( m_{i} c_{w} \Delta T_{w} )$
- $Q_{i} = ( 0.12 \times ( 1.9 \times 10 ^{3} ) \times ( 0 - - 7.2 ) ) + ( 0.12 \times ( 442 \times 10 ^{3} ) ) + ( 0.12 \times ( 5.7 \times 10 ^{3} ) T_{f} )$
- $Q_{i}=54681.6+684T_{f}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine an equation for the energy change in the water, *Q*<sub>*w*</sub>:

- Energy lost by water, $Q_{w} = m_{w} c_{w} ( T_{w} - T_{f} )$
- $Q_{w} = 0.75 \times ( 5.7 \times 10 ^{3} ) \times ( 22.2 - T_{f} )$
- $Q_{w}=94905-4275T_{f}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the final temperature of the water, *T*<sub>*f*</sub>:

- Energy gained by ice = energy lost by water
- $54681.6+684T_{f}=94905-4275T_{f}$
- $4959T_{f}=40223.4$
- $T_{f}=8.11^{\circ}C$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Energy gained by ice = energy required to heat ice + energy required to melt ice + energy required to heat water*

> *because "energy required to heat water" is the energy lost by the ice on the water*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The ice spheres have a radius of 20 mm and a density of 870 kg m^−3^.
Volume of one sphere = 3.35 × 10^−5^ m^3^ (from part (b))
Radius of sphere, r = 20 × 10^−3^ m (from part (b))

The experiment is repeated with four identical cubes of ice. The cubes have equal volume, mass and density to the spheres from parts **(a) **and **(b)**.

Determine through calculation whether the final temperature would be obtained quicker when using the cubes instead of the spheres.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine through calculation whether the final temperature would be obtained quicker when using the cubes instead of the spheres:

List the known quantities:

- Volume of one sphere = 3.35 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m<sup>3</sup> (from part (b))
- Radius of sphere, *r *= 20 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m (from part (b))

Explanation:

- The greater the surface area to volume ratio of the ice pieces then the quicker thermal transfer will take place; ** [1 mark]**

Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the spheres:

- Surface area of one sphere = $4 \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{r}^{2} = 4 \mathrm{\pi } \\times ( 20 \\times 10^{- 3} )^{2} = 5.03 \\times 10^{- 3} \mathrm{m}^{2}$
- $\frac{surfacearea}{volume}=\frac{5.03\times10^{-3}}{3.35\times10^{-5}}=150.15m^{-1}$ ** [1 mark]**

Calculate the side length of the cubes:

- Volume of sphere = volume of cube
- Volume of cube = *l*<sup>*3*</sup>
- So, $l = \sqrt[3]{v o l u m e o f s p h e r e} = \sqrt[3]{ ( 3.35 \times 10^{ - } 5 ) }$
- $l=0.032m$ ** [1 mark]**

Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cubes:

- Surface area of one cube = $6 \times ( 0.032 ) ^{2} = 6.14 \times 10^{ - } 3 \mathrm{m} ^{2}$
- $\frac{surfacearea}{volume}=\frac{6.14\times10^{-3}}{3.35\times10^{-5}}=183.3m^{-1}$** [1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- The ice cubes have a higher surface area to volume ratio, so the final temperature would be obtained quicker;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
As part of a model village pyrotechnics display a 33 g iron ball bearing, cooled to a soecific initial temperature of −2.1592 °C, is dropped into a pool. The ball begins to accelerate uniformly from a height of 0.75 m above the surface of the pool with a velocity of 20 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Assume that the ball falls with a constant acceleration due to free fall but a thermal energy transfer takes place between the ball and the air.

The iron ball has a specific heat capacity of 440 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the temperature of the ball immediately before it hits the water.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the temperature of the ball immediately before it hits the water:

List the known quantities:

- Height of fall, *h *= 0.75 m
- Initial velocity of ball, *u *= 20 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Acceleration due to free-fall, *g *= 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>
- Initial temperature of ball, *T*<sub>*i*</sub> = −2.1592 °C

Calculate the final velocity of the ball just before it hits the surface of the water, *v*:

- Recall an equation of uniform motion: $v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$
- So, $v = \sqrt{u ^{2} + 2 a h} = \sqrt{20 ^{2} + ( 2 \times 9.81 \times 0.75 ) } = 20.36 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s} ^{ - } 1$ **[1 mark]**

Consider the energy transfer taking place as the ball falls:

- Initial gravitational potential energy + initial kinetic energy = final gravitational potential energy + final kinetic energy + thermal energy transferred to surroundings
- $mgh+\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}=0+\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+mc\DeltaT$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the change in temperature of the ball bearing, Δ*T*:

- $\DeltaT=\frac{2gh+u^{2}-v^{2}}{2c}$
- $\Delta T = \frac{ ( 2 \times 9.81 \times 0.75 ) + 20 ^{2} - 20.36 ^{2} }{ ( 2 \times 440 ) }$
- $\DeltaT=2.1068\times10^{-4}^{\circ}C$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the temperature of the ball immediately before it hits the water, *T*<sub>*f*</sub>:

- $\DeltaT=T_{f}-T_{i}$
- $T_{f} = \Delta T + T_{i} = ( 2.1068 \times 10^{ - } 4 ) + ( - 2.1592 ) = - 2.1590 ^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

As part of a model village pyrotechnics display a 33 g iron ball bearing, cooled to a soecific initial temperature of −2.1592 °C, is dropped into a pool. The ball begins to accelerate uniformly from a height of 0.75 m above the surface of the pool with a velocity of 20 m s^−1^.

The iron ball has a specific heat capacity of 440 J kg^−1^ °C^−1^.

The iron ball bearing from **(a)** falls into the pool. The pool has dimensions of 5 cm, 10 cm and 30 cm. The density of the water in the pool is 1030 kg m<sup>−3</sup> and has a specific heat capacity of 4300 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>. The initial temperature of the water in the pool is 22.5173 °C.

Calculate the final temperature of the ball and the water after impact.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the final temperature of the ball and the water after impact:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of ball bearing, *m*<sub>*b*</sub> = 33 g = 33 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg (from part (a))
- Volume of pool, *V *= 0.05 × 0.1 × 0.3 = 1.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- Density of water, *ρ* = 1030 kg m<sup>−3</sup>
- Specific heat capacity of water, *c*<sub>*w*</sub> = 4300 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>
- Specific heat capacity of ball, *c*<sub>*b*</sub> = 440 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))
- Initial temperature of water, *T*<sub>*w*</sub> = 22.5173 °C
- Temperature of ball upon hitting the water, *T*<sub>*b*</sub> = −2.1590 °C (from part (a))

Calculate the mass of the water in the pool, m<sub>w</sub>:

- Recall the equation for density, $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ so $m_{w}=ρV$
- $m_{w} = 1030 \times ( 1.5 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) = 1.545 kg$ **[1 mark]**

Consider the energy transfer taking place when the ball is in the water:

- Energy gained by ball = energy lost by water
- $m_{b} c_{b} ( T - T_{b} ) = m_{w} c_{w} ( T - T_{w} )$
- $m_{b}c_{b}T-m_{b}c_{b}T_{b}=m_{w}c_{w}T-m_{w}c_{w}T_{w}$

- $( m_{b} c_{b} - m_{w} c_{w} ) T = m_{b} c_{b} T_{b} - m_{w} c_{w} T_{w}$
- $T = \frac{m_{b} c_{b} T_{b} - m_{w} c_{w} T_{w}}{ ( m_{b} c_{b} - m_{w} c_{w} ) }$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the final temperature of the ball and the water, *T*:

- $T = \frac{ ( ( 33 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times 440 \times - 2.1590 ) - ( 1.545 \times 4300 \times 22.5137 ) }{ ( ( 33 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times 440 ) - ( 1.545 \times 4300 ) }$
- $T=22.6577^{\circ}C$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A professional cyclist of mass 50 kg is testing a new hydraulic brake system on his racing bike of mass 5 kg. He is travelling at a constant speed of 25 m s<sup>−1</sup> when he has to brake suddenly.

The four brake discs on the bike each have a mass of 250 g, included in the mass of the bike. The specific heat capacity of the mineral oil in the brake system is 1.77 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the overall increase in the temperature of the brake discs.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the overall increase in the temperature of the brake discs:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of cyclist, m<sub>c</sub> = 50 kg
- Mass of bike, *m*<sub>*b*</sub> = 5 kg
- Constant speed, *v *= 25 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Mass of 1 brake disc, *m*<sub>*d*</sub>* *= 250 g = 0.25 kg
- Specific heat capacity or brake fluid, *c* = 1.77 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup>.= 1.77 × 10<sup>3 </sup>J kg<sup>−1</sup>

Obtain an equation for the conservation of energy as the cyclist comes to a stop:

- $m=m_{b}+m_{c}=55\mathrm{kg}$
- Kinetic energy lost by cyclist and bike = thermal energy gained by 4 brake discs
- $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=4m_{d}c\DeltaT$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the increase in temperature of the brake discs, Δ*T:*

- $\DeltaT=\frac{mv^{2}}{8m_{d}c}$
- $\Delta T = \frac{55 \times 25 ^{2} }{8 \times 0.25 \times ( 1.77 \times 10 ^{3} ) }$
- $\DeltaT=9.71^{\circ}C$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

To determine the number of molecules, *N*:

  - $n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}\rightarrowN=nN_{A}$
- $N = 3.33 \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $N=2.01\times10^{24}=2\times10^{24}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Use the following information to determine the molar mass of glucose, C6H12O6. The atomic mass of hydrogen is 1. The atomic mass of carbon is 12. The atomic mass of oxygen is 16.

Determine how many molecules of glucose there are in 600 g of glucose. N = 3.33 × (6.02×10^23), N = 2.01×10^24 = 2×10^24

Determine the mass of carbon in 600 g of glucose.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the mass of carbon in 600 g of glucose:

List the known quantities:

- Atomic mass of carbon = 12
- Number of glucose molecules, *N* = 2.01 ×10<sup>24</sup> (from part (c))
- Unified atomic mass unit, 1 u = 1.66×10<sup>−27</sup> kg (from the data page)

Determine the number of carbon atoms in 600 g of glucose:

- There are 6 carbon atoms per C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> molecule
- Therefore, there are 6*N* carbon atoms in 600 g of glucose

  - Number of C atoms = $6\times2.01\times10^{24}$** [1 mark]**
  - Number of C atoms = $1.206\times10^{25}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the total mass of carbon atoms:

- Mass of 1 carbon atom = 12 u = $12\times1.66\times10^{-27}=1.992\times10^{-26}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**
- Total mass of carbon atoms = mass of 1 carbon atom × number of carbon atoms

  - Total mass of carbon atoms = $( 1.992 \times 10^{ - } 26 ) \times ( 1.206 \times 10^{25} )$ **[1 mark]**
  - Total mass of carbon atoms = $0.240\mathrm{kg}$  **OR** 240 g** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Determine the number of atoms in 4.0 g of Nitrogen-14.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Atomic mass of nitrogen-14 = mass of 1 mole of nitrogen-14 = 14 g
- Mass of nitrogen sample, *m *= 4.0 g
- Avogadro's constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23 </sup>mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the number of moles in 4.0 g:

- $n=\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{sample}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}$** [1 mark]**
- $n=\frac{4}{14}=0.2857$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of atoms, *N*:

- *N *= *n *× *N*<sub>*A*</sub> **[1 mark]**
- *N* = 0.2857 × (6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>)
- *N *= 1.72 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.7 × 10<sup>23</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *When doing molar calculations it is important to leave the unrounded **n** number in your calculator to use in the **N** calculation. Because you are multiplying by such a large number (6.02 × 10*<sup>*23*</sup>*) any rounding errors are greatly magnified. If you use the unrounded value for n, then **N **= 1.72 × 10*<sup>*23*</sup>* but if you use **n** = 0.29 then **N **= 1.746 × 10*<sup>*23*</sup>* = 1.75 × 10*<sup>*23 *</sup>*which may lose you the mark.*

parts.problemMd: Explain the difference in the nuclear composition of nitrogen-14 and nitrogen-15.
parts.solutionMd:
An isotope is:

- An atom of the same element that has the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in the nucleus; **[1 mark]**

Nitrogen-14 is:

- An isotope of nitrogen that has 14 nucleons; **[1 mark]**
- 7 protons and 7 neutrons; **[1 mark]**

Nitrogen-15 is:

- An isotope of nitrogen that has 15 nucleons; **[1 mark]**
- 7 protons and 8 neutrons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

Atomic mass of nitrogen-14 = mass of 1 mole of nitrogen-14 = 14 g
Nitrogen-14 has 14 nucleons (7 protons and 7 neutrons); Nitrogen-15 has 15 nucleons (7 protons and 8 neutrons).

State whether there are more atoms in 4 g of nitrogen-14 than in nitrogen-15. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The number of atoms in nitrogen-15 is:

- Less than the number of atoms in nitrogen-14; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- The molar mass of nitrogen-15 is bigger than the molar mass of nitrogen-14 so the number of moles *n  *will be less; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Carbon-12 and oxygen-16 form the most abundant compound of carbon dioxide.

Determine the relative atomic mass of carbon dioxide.
parts.solutionMd:

- Carbon-12 has a relative atomic mass = 12 g **AND**
- Oxygen-16 has a relative atomic mass = 16 g **[1 mark]**

Determine the relative atomic mass of carbon dioxide, CO<sub>2</sub>:

- 12 + (2 × 16) = 44 g **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Remember that CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* is made up of one atom of carbon and two atoms of oxygen.*

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
The following information on the isotopes of the elements in methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) is available:

- Carbon-12
- Hydrogen-1
- Sulphur-32
- Oxygen-16

(i) Determine the ratio of the molar mass of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>).

[3]

(ii) State the number of moles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) required to equal the same mass of sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the molar mass of methane, CH<sub>4</sub>:

- Molar mass of carbon-12 = 12 g
- Molar mass of hydrogen-1 = 1 g
- Molar mass of CH<sub>4 </sub>= 12 + (4 × 1) = 16 g **[1 mark]**

Determine the molar mass of sulphur dioxide, SO<sub>2</sub>:

- Molar mass of sulphur-32 = 32 g
- Molar mass of oxygen-16 = 16 g
- Molar mass of SO<sub>2 </sub>= 32 + (16 × 2) = 32 + 32 = 64 g **[1 mark]**

Obtain a ratio for the molar mass of methane and sulphur dioxide:

- $\frac{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{methane}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{sulphur} \mathrm{dioxide}}=\frac{16}{64}=0.25$** [1 mark]**

(ii) State the number of moles of methane required to equal the same mass of sulphur dioxide:

- 4 moles of methane are required;** [1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:

- Oxygen-16

Determine the number of moles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) contained within the gas.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Molar mass SO<sub>2</sub> = 64 g
- Molar mass CH<sub>4</sub> = 16 g
- Mass of mixed gas, *m  *= 880 g

Determine the combined molar mass of SO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub>:

- Combined molar mass = 64 + 16 = 80 g **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of moles of SO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub>:

- Number of moles = $\frac{880}{80}=11$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of moles of CH<sub>4</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub>:

- Gases are mixed in equal parts, so there are <u>11 moles</u> of <u>both</u> CH<sub>4</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Don't let part (a) confuse you. The gases have been combined as one molecule of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* with one molecule of CH*<sub>*4*</sub>*.*

parts.problemMd:

In a new mix of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) of mass 896 g. The two gases have been mixed in the ratio 4:1 methane to sulphur dioxide.

Determine the number of moles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) contained within the gas.
parts.solutionMd:

- Ratio is CH<sub>4 </sub>: SO<sub>2 </sub>, 4:1
- Molar mass fits this ratio (4 × 16 g = 64 g): (1 × 64 g) therefore, in terms of mass the gases are equally split

  - $\frac{896}{2}=448$ g SO<sub>2</sub> and 448 g CH<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of moles of each substance:

- Moles of CH<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{448}{16}=28$ **[1 mark]**
- Moles of SO<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{448}{64}=7$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Hopefully, you recognised that the ratio given is the same as the ratio already calculated in part (a). So no additional sums are needed here.  There are several ways to complete this question but this method follows the most logical steps for 3 marks. *

parts.problemMd:
An ideal gas is in a container of volume 0.005 m<sup>3</sup>. The gas is at a temperature of 10°C and a pressure of 4 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.

Calculate the pressure of the ideal gas in the same container when it is heated to 30 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the pressure of the ideal gas in the same container when it is heated to 30 °C:

List the known quantities:

- Initial temperature, *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 10 °C
- Initial pressure, *P*<sub>*1*</sub>* = *4 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Final temperature, *T*<sub>*2*</sub> = 30 °C

Convert the temperatures into Kelvin:

- *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 10 + 273 = 283 K
**AND**
- *T*<sub>*2*</sub> = 30 + 273 = 303 K **[1 mark]**

Determine the correct gas law required to calculate the final pressure, *P*<sub>*2*</sub>:

- Use the pressure law

  - $\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

  - $P_{2}=\frac{P_{1}T_{2}}{T_{1}}$

Substitute the known quantities and calculate *P*<sub>*2*</sub>:

- $P_{2} = \frac{ ( 4 \times 10^{5} ) \times 303}{283}$ **[1 mark]**
- $P_{2}=4.3\times10^{5}\mathrm{Pa}$** [1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A cylinder used for scuba diving contains an ideal gas with a volume of 2.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>. The gas is at a temperature of 10°C and a pressure of 4.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> Pa.

Calculate the amount of gas in the cylinder, in moles.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the amount of gas in the cylinder, in moles:

List the known quantities:

- Volume, *V* = 2.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- Temperature, *T *= 10°C + 273 = 283 K
- Pressure, *p* = 4.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> Pa
- Molar gas constant, *R* = 8.31 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

Use the ideal gas equation in terms of number of moles *n*:

- $pV=nRT$
- $n=\frac{pV}{RT}$ **[1 mark]**
- $n = \frac{ ( 4.0 \times 10 ^{2} ) \times ( 2.0 \times 10 ^{3} ) }{8.31 \times 283}$ **[1 mark]**
- $n=340.18=340\mathrm{mol}$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *All of the quantities in the question are written to **2 s.f.,** and your final answer should be too. *

parts.problemMd:
A canister of oxygen mixed with air has a volume of 0.0349 m<sup>3</sup> and a pressure of 1.50 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa. The canister is stored in a hospital basement at a temperature of 20°C.

Determine the number of moles of gas in the canister.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the number of moles, *n*, of gas in the canister:

List the known quantities:

- Volume, $V=0.0349m^{3}$
- Pressure, $P=1.50\times10^{6}\mathrm{Pa}$
- Temperature, $T=20^{\circ}C$
- Molar gas constant, $R=8.31JK^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Convert temperature into Kelvin:

- $T=20^{\circ}C+273=293K$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the ideal gas equation and rearrange to make *n* the subject:

- $PV=nRT\rightarrown=\frac{PV}{RT}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $n = \frac{ ( 1.50 \times 10^{6} ) \times 0.0349}{ 8.31 \times 293}$** **
- $n=21.5\mathrm{mol}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember to convert any temperatures to Kelvin. You can do this within your calculation or when you list the known quantities if you prefer.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A canister of oxygen mixed with air has a volume of 0.0349 m^3 and a pressure of 1.50 × 10^6 Pa. The canister is stored in a hospital basement at a temperature of 20°C.

The canister is brought up to a ward for use. Once the gas has reached equilibrium with the temperature of the hospital ward, the temperature of the canister is 32°C.

Determine the pressure of the gas at this temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the pressure of the gas at 32°C:

List the known quantities:

- Volume, $V=0.0349m^{3}$
- Initial temperature, $T_{1}=20^{\circ}C+273=293K$
- Final temperature, $T_{2}=32^{\circ}C+273=305K$
- Initial pressure, $P_{1}=1.50\times10^{6}\mathrm{Pa}$
- Molar gas constant, $R=8.31JK^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Recall the pressure law and rearrange to make *P*<sub>2</sub> the subject:

- $\frac{p_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{p_{2}}{T_{2}}\rightarrowp_{2}=\frac{p_{1}T_{2}}{T_{1}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $p_{2} = \frac{ ( 1.50 \times 10^{6} ) \times 305}{293}$ **[1 mark]**
- $p_{2}=1.56\times10^{6}\mathrm{Pa}$ (3 s.f.)** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain the effect on the pressure of the gas when the temperature was increased.
parts.solutionMd:
As the temperature of the gas increases...

- The average kinetic energy of the molecules increases; **[1 mark]**
- So the molecules collide with the surface of the container more frequently **AND** with a greater force; **[1 mark]**
- Since <u>pressure is force per unit area</u>, the pressure increases; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The ideal gas equation in terms of the number of moles, *n*, is written as

$pV=nRT$

where *R* is the molar gas constant.

Show that the ideal gas equation can also be written as

$pV=NkT$

where *N* is the number of molecules and *k* is the Boltzmann constant.
parts.solutionMd:
The ideal gas equation can also be written as $pV=NkT$ by:

State the definition of the Boltzmann constant, *k*:

- $k=\frac{R}{N_{A}}$

Determine the equation for the number of moles, *n*:

- $n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}$

Substitute this into the ideal gas equation:

- $p V = n R T = ( \frac{N}{N} _{A} ) R T$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the Boltzmann constant:

- $k=\frac{R}{N_{A}}\RightarrowR=kN_{A}$
- $p V = ( \frac{N}{N} _{A} ) \\times k N_{A} \\times T = N k T$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A cylinder for an ideal gas has a radius of 120 mm and a height of 1350 mm. The gas is at a temperature of 14 °C and a pressure of 1.7 × 10<sup>7</sup> Pa.

![15-1-1b-m-ideal-gas-cylinder](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/15-ideal-gases/15-2-equation-of-state/assets/008-15-1-1b-m-ideal-gas-cylinder.png)

Show that the amount of gas in the cylinder is 430 mol.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the amount of gas in the cylinder is 430 mol

List the known quantities:

- Radius of the cylinder, *r* = 120 mm = 120 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m
- Height of the cylinder, *h* = 1350 mm 1350 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m
- Temperature of the gas, *T* = 14 °C = 14 + 273 = 287 K
- Pressure, *p* = 1.7 × 10<sup>7</sup> Pa

Calculate the volume of the gas, *V*:

- $V=A\timesh=πr^{2}\timesh$
- $V = \mathrm{\pi } ( 120 \\times 10^{- 3} )^{2} \\times ( 1350 \\times 10^{- 3} ) = 0.061 \mathrm{m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the ideal gas equation for the number of moles, *n*:

- $p V = n R T \Rightarrow n = \frac{pV}{RT}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $n = \frac{ ( 1.7 \times 10^{7} ) \times 0.061}{8.31 \times ( 287 ) } = 434.8 = 430 \text{mol}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You will be expected to remember the volume of common 3D shapes such as cubes, cylinders and spheres.*

> *T** in the ideal gas equation is always in Kelvin, do not miss out this conversion if you are given a temperature in °C.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A cylinder for an ideal gas has a radius of 120 mm and a height of 1350 mm. The gas is at a temperature of 14 °C and a pressure of 1.7 × 10^7^ Pa. Show that the amount of gas in the cylinder is 430 mol. [Mark scheme: n = 434.8 = 430 mol]

The gas leaks slowly from the cylinder at an average rate of 8.3 × 10<sup>15</sup> atoms s<sup>–1 </sup>so that, after a time of 51 days, the pressure reduces. The temperature remains constant.

Calculate the percentage of the number of moles lost from the cylinder.
parts.solutionMd:
The percentage of the number of moles lost from the cylinder is:

- Rate of loss of atoms = 8.3 × 10<sup>15</sup> atoms s<sup>–1</sup>
- Time, *t* = 51 days
- Initial number of moles, *n * = 434.8 mol (from part b)

Calculate the number of lost atoms:

- $a t o m s l o s t = ( 8.3 \times 10^{15} ) \times ( 51 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 )$
- $atomslost=3.657\times10^{22}\mathrm{atoms}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of lost moles, *n*:

- $n=\frac{3.657\times10^{22}}{6.02\times10^{23}}=0.059\mathrm{mol}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the percentage of the number of moles lost:

- $\% m o l e s l o s t = \frac{0.059 }{434.8} \times 100 \%$
- $\% m o l e s l o s t = 0.01356 \% = 0.014 \%$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *If the rate is in **s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* then the time you must multiply this by must be in **s **so the final units are **atoms**. Take care for small unit conversions like this, which are very easy to lose marks from.*

parts.problemMd: Calculate the number of molecules in a gas containing 120 g of ${}_{8}^{16}\mathrm{O}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The number of molecules in a gas containing 120 g of ${}_{8}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ is:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of sample, *m* = 120 g
- Molar mass of oxygen-16, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 16 g mol<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the number of moles, *n*:

- $n=\frac{m}{M_{r}}=\frac{120}{16}$
- $n=7.5\mathrm{mol}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of molecules, *N*:

- $n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}\RightarrowN=nN_{A}$
- $N = 7.5 \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} ) = 4.5 \times 10^{24}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A different ideal gas has an initial volume of 6.00 × 10<sup>4</sup> m<sup>3</sup> at a pressure of 1.42 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa and a temperature of 8 °C

It is heated at a constant volume so that, in its final state, the pressure is 1.70 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa at a temperature of 63 °C.

Show that these two states prove it behaves as an ideal gas.
parts.solutionMd:
The two states prove it behaves as an ideal gas because:

List the known quantities:

- Initial (and final) volume, *V*<sub>1</sub> = 6.00 × 10<sup>4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- Initial pressure, *p*<sub>1</sub> = 1.42 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Initial temperature, *T*<sub>1</sub> = 8 °C = 8 + 273 = 281 K
- Final pressure, *p*<sub>2</sub> = 1.70 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Final temperature, *T*<sub>2</sub> = 63 °C = 63 + 273 = 336 K

Determine an equation linking *p*, *V* and *T*:

- $pV\proptoT\Rightarrow\frac{pV}{T}=constant$

Substitute in the initial values:

- $\frac{p_{1} V_{1}}{T_{1}} = \frac{ ( 1.42 \times 10^{5} ) \times ( 6.00 \times 10^{4} ) }{281} = 3.03 \times 10^{7}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute in the final values:

- $\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{T_{2}} = \frac{ ( 1.70 \times 10^{5} ) \times ( 6.00 \times 10^{4} ) }{336} = 3.03 \times 10^{7}$** [1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- This is an ideal gas because $\frac{pV}{T}=constant$;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The temperature must be in **Kelvin **when using the ideal gas equation.*

> *Anytime you want to change a proportionality into an equation:*

- *Turn the proportionality sign into an = sign and add a **constant** (e.g. k) *$pV=kT$

Calculate the number of atoms:

parts.problemMd:

temperature = .......................... °C
parts.solutionMd:
The temperature of the air in the tyre is:

List the known quantities:

- Volume, *V* = 3.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> mm<sup>3</sup>
- Pressure, *p* = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Number of moles, *n* = 0.29 mol

Convert the volume from mm<sup>3</sup> to m<sup>3</sup>:

- 1 mm<sup>3</sup> = 1 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- 3.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> mm<sup>3</sup> = (3.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × 10<sup>–9</sup> = 0.0035 m<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

Determine the equation for the temperature, *T *and substitute in the values:

- $pV=nRT\RightarrowT=\frac{pV}{nR}$
- $T = \frac{ ( 2.0 \times 10^{5} ) \times 0.0035 }{0.29 \times 8.31} = 290.46 \mathrm{K}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The air in a bicycle tire has a constant volume of 3.5 × 10^6 mm^3. The pressure of 0.29 mol of the air is 2.0 × 10^5 Pa. The air may be considered to be an ideal gas. Calculate the temperature of the air in the tire. [Answer: temperature = 17 °C = 290 K]

The pressure of the tire is increased using a pump. On each stroke of the pump, 0.0045 mol of air is forced into the tire.

Calculate the number of moles of air in the tire when the pressure increases to 2.7 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa and the temperature increases by 10 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
The number of strokes of the pump to increase the pressure to 3.9 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa at a temperature increase of 12 °C is:

- Initial number moles, *n*<sub>1 </sub>= 0.29 mol
- Initial pressure, *p*<sub>1</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Initial temperature, *T*<sub>1</sub> = 17 °C = 17 + 273 = 290 K
- Final pressure, *p*<sub>2</sub> = 2.7 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Final temperature, *T*<sub>2</sub> = 290 + 10 = 300 K

Determine an equation for the new number of moles, *n*<sub>2</sub>:

- $pV=nRT\Rightarrown=\frac{pV}{RT}$ where $\frac{V}{R}$is a constant
- $n=constant\times\frac{p}{T}$
- $\frac{n_{1}T_{1}}{p_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}T_{2}}{p_{2}}$
- $n_{2}=\frac{n_{1}p_{2}T_{1}}{p_{1}T_{2}}=n_{1}\times\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\times\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$

Substitute in the values:

- $n_{2} = 0.29 \\times ( \frac{2.7 \\times 10^{5} }{2.0 \\times 10^{5} } ) \\times ( \frac{290}{300} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $n_{2}=0.378=0.38\mathrm{mol}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Determining the equation for the final number of moles is quite tricky here. The trick is it to see which variables in the equation are **constant**, and then you can convert this into an equation for the variables **before** (with a subscript '1') and the variables **after** (with a subscript '2'). This comes up many times in A-level physics, especially in the ideal gases topic.*

parts.problemMd:
The pressure exerted by an ideal gas of 8.4 × 10<sup>20</sup> molecules in a container of volume 1.6 × 10<sup>–5</sup> m<sup>3</sup> is 3.2 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.

Calculate the temperature of the gas in the container in ºC.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Pressure, *p* = 3.2 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Volume, *V* = 1.6 × 10<sup>–5 </sup>m<sup>3</sup>
- Number of molecules, *N* = 8.4 × 10<sup>20</sup>

From data booklet:

- The Boltzmann constant, *k *= 1.38 × 10<sup>–23</sup> J K<sup>–1</sup>
- The Avogadro constant,  $N_{A}$ = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J mol<sup>–1</sup> K<sup>–1</sup>

**Method 1: **Calculate temperature using the number of molecules, *N*:

- *pV = NkT*
- *T* = $\frac{pV}{Nk}$ = $\frac{ ( 3.2 \times 10^{5} ) \times ( 1.6 \times 10^{ - } 5 ) }{ ( 8.4 \times 10^{20} ) \times ( 1.38 \times 10^{ - } 23 ) }$  **[1 mark]**
- *T* = 441.68 K **[1 mark]**

Convert temperature into ºC:

- *T* = 441.68 – 273.15 = 168.53 = 169 ºC **[1 mark]**** **

**Final answer:** **OR**

**Method 2:** Calculate temperature using number of moles, *n*:

- *pV = nRT*
- *n* =$\frac{N}{N_{A}}$ = $\frac{8.4\times10^{20}}{6.02\times10^{23}}$ = 1.395 × 10<sup>–3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**
- *T* = $\frac{pV}{nR}$ =$\frac{ ( 3.2 \times 10^{5} ) \times ( 1.6 \times 10^{ - } 5 ) }{ ( 1.395 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times 8.31}$ = 441.67 K **[1 mark]**

Convert temperature into ºC:

- *T* = 441.67 – 273.15 = 168.54 = 169 ºC **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the root mean square speed r.m.s. of the particles in the system when the conical flask is surrounded by ice in the beaker in the freezer:

List the known quantities:

- Specific latent heat of vapourisation, *L*<sub>*v*</sub> = 2160 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> = 2160 × 10<sup>3</sup> J kg<sup>−1</sup>
- Specific latent heat of fusion, *L*<sub>*f*</sub> = 324 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> = 324 × 10<sup>3</sup>J kg<sup>−1</sup>
- Specific heat capacity of water, *C* = 4084 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>
- Change in temperature of the water, Δ*θ* = 100 °C
- Mass of gas, *m *= *m*
- Mass of ice / water, *M* = 240*m*

Obtain an expression for the energy of the system:

- Kinetic energy of molecules in conical flask = Energy lost from the system
- KE = Energy lost when water is still boiling + energy lost when water is cooling + energy lost when water is freezing
- $\langle 1 \frac{1}{2} m c^{2} = M L_{v} + M C \\Delta \theta + M L_{f} \rangle$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the r.m.s:

- $\langle 1 \frac{1}{2} m c^{2} = 240 m L_{v} + 240 m C \\Delta \theta + 240 m L_{f} \rangle$
- $c = \sqrt{2 \times 240 ( L_{v} + c \Delta \theta + L_{f} ) }$
- $c = \sqrt{2 \times 240 ( ( 2160 \times 10 ^{3} ) + ( 4084 \times 100 ) + ( 324 \times 10 ^{3} ) ) }$

$E_{K}=\frac{3}{2}kT$
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the average translational kinetic energy is $E_{K}=\frac{3}{2}kT$:

- Ideal gas equation:  $pV=NkT$  and  $pV=\frac{1}{3}Nm<c^{2}>$
- ∴ $NkT=\frac{1}{3}Nm<c^{2}>$ **[1 mark]**
- $\cancel{N} k T = 1 \frac{1}{3} \cancel{N} m < c^{2} > \Leftrightarrow 3 k T = m < c^{2} >$
- Divide both sides by 2:  $\frac{3}{2}kT=\frac{1}{2}m<c^{2}>$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}m<c^{2}>$ therefore,** **$E_{K}=\frac{3}{2}kT$

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The expression gives the **average **translational kinetic energy, so the expression *$3kT=m<c^{2}>$* must be ÷ 2*

> *The kinetic energy equation from mechanics = *$\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$* where *$v^{2}=<c^{2}>$

> *Hence, *$E_{k}=\frac{3}{2}kT=\frac{1}{2}m<c^{2}>$

parts.solutionMd:

- Original r.m.s. speed of molecules = $c_{1}$

parts.problemMd: State two assumptions of the simple kinetic model of a gas.
parts.solutionMd:
Assumptions of the simple kinetic model of a gas:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two ****from:**

- The gas contains a large number of molecules / atoms / particles; **[1 mark]**
- The molecules are in random motion; **[1 mark]**
- There are no intermolecular forces between the molecules; **[1 mark]**
- The collisions between the molecules are elastic; **[1 mark]**
- The time of the collisions is much less than the time between the collisions; **[1 mark]**
- The volume of molecules is much less than the volume of the containing vessel; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Use the kinetic model of gases and Newton’s laws of motion to explain how a gas exerts a pressure on the sides of its container.
parts.solutionMd:
A gas exerts a pressure on the sides of its container because:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three ****from:**

- The molecules collide with the walls; **[1 mark]**
- The <u>change in momentum</u> of the molecules (on collision with the walls) means there is a force (on the molecules); **[1 mark]**
- The molecules exert an equal and opposite force on the walls (of the container); **[1 mark]**
- Pressure is the average of the force from the collisions per surface area on the walls;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

1.42 × 10<sup>3</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>

For these four atoms, calculate the r.m.s. to three significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:

- Mean square speed:  $< c ^{2} > = \frac{s u m o f ( 4 v a l u e s ) ^{2} }{4}$
- $< c ^{2} > = \frac{ ( 1420 ) ^{2} + ( 1510 ) ^{2} + ( 1560 ) ^{2} + ( 1540 ) ^{2} }{4}$ **[1 mark]**

- $r.m.s.=\sqrt{<c^{2}>}$
- $r.m.s.=\sqrt{2.275\times10^{6}}$ **[1 mark]**

The collisions the particle has with the container walls are **elastic**.

Determine an expression for the change in momentum of the molecule as it hits a wall perpendicularly.
parts.solutionMd:
Consider the change in momentum of the molecule as it hits the wall perpendicularly:

- Change in momentum = momentum after − momentum before
- $\Delta p = - m c - ( + m c )$
- $\Deltap=-2mc$** [1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A single molecule is in a cube-shaped box with sides of equal length \$\$l\$\$. The molecule has a mass \$\$m\$\$ and moves with a speed \$\$c\$\$ parallel to one side of the box. It collides at regular intervals with the ends of the box, exerting a force and contributing to the pressure of the gas. The collisions the particle has with the container walls are elastic. Change in momentum of the molecule as it hits a wall perpendicularly: \$\$\Delta p = -2mc\$\$

(i) Show that the time between collisions of the molecule on the container wall is given by:

$timebetweencollisions=\frac{2l}{c}$

[2]

(ii) Determine an expression for the change in momentum per second.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Write an expression for the time between collisions with the wall:

- The molecule travels from one side of the cube to the surface it collides with, this is a distance $l$
- After the collision, the molecule travels back across one side of the cube, the same distance $l$
- Hence, the molecule travels a total distance of $2l$ **[1 mark]**

Obtain an expression for the time between collisions:

- $time=\frac{distance}{speed}$
- $timebetweencollisions=\frac{distancebetweencollisions}{speedofmolecule}=\frac{2l}{c}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Write an expression for the rate of change in momentum:

- Rate of change of momentum:  $\frac{changeinmomentum}{timebetweencollisions}=\frac{\Deltap}{\Deltat}$ **[1 mark]**
- Rate of change of momentum:  $\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{2 m c}{ ( \frac{2 l}{c} ) } = \frac{m c ^{2} }{l}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A single molecule is in a cube-shaped box with sides of equal length l. The molecule has a mass m and moves with a speed c parallel to one side of the box. It collides at regular intervals with the ends of the box, exerting a force and contributing to the pressure of the gas. The collisions the particle has with the container walls are elastic.

(ii) Rate of change of momentum: Δp/Δt = 2mc/(2l/c) = mc²/l

Consider *N *molecules identical to the single molecule in parts **(a) **and **(b) **in the same cube-shaped box.

Each molecule has a different velocity that contributes to the pressure.

Calculate the total pressure from the *N *particles in the box.
parts.solutionMd:
The total pressure from the *N *particles in the box is:

- All the collisions take place on one face of the cube
- Area of the collision:  $l\timesl=l^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Obtain an expression for pressure and substitute for force and area:

- Force = rate of change of momentum
- $p r e s s u r e = \frac{f o r c e}{a r e a} = \frac{ ( \frac{m c ^{2} }{l} ) }{l ^{2} }$ **[1 mark]**

Obtain an expression that considers the different velocities of the molecules:

- Total pressure of the molecules: $p=\frac{Nmc^{2}}{l^{3}}$ **[1 mark]**
- The different velocities can be described by the mean square of the velocities $<c^{2}>$
- Hence, $p=\frac{Nm<c^{2}>}{l^{3}}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

Hence, p = N m <c²> / l³

A single molecule is in a cube-shaped box with sides of equal length l. The molecule has a mass m and moves with a speed c parallel to one side of the box.

Hence, show that the kinetic theory of gases equation is:

$pV=\frac{1}{3}Nm<c^{2}>$
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the kinetic theory of gases equation is $pV=\frac{1}{3}Nm<c^{2}>$:

- Velocity components in 3 dimensions:  $c ^{2} = ( c_{x} ) ^{2} + ( c_{y} ) ^{2} + ( c_{z} ) ^{2}$
- Because of symmetry, it can be assumed that  $< ( c_{x} ) ^{2} > = < ( c_{y} ) ^{2} > = < ( c_{z} ) ^{2} >$
- Mean square speed:  $< ( c_{x} ) ^{2} > = \frac{1}{3} < c ^{2} >$ **[1 mark]**

Consider the volume of the cube:

- The cube is an $l\timesl\timesl$* *box
- Hence, volume $V=l^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the expression for pressure:

- $p=\frac{Nm<c^{2}>}{l^{3}}$
- $p=\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{Nm<c^{2}>}{V}$ **[1 mark]**
- Hence,** **$pV=\frac{1}{3}Nm<c^{2}>$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *It can be tricky to think about the **different components** of **velocity**:*

parts.problemMd:
A sealed container A has the shape of a rectangular prism and contains an ideal gas. The dimensions of the container are *x*, *y *and z as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![15-2-1a-h-derivation-cube-hsq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/15-ideal-gases/15-3-kinetic-theory-of-gases/assets/011-15-2-1a-h-derivation-cube-hsq-cie-a-level.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

- The average force exerted by the gas on the bottom wall of the container is *F*
- There are *n *moles of gas in the container
- The temperature of the gas is *T *

Obtain an expression for the height of the container in terms of* F,* *n *and *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
Obtain an expression in terms of* F,* *n *and *T *for the height of the container:

- Surface pressure:  $P=\frac{F}{A}$
- Ideal gas equation:  $PV=nRT$
- Combine the equations:  $( \frac{F}{A} ) V = n R T$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute and rearrange the dimensions *l*, *h*, and *w *into the equation:

- Area:  $A=xy$
- Volume:  $V=xyz$*  *
- Substitute:   $\frac{F\timesxyz}{xy}=nRT\RightarrowFz=nRT$
- Rearrange for the height:  $z=\frac{nRT}{F}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A second container B contains the same ideal gas.

The following information is known:

- The pressure in B is a quarter of the pressure in A
- The volume of B is five times the volume of A
- Container B contains half the number of molecules as A
- The temperature of container B is 800 K

Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas of container A.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas of container A:

List the known quantities:

- Pressure of gas in B:  $P_{B}=\frac{1}{4}P_{A}$
- Volume of B:  $V_{B}=5V_{A}$
- Number of molecules in B:  $n_{B}=\frac{1}{2}n_{A}$
- Temperature of gas in B:  *T*<sub>B</sub> = 800 K
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Boltzmann constant, *k *= 1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J K<sup>−1</sup>

Write expressions in terms of the ideal gas equation for the gas contained in A and B:

- Gas in container A:  $P_{A}V_{A}=n_{A}RT_{A}$
- Gas in container B:  `P _ B V _ B = n _ B R T _ B <-> ( P _ A / 4 ) x ( 5 V _ A ) = ( n _ A / 2 ) R x 800` **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $\frac{5}{4}P_{A}V_{A}=400n_{A}R\RightarrowP_{A}V_{A}=320n_{A}R$

Equate the equations in terms of *R *to find the temperature in container A:

- Gas in container A:  $P_{A}V_{A}=n_{A}RT_{A}\RightarrowR=\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{n_{A}T_{A}}$
- Gas in container B:  $P_{A}V_{A}=320n_{A}R\RightarrowR=\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{320n_{A}}$
- Equate & simplify:  $\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{n_{A}T_{A}}=\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{320n_{A}}$
- Temperature of gas A:  $T_{A}=320K$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas of container A:

- Average kinetic energy:  $E_{k}=\frac{3}{2}kT$
- $E_{k} = \frac{3}{2} \times ( 1.38 \times 10^{ - } 23 ) \times 320$
- $E_{k}=6.624\times10^{-21}J$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The kinetic theory of gases assumes that collisions between particles and between particles and the walls of their container are perfectly elastic.

(i) Describe what is meant by a *perfectly elastic collision*

[1]

(ii) Describe the nature of the forces between the molecules

[1]

(iii) Describe, with a reason, the type of speed of the molecules considered in the kinetic theory.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) A perfectly elastic collision is when:

- Kinetic energy is conserved during the collision **OR**
- No kinetic energy is permanently transformed into internal energy (heat, deformation, sound); **[1 mark]**

(ii) The forces between the molecules are:

- There are no long-range intermolecular forces **OR**
- Forces between molecules are negligible except during collisions **[1 mark]**

(iii) The speed of the molecules considered in the kinetic theory is:

- The Root Mean Square (RMS) speed; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- Because the macroscopic properties of the gas (like Temperature and Pressure) are related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules, which depends on the square of the speed;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A gas collimator is used to measure the average velocity of particles in a gas.

The collimator in Fig. 1.1 controls the pressure and the volume and it maintains a gas at a constant temperature.

![15-2-2b-h-collimator-kinetic-theory-hsq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/15-ideal-gases/15-3-kinetic-theory-of-gases/assets/010-15-2-2b-h-collimator-kinetic-theory-hsq-cie-a-le.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Explain why two narrow apertures are required in the collimator to measure the velocity of the particles inside.
parts.solutionMd:
Two narrow apertures are required in the collimator to measure the velocity of the particles inside because:

- Particles in the main chamber move in a constant random  thermal motion; **[1 mark]**
- Only particles travelling in a straight line along the axis / parallel to the beam can pass through both apertures to reach the detector; **[1 mark]**
- This ensures the velocity measured is strictly the velocity in the direction of the beam; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Understanding how a collimator works is **not **part of your **exam** syllabus, **but **hard questions will ask you to **apply** your **knowledge** from the syllabus to a new situation. *

parts.problemMd:
A paint manufacturer is measuring the root mean square speed of a sample of propane particles used to make spray paint. At a temperature of 9 °C the propane molecules have a velocity of 399.00 m s<sup>−1</sup>  with an uncertainty of 0.5 %.

Propane has a molecular mass of 44.097 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.

Determine whether the propane sample behaves as an ideal gas.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine whether the propane sample behaves as an ideal gas:

- Molar mass of propane, *M*<sub>*r*</sub> = 44.097 g mol<sup>−1</sup> = 44.097 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Average velocity of particles, *c* = 399.00 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Uncertainty in velocity = 0.5 %
- Temperature, *T *= 9 °C = 9 + 273.15 = 282.15 K
- Avogadro constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Boltzmann constant, *k* = 1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J K<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the mass of one molecule, $m$

- $m=\frac{M_{r}}{N_{A}}=\frac{44.097\times10^{-3}}{6.02\times10^{23}}$
- $m=7.325\times10^{-26}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the RMS speed, $c_{rms}$

- $c_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}}$
- $c_{r m s} = \sqrt{ \frac{3 \\times ( 1.38 \\times 10^{- 23} ) \\times 282.15}{7.325 \\times 10^{- 26} } }$
- $c_{rms}=399.20ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Compare to the measured value

- Measured value = 399.00 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculated value = 399.20 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- $\% \text{uncertainty} = \frac{ \text{calculated velocity} - \text{known velocity} }{ \text{known velocity} } \times 100$
- $\% \text{uncertainty} = \frac{399.20 - 399.00}{399.00} \times 100$
- $\% uncertainty = 0.05 \%$ **[1 mark]**
- The difference between the theoretical and measured speeds is about 0.05%, which is much smaller than the 0.5% experimental uncertainty, therefore, the measured speed is consistent with the value predicted for an ideal gas; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A sealed box contains 3.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. The average translational kinetic energy of the gas is 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> J.

Calculate the average temperature of the gas.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average temperature of the gas:

List the known quantities:

- Number of moles, *n *= 3.0
- Pressure, *p *= 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas, *E*<sub>*k-total*</sub> = 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> J
- Avogadro constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Boltzmann constant, *k *= 1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J K<sup>−1</sup>
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the translational kinetic energy of one molecule in the gas, *E*<sub>*k-total*</sub>:

- The gas contains 3 moles, so *n *= 3
- Each mole of gas contains Avogadro's number of molecules, *N*<sub>*A*</sub>
- Therefore, the translational kinetic energy of one molecule in the gas is given by the equation: $E_{k}=\frac{E_{k-total}}{nN_{A}}$
- $E_{k} = \frac{1 \times 10^{4} }{3 \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} ) }$
- $E_{k}=5.537\times10^{-21}J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the temperature of the gas:

- Average kinetic energy:  $E_{k}=\frac{3}{2}kT\RightarrowT=\frac{2E_{k}}{3k}$
- $T = \frac{2 E_{k}}{3 k} = \frac{2 \times ( 5.537 \times 10^{ - } 21 ) }{3 \times ( 1.38 \times 10^{ - } 23 ) } = 267.5 \mathrm{K}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:

List the known quantities:

- Average translational kinetic energy of one molecule, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = 5.54 × 10<sup>−21</sup> J (From part (a))
- Molar mass, *M*<sub>*r*</sub> = 5.9 g mol<sup>−1</sup> = 5.9 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Avogadro constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the mass of one molecule, *m*:

- $m=\frac{M_{r}}{N_{A}}$
- $m = \frac{ ( 5.9 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) }{ ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} ) }$
- $m=9.8\times10^{-27}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule to calculate the average velocity, *c*:

- $\langle E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} m c^{2} \rangle$
- $c=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m}}$
- $c = \sqrt{ \frac{2 \\times ( 5.54 \\times 10^{- 21} )}{9.8 \\times 10^{- 27} } }$
- $c=1063ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the magnitude of the impulse of the gas atoms:

- The collision of the particles with the walls is perfectly elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved before and after each collision
- Consider the change in direction of the particle before and after the collision

  - Before the collision: the particle moves towards the wall and the velocity is positive
  - After the collision: the particle moves away from the wall and the velocity is negative

- Impulse = change in momentum = *mv *− *mu*
- Impulse =* mc − *(−*mc*)* *= 2*mc*
- Impulse = 2 × (9.8 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) × (1063)
- Impulse = 2.08 × 10<sup>−23</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

A sealed box contains 3.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. The average translational kinetic energy of the gas is 1 × 10^4 J. Calculate the average temperature of the gas. [Answer: T = 267.5 K]

The pressure of the ideal gas in the box is 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. The box is opened and additional molecules enter. The number of gas atoms is increased by *y *%.

The box is then resealed and the temperature of the remaining gas atoms increased by 102.5 °C. The new pressure in the box is 2% of the original pressure. The box has a volume 0.819 m<sup>3</sup>.

Find the value of *y*.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the value of *y:*

List the known quantities:

- Original number of moles, *n *= 3.0
- Original pressure, *p*<sub>*1*</sub>* *= 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Volume of gas, *V* = 0.819 m<sup>3</sup>
- Original temperature, *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 267.5 K (from **(a)**)
- New temperature, *T*<sub>*2*</sub> = 267.5 + 102.5 = 370 K
- New pressure, *p*<sub>*2*</sub> = 0.02 × *p*<sub>*1*</sub> = 0.02 × (6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup>) = 1.22 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the new number of moles, *n*:

- Ideal gas equation: $pV=nRT\Rightarrown=\frac{p_{2}V}{RT_{2}}$
- $n = \frac{ ( 1.22 \times 10^{4} ) \times 0.819}{8.31 \times 370} = 3.25 \text{mol}$** [1 mark]**

Calculate *y*:

- $y = \frac{d i f f e r e n c e i n m o l e s}{o r i g i n a l n u m b e r o f m o l e s} \times 100 \%$
- $y = \frac{3.25 - 3}{3} \times 100 = 8.3 \%$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
For an ideal gas, internal energy is directly proportional to temperature in kelvin.

A sample of ideal gas is in a perfectly insulated box of fixed volume.

The temperature of the sample rises from 400 K to 600 K. Its internal energy was initially 2800 J.

Calculate its new internal energy.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the new internal energy:

List the known quantities:

- Initial temperature, *T*<sub>*i*</sub>  = 400 K
- Final temperature, *T*<sub>*f*</sub>  = 600 K
- Initial internal energy, *U*<sub>*i*</sub>  = 2800 J

Use direct proportionality:

- $T\proptoU$
- Therefore, $\frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}=\frac{U_{f}}{U_{i}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities to find the new internal energy, *U*<sub>*f*</sub> :

- $U_{f}=U_{i}\times\frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}=2800\times\frac{600}{400}$ **[1 mark]**
- $U_{f}=4200J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The equation *$\frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}=\frac{U_{f}}{U_{i}}$* is essentially saying 'if temperature doubles, internal energy also doubles'. This is direct proportionality, but you could have also used the initial temperature and initial internal energy to find a constant of proportionality and found final internal energy that way. Both methods are equivalent.*

parts.problemMd:
A container of fixed volume holds 15.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. This is 9.03 × 10<sup>24</sup> atoms in total.

Each atom has a mass of 6.64 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg.

The gas is held at a temperature such that the root-mean-square speed is 1680 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate this temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the temperature:

List the known quantities:

- Number of moles, *n*  = 15.0 mol
- Number of atoms, *N* = 9.03 × 10<sup>24</sup>
- Root-mean-square speed, $\langle \sqrt{ c^{2} } \rangle$ = 1680 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Mass of an individual atom, *m* = 6.64 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg
- Molar gas constant, *R*  = 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Recall the ideal gas law:

- $pV=nRT$

Use the pressure of an ideal gas equation from the formulae page:

- $\langle p = 1 \frac{1}{3} \frac{N m}{V} c^{2} \rangle$

Combine the two to eliminate pressure and volume:

- $\langle p V = ( 1 \frac{1}{3} \frac{N m}{ \cancel{V} } c^{2} ) \\times \cancel{V} = n R T \rangle$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for temperature:

- $\langle n R T = \frac{N m c^{2}}{3} \rangle$
- $\langle T = \frac{N m c^{2}}{3 n R} = \frac{( 9.03 \\times 10^{24} ) \\times ( 6.64 \\times 10^{-27} ) \\times 1680^{2}}{3 \\times 15 \\times 8.31} \rangle$ **[1 mark]**
- $T=453K$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Combining these two known equations requires some careful algebra. Additionally, a common pitfall is to forget to square the root-mean-square speed when using the pressure of an ideal gas equation. You had to square the 1680 m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* to get the correct answer.*

> *Root-mean-square speed is written as *$\langle \sqrt{ c^{2} } \rangle$*and has units of speed, m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>*.*

> *Mean-square speed is written as *$< c^{2} >$* and has units of speed-squared, m*<sup>*2*</sup>* s*<sup>*−2*</sup>*.*

- $T=\frac{pV}{nR}$

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
A monatomic gas, contained within a balloon, gains 43 kJ of internal energy.

This process involves 25 kJ of thermal energy being transferred to the gas.

Calculate the work done through this process, including the whether work is done on or by the balloon.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculating the work done by the gas:

List the known quantities:

- Change in internal energy, Δ*U* = +43 kJ
- Thermal energy transferred, *Q* = +25 kJ

Recall the first law of thermodynamics:

- $ΔU=q+W$

Substitute the known quantities and find *W *:

- $W=+18\mathrm{kJ}$ **[1 mark]**
- Work is done <u>on the balloon</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In thermodynamics, the sign in front of an energy implies a direction of transfer. In CIE, the convention is:*

- *Work done **on** the system (gas compressed) is positive*
- *Work done **by** the system (gas expands) is negative*

> *Not every website or exam board uses CIE's sign convention for thermodynamics, so be aware of this if attempting practice questions from a range of exam boards or websites.*

Write an algebraic expression relating change in internal energy and work done.
parts.solutionMd:
To write an expression for internal energy and work done:

Recall the first law of thermodynamics:

- $ΔU=q+W$ **[1 mark]**

  - where Δ*U*  is change in internal energy
  - *q*  is energy transferred to the system by heating
  - *W*  is work done

Consider the heat transferred:

- The system is perfectly insulated
- $q=0J$* ***[1 mark]**

Relate change in internal energy and work:

- $ΔU=W$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In questions on the first law, phrases like 'insulated' or 'no energy enters of leaves the system' are your hints that **q** is zero and you may equate change in internal energy and work done. Knowing the definitions of each term in the equation will help you identify these clues.*

parts.problemMd: Suggest, with a reason, how the specific latent heat of vapourisation of water at a pressure greater than atmospheric pressure compares with its value at atmospheric pressure.
parts.solutionMd:
When the atmospheric pressure is greater then the specific latent heat of vapourisation will be as follows:

- The greater the atmospheric pressure, the higher the boiling point; **[1 mark]**
- So a larger amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces (between the water molecules); **[1 mark]**

Consider the effect on the specific latent heat of vapourisation:

- Thermal energy, $q=mL_{v}$
- Hence, specific latent heat of vapourisation also increases;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

*This is a **difficult question**. The **atmospheric pressure** above the water is **higher**, so the water requires **more energy** to overcome this.*

> *As **atmospheric pressure decreases**, you walk **higher up** a mountain, then the **boiling temperature** of your **water decreases**, so the time it takes your water to boil is less and the **energy required to boil** is also **less**. This can be an easier way to think about this question. *

parts.problemMd: State the first law of thermodynamics and include any relevant units.
parts.solutionMd:
The first law of thermodynamics states:

- Increase in internal energy, *ΔU* = energy supplied to the system by heating, *q* + work done on the system, *W; ***[1 mark]**
- Units are J; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A fixed mass of water is in a beaker at atmospheric pressure. The initial temperature of the water is 0 °C. The water is supplied with thermal energy *q*, so that its temperature increases to 10 °C. There is no net change in the volume of the water.

Determine the work done and the increase in internal energy of the water by completing **Table 1.1**, considering the first law of thermodynamics.

| Work done on water | thermal energy supplied to water | increase in internal energy of water |
|---|---|---|
|   | + *q* |   |
parts.solutionMd:

| work done on water | thermal energy supplied to water | increase in internal energy of water |
|---|---|---|
| **Final answer:** **0** | + *q* | **Final answer:** **+ ΔU** |

- The volume of the water does not change, so the work done on the water = 0; **[1 mark]**
- The water remains at atmospheric pressure, and the only energy supplied is thermal energy, so the internal energy of the water increases by *+ΔU;* **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A fixed mass of water is in a beaker at atmospheric pressure. The initial temperature of the water is 0 \u00b0C. The water is supplied with thermal energy q, so that its temperature increases to 10 \u00b0C. There is no net change in the volume of the water.

Determine the work done and the increase in internal energy of the water by completing Table 1.1, considering the first law of thermodynamics.

Table 1.1: work done on water = 0; thermal energy supplied to water = +q; increase in internal energy of water = +\u0394U. The volume of the water does not change, so the work done on the water = 0. The water remains at atmospheric pressure, and the only energy supplied is thermal energy, so the internal energy of the water increases by +\u0394U.

The water from part (b) is now heated so it's temperature increases by a further 10 °C to a final temperature of 20 °C. This process causes the volume of the water to increase so that work *W *is done.

Assume that the change in internal energy is the same as in part (b).

Determine the work done, thermal energy supplied and the increase in internal energy of the water by completing **Table 1.2**, considering the first law of thermodynamics.

| Work done on water | thermal energy supplied to water | increase in internal energy of water |
|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
A table that would score 2 marks should look like this:

| Work done on water | thermal energy supplied to water | increase in internal energy of water |
|---|---|---|
| **Final answer:** **−W** | **Final answer:** **+W +ΔU** | **Final answer:** **+ΔU** |

- Work, *W* is done on the water to increase the volume, so the work done by the water = −*W* **AND**
- The change in internal energy = same as part (b) = *+*Δ*U*; **[1 mark]**

- Work done + thermal energy supplied = increase in internal energy

  - So −*W* + thermal energy supplied = +Δ*U*
  - Hence, thermal energy supplied = +*W* +Δ*U*;* ***[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
The average specific heat capacity of water between 10 °C and 20 °C compares with its average value between 0 °C and 10 °C:

- The change in thermal energy is higher; **[1 mark]**
- So the specific heat capacity is higher; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The change in thermal energy from 0 °C to 10 °C = +**q** *

> *The change in thermal energy from 10 °C to 20 °C = +**W **+Δ**U*

> *Hence, +W **+ΔU **> +**q** *

> *It can be easier to consider these values using the specific heat capacity equation:*

> *Δ**Q** = **mc**Δ**θ** *

> *So specific heat capacity, *$c=\frac{\DeltaQ}{m\Deltaθ}$

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A fixed mass of an ideal gas is initially at a temperature of 20 °C. The gas has a volume of 0.12 m^3 and a pressure of 0.6 × 10^5 Pa.

The gas undergoes three successive changes, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![16-1-2b-m-thermodynamics-cycle-of-change-grid-sq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/16-thermodynamics/16-2-the-first-law-of-thermodynamics/assets/001-16-1-2b-m-thermodynamics-cycle-of-change-grid-sq.png)

The initial state of the gas is represented by point X. The gas is cooled at constant pressure to point Y by the removal of 24.0 kJ of thermal energy.

The gas is then heated at constant volume to point Z.

Finally, the gas expands at constant temperature back to its original pressure and volume at point X. During the expansion, the gas does 15.8 kJ of work.

Calculate the magnitude of the work done in kJ during the change XY.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the work done in kJ during the change XY

List the known quantities:

- For X and Y pressure, *p *= 0.6 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- For X, volume, *V*<sub>*X*</sub> = 0.12 m<sup>3</sup>
- For Y, volume, *V*<sub>*Y*</sub> = 0.04 m<sup>3</sup>

Use the work done on a gas equation:

- $W=p\DeltaV$ **[1 mark]**
- $W = p ( V_{X} - V_{Y} )$
- $W = ( 0.6 \times 10^{5} ) \times ( 0.12 - 0.04 )$
- $W=4800J=4.8\mathrm{kJ}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The gas undergoes three successive changes, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The initial state of the gas is represented by point X. The gas is cooled at constant pressure to point Y by the removal of 24.0 kJ of thermal energy. The gas is then heated at constant volume to point Z. Finally, the gas expands at constant temperature back to its original pressure and volume at point X. During the expansion, the gas does 15.8 kJ of work.
Calculate the magnitude of the work done in kJ during the change XY: W = pΔV = (0.6 × 10^5) × (0.12 − 0.04) = 4800 J = 4.8 kJ

Complete Table 1.1 to show the work done on the gas, the thermal energy supplied to the gas and the increase in internal energy of the gas, for each of the changes XY, YZ and ZX.

**Table 1.1**

| change | increase in internal energy of gas / kJ | thermal energy supplied to gas / kJ | work done on gas / kJ |
|---|---|---|---|
| XY |   | −24.0 |   |
| YZ |   |   |   |
| ZX |   |   | −15.8 |
parts.solutionMd:
**During XY**

- Work done on gas for XY = +4.8 kJ (from (b))
- Increase in internal energy Δ*U* = − 24 + 4.8 = −19.2 kJ calculated from the equation $\DeltaU=q+W$

**During YZ**

- Work done for YZ = 0 kJ (as there is no change in volume)
- Increase in internal energy Δ*U* =  +19.2 kJ because the total increase in internal energy of the system (XYZX) = 0
- Hence, thermal energy gained = 19.2 kJ

**During ZX**

- Work done for ZX = −15.8 kJ (given in table)
- Increase in internal energy = 0 kJ (temperature and state do not change along ZX so the system is not heated . For the isothermal expansion ZX, the internal energy does not change (Δ*U* = 0), so by $\DeltaU=q+W$, $q=-W=+15.8$ kJ — thermal energy is supplied to maintain constant temperature)
- Hence, thermal energy = 15.8 kJ

A correctly completed table should look like this:

| change | increase in internal energy of gas / kJ | thermal energy supplied to gas / kJ | work done on gas / kJ |
|---|---|---|---|
| XY | **Final answer:** **−19.2** | −24.0 | **Final answer:** **4.8** |
| YZ | **Final answer:** **19.2** | **Final answer:** **19.2** | **Final answer:** **0** |
| ZX | **Final answer:** **0** | **Final answer:** **15.8** | −15.8 |

- **1 mark for each correct row**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The curved line ZX is called an isotherm. It is common for you to be asked to recognise that, if temperature and state of an **ideal gas **do not change, the internal energy does not change. The particles of an ideal gas do not interact so the only internal energy is the sum of kinetic energies (i.e. temperature).*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a chamber containing 5.2 kg of a gas, with a 0.75 kg piston above the gas.

![thermodynamics-1ah-ib-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/16-thermodynamics/16-2-the-first-law-of-thermodynamics/assets/002-thermodynamics-1ah-ib-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

When the gas is supplied with 32.4 kJ of heat, the piston experiences an average upwards acceleration 3.5 m s<sup>−2</sup> over a distance of 12 cm.

Calculate the work done by the gas.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the work done by the gas:

List the known quantities:

- Heat supplied to gas, *q*  = 32.4 kJ
- Upwards acceleration, *a*  = 3.5 m s<sup>−2</sup>
- Mass of piston, *m*  = 0.75 kg
- Distance moved, *s*  = 12 cm = 0.12 m
- Acceleration of free fall, *g*  = 9.81 m s<sup>−2 </sup>(from the data page)

Apply Newton's second law:

- The resultant force, *F*<sub>*res*</sub> , on the piston is:

  - $F_{res}=ma$
- The gas exerts an upward force, *F*<sub>*res*</sub> , and the piston's weight, *mg* , acts downwards

  - $F_{res}=F_{gas}-mg$
- Combine the two equations

  - $F_{gas}-mg=ma$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the force from the gas:

- $F_{g} a s = m ( a + g ) = 0.75 ( 3.5 + 9.81 )$
- $F_{gas}=9.983N$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the work done, *W *:

- Recall that distance moved parallel to the force was 12 cm
- $W=F_{gas}s=9.983\times0.12$
- $W=1.2J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Work done pops up in a lot of different areas of physics - you may have gone to the first law of thermodynamics initially. This question, however, makes use of Newton's second law to find a resultant force and then calculate mechanical work.  Annotate the diagram, list your known quantities, and the method will become much clearer.*

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the frequency of the oscillation:

parts.problemMd:
A mass of 0.42 kg is attached to a spring and the system is made to oscillate with simple harmonic motion (SHM) on a horizontal, frictionless surface. The mass passes through the equilibrium position 200 times per minute.

The kinetic energy of the mass as it passes through the equilibrium position is 500 mJ. There are two points where the restoring force acting on the mass is at its maximum.

Show that the distance between these points is approximately 29 cm.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 0.42 kg
- Passes through equilibrium 200 minute<sup>–1</sup>
- Kinetic Energy at *x* = 0, $E_{k}$= 500 mJ = 0.5 J

Determine the time period of the mass:

- The mass passes through the equilibrium position twice in one time period

  - There are 100 complete oscillations per minute
- *T* = $\frac{1}{f}$where *f* = $\frac{100}{60}$ s<sup>-1</sup>
- *T* = $\frac{60}{100}$= 0.6 s **[1 mark]**

Determine the angular velocity of the mass:

- *ω *= $\frac{2π}{T}$= $\frac{2π}{0.6}$ = 10.472 rad s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Kinetic energy (and velocity) is maximum when displacement is zero:

- $E_{k}$=$\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>2</sup>
- $v_{max}=ωx_{0}$* * where *x*<sub>0</sub>  is amplitude
- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- 0.5 = $\frac{1}{2}$× 0.42 × (10.472)<sup>2 </sup>× *x*<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>

Rearrange for amplitude *x*<sub>0</sub> and substitute in the values:

- Amplitude, *x*<sub>0 </sub>=$\sqrt{ \frac{2 \\times 0.5}{0.42 \\times ( 10.472 )^{2}} }$ = 0.147 m = 14.7 cm **[1 mark]**

Calculate the distance:

- Distance between the two maxima is twice the amplitude
- *d *= 14.7 × 2 = 29.3 = 29 cm (2 sf) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *There are several useful formulae for the simple harmonic oscillation on the formula page. The equation *$v_{max}=ωx_{0}$* can be derived from:*

$v=\pmω\sqrt{x_{0}^{2}-x^{2}}$

> *by realising that speed is at a maximum at the equilibrium position, when **x**  is zero. Here, **x*<sub>*0*</sub>*  is maximum displacement (the amplitude).*

parts.solutionMd:
Derive equation for frequency of a pendulum:

- *f =*$\frac{1}{T}$* *=  $\frac{1}{2π}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$

Consider the effect of a stronger gravitational field:

- Period is independent of gravitational acceleration / there is no *g* term, so change in *g* will not affect frequency; **[1 mark]**

Consider the effect of 3 additional springs in parallel:

- 4 springs will require 4 times the force to extend the same distance, so <u>*k*</u><u> in this experiment is quadrupled</u> (× 4); **[1 mark]**
- Frequency is proportional to $\sqrt{k}$, so the <u>frequency is doubled</u>; **[1 mark]**

![6-2-s-q--q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-1-simple-harmonic-oscillations/assets/010-6-2-s-q-q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

(i) Label on the graph with the letter X a point where the speed of the pendulum is half that of its initial speed.

[1]

(ii) Calculate, in metres, the length of the thread, if the period *T*  is given by the equation:

$T=2π\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$

where *l*  is the pendulum length and *g*  is the acceleration of free fall.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To mark on the graph a point where velocity is half its initial value:

- Kinetic energy is proportional to velocity<sup>2</sup>
- If the velocity is halved, then the kinetic energy is a quarter of the initial $( \frac{1}{2} ^{2} )$
- Any point on the graph at 5 mJ marked; **[1 mark]**

![6-2-s-q--q5a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-1-simple-harmonic-oscillations/assets/011-6-2-s-q-q5a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

(ii) To calculate the length of the pendulum:

- From the graph, the time period is 2.25 s
- Acceleration of free fall, *g*  = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup> (from the data page)
- Period, $T=2π\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$
- Length, *l = *$\frac{T^{2}g}{4π^{2}}$*= *$\frac{( 2.25 )^{2} \\times 9.81}{4 \mathrm{\pi }^{2}}$* ***[1 mark]**
- *l = *1.26 m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Don't forget that kinetic energy reaches a maximum value **twice** in a single period, as the pendulum passes through the centre (maximum kinetic energy) from one side and then back again from the other. *

parts.solutionMd:

parts.solutionMd:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, $m$ = 20 g = 0.02 kg

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a mass-spring system which undergoes simple harmonic motion.

The mass of 75 g is connected between two identical springs. The mass-spring system rests on a frictionless surface. A force of 0.025 N is needed to compress or extend the spring by 1.0 mm.

The mass is pulled from its equilibrium position to the right by 0.055 m and then released. The mass oscillates about the equilibrium position in simple harmonic motion.

![9-1-hl-sq-medium-3a-mass-spring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-2-energy-in-simple-harmonic-motion/assets/007-9-1-hl-sq-medium-3a-mass-spring.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the acceleration of the mass at the moment of release.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the acceleration at the moment of release:

List the known quantities:

- Mass,* m*<sub>*m*</sub> = 75 g = 0.075 kg
- Force per mm, *F* = 0.025 N mm<sup>−1</sup>
- Amplitude of oscillations, $x_{0m}$ = 0.055 m = 55 mm

Determine the force required to pull the mass 0.055 m to the right:

- Force = force per mm × amplitude of oscillation
- F = 0.025 × 55 = 1.4 N per spring
- There are two springs so 2 × 1.4 N = 2.8 N

Calculate the acceleration at the moment of release:

- Rearrange *F* = *ma*
- *a *=* *$\frac{F}{m}$* = *$\frac{2.8}{0.075}$* *= 37 m s<sup>−2</sup> **[1 mark]**

Consider the direction of motion:

- Since *a* ∝ −$x$, *a* will be negative
- *a* = −37 m s<sup>−2 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

To estimate the maximum kinetic energy of the ion:

parts.problemMd:
The amplitude of the pendulum is 60 cm when it swings with a frequency of 0.7 Hz. During this oscillation, the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum is 23 J.

Determine the mass of the pendulum bob.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the mass of the pendulum bob:

List the known quantities:

- Amplitude, $A=x_{0}=60\mathrm{cm}=0.6m$
- Frequency, $f=0.7\mathrm{Hz}$
- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}=23J$

Recall the total energy equation and rearrange to solve for *m*:

- $E=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- $m=\frac{2E}{ω^{2}x_{0}^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the equation for angular velocity into the total energy equation:

- $ω=\frac{2π}{T}=2πf$
- $m = \frac{2 E}{( 2 \mathrm{\pi } f )^{2} x_{0}^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate mass:

- $E_{Kmax}=E$ **[1 mark]**
- $m = \frac{2 \\times 23}{( 2 \mathrm{\pi } \\times 0.7 )^{2} \\times ( 0.6 )^{2}}$
- $m=6.6\mathrm{kg}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The amplitude of the pendulum is 60 cm when it swings with a frequency of 0.7 Hz. During this oscillation, the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum is 23 J.
Determine the mass of the pendulum bob. (m = 6.6 kg)

Calculate the kinetic energy of the pendulum when the pendulum bob is at a distance of $0.4x_{0}$ from its point of maximum displacement.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the kinetic energy of the pendulum bob:

List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}=23J$ (from part (b))
- Amplitude, $A=x_{0}=0.6m$ (from part (a))
- Frequency, $f=0.7\mathrm{Hz}$ (from part (a))
- Mass of pendulum, $m=6.6\mathrm{kg}$ (from part (b))

Determine the displacement from the equilibrium position:

- The question states that the pendulum is $0.4x_{0}$ from its maximum displacement ![9-1-hl-mcq-m5-ms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-2-energy-in-simple-harmonic-motion/assets/023-9-1-hl-mcq-m5-ms.jpg)

  - Therefore, it is $0.6x_{0}$ from its equilibrium position **OR** $x=0.6\times0.6=0.36m$ **[1 mark]**

Using the kinetic energy equation to determine the kinetic energy at this displacement:

- $E_{K} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega ^{2} ( x_{0} ^{2} - x ^{2} ) = \frac{1}{2} m ( 2 pi f ) ^{2} ( x_{0} ^{2} - x ^{2} )$
- $E_{K} = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.6 \times ( 2 pi \times 0.7 ) ^{2} \times ( 0.6 ^{2} - 0.36 ^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{K}=14.72J$** [1 mark]**

**OR**

- $E_{K} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega ^{2} ( x_{0} ^{2} - x ^{2} ) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega ^{2} ( x_{0} ^{2} - ( 0.6 x_{0} ) ^{2} )$
- $E_{K} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega ^{2} x_{0} ^{2} ( 1 - 0.6 ^{2} ) = 23 ( 1 - 0.6 ^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

- $E_{K}=14.72J$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *We can use the total energy equation in this instance because we know the value of the maximum kinetic energy which is equal to the total energy of the system. Always choose equations based on the known quantities you are given (or can calculate from what you are given!)*

When the water is pushed down a distance *x*<sub>*max*</sub> on one side of the tube then the water on the opposite side rises. List the known quantities:

- Cross-sectional area of liquid = *A*
- Mass of liquid = *m*
- Density of liquid = *ρ*
- Volume of liquid = *V*
- Length of liquid column =* L*

Recall the equations for maximum kinetic energy *E*<sub>*k (max)*</sub>, volume *V* and density *ρ*:

- $E_{k} ( m a x ) = \frac{1}{2} m v_{m} a x ^{2}$ **AND**
- *V *= *AL* **AND**

Rearrange and substitute the equations for mass *m *and volume *V*:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ $\rightarrow$ $m=ρV$

- $E_{k} ( m a x ) = \frac{1}{2} ( \text{rho} A L ) v_{m} a x ^{2}$
