- Mass of liquid = *m*
- Density of liquid = *ρ*
- Volume of liquid = *V*
- Length of liquid =* L*

Obtain an expression in terms of cross-sectional area *A* and density *ρ* for the mass *m* of the liquid:

- *m *= *Vρ*
- Let *x*<sub>*max*</sub> be amplitude / maximum displacement of the oscillation above the equilibrium position where gravitational potential energy is gained
- So, *m *= *Ax*<sub>*max*</sub>*ρ ***[1 mark]**

Obtain an expression for gravitational potential energy *E*<sub>*p*</sub><sub> (max)</sub> in terms of cross-sectional area *A *and density of liquid *ρ*:

- At maximum displacement, the gravitational potential energy of the water is the energy needed to lift a section of the water a height *x*<sub>*max*</sub> above the equilibrium position = *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = *mgx*<sub>*max*</sub>
- *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = (*Ax*<sub>*max*</sub>*ρ*) × *gx*<sub>*max*</sub>
- *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = *Aρgx*<sub>*max*</sub><sup>*2*</sup><sup> </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Gravtiational potential energy is gained when the water is a height of **x*<sub>*max*</sub>* above the equilibrium position hence the equation for the mass of the water moving above this position contains **x*<sub>*max*</sub>*. The SHM equation for **v*<sub>*max*</sub>* is **v*<sub>*max*</sub>* = **ωA** where **A **is amplitude and not cross-sectional area. Don't let this confuse you! *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A U shaped tube with cross-sectional area A contains a liquid of mass m, density ρ and volume V as shown in Fig. 1.1. When the water of length L is in equilibrium in the tube the levels of water on either side are equal. When the water is pushed down a distance x_max on one side of the tube then the water on the opposite side rises. Upon release the water undergoes simple harmonic motion as the water levels on each side rise and fall about the equilibrium position.
E_k(max) = 1/2 ALρ(v_max)^2 (From part a)
E_p(max) = Aρg(x_max)^2 (From part b)

Show that the time period of the oscillation of the liquid in the U shaped tube of Fig. 1.1 is given by the equation

$T=2π\sqrt{\frac{l}{2g}}$
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- $E_{k} ( m a x ) = \frac{1}{2} A L \text{rho} v_{m} a x ^{2}$ (From part a))
- *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = *Aρgx*<sub>*max*</sub><sup>*2 *</sup>(From part b))

Combine the expressions and rearrange to get an expression for $\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}$:

- $\frac{1}{2}ALρv_{max}^{2}=Aρgx_{max}^{2}$
- $\frac{v_{max}^{2}}{x_{max}^{2}}=\frac{2Aρg}{ALρ}$
- $\frac{v_{max}^{2}}{x_{max}^{2}}=\frac{2g}{L}$
- $\frac{v_{max}}{x_{max}}=\sqrt{\frac{2g}{L}}$
- $\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for *v*<sub>*max*</sub> to substitute in for *ω*:

- Recall: *v*<sub>*max *</sub>= *ωx*<sub>*max *</sub>(for amplitude *x*<sub>*max*</sub>)
- $ω=\frac{v_{max}}{x_{max}}$ $\rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{ω}=\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}$
- $\frac{1}{ω}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation for angular velocity, *ω *in terms of time period *T *and obtain the required equation:

- Recall: $ω=\frac{2π}{T}$
- So, $\frac{1}{ω}=\frac{T}{2π}$
- $\frac{T}{2π}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $T=2π\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You do not need to know this equation for your course, so don't learn it. These types of hard questions are common when they take you beyond the syllabus. *

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{k}$= 0.25 mJ (from part b)

Determine the equation for potential energy, $E_{P}$:

- The total energy of the system, $E_{T}$ = Kinetic energy,  $E_{k}$+ Potential energy $E_{P}$
- Therefore, $E_{P}=E_{T}-E_{K}$

  - When the kinetic energy is 0, the potential energy is at a maximum

Determine *v*  from the graph at *t* = 6 s:

- When$t$ = 6 s the velocity, $v$ = 0

  - This means $E_{k}$= 0 ![ma2d_oscillations_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-2-energy-in-simple-harmonic-motion/assets/004-ma2d-oscillations-ib-sl-physics-sq-medium.png)

- *v* = 0 at the maximum or minimum amplitude of the oscillation

- Therefore $E_{P}=E_{T}$ = 0.25 mJ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A mass of m = 50 g is attached to the mass-spring system. The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows the variation with time of the velocity of the block. Fig. 1.1. Determine the total energy of the system when it is oscillating with a mass of 50 g.
From the graph, v_max = 0.1 m s^–1. The total energy of the system is equal to the maximum kinetic energy: E_T = E_Kmax = 1/2 m v_max^2 = 1/2 × 0.05 × (0.1)^2 = 0.25 mJ. Time period T = 4 s (from graph).

The mass-spring system is now fixed so the mass and spring oscillate vertically. The mass remains at 50 g and the angular velocity and time period the same as before.

Show that the total energy of the system is still the same as in part (b).
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m *= 50 g = 0.05 kg
- Total energy of system in part b), *E*<sub>*T*</sub> = 0.25 mJ
- Time period of oscillation, *T *= 4 s (from part b)
- *v*<sub>*max*</sub> = 0.1 m s<sup>−1</sup> (From part b)

Determine the angular velocity of the oscillation, *ω*:

- Recall: $ω=\frac{2π}{T}$
- $ω=\frac{2π}{4}=\frac{π}{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the amplitude of oscillation, *x*<sub>*0*</sub>:

- Recall: $v_{max} = ω x_{0}$
- $x_{0}=\frac{0.1}{\frac{π}{2}}=0.06366m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total energy of the system, *E*<sub>*T*</sub>:

- Recall: $E_{T}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- $E_{T} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \\times 0.05 \\times ( \frac{\mathrm{\pi }}{2} )^{2} \\times 0.06366^{2} = 2.5 \\times 10^{- 4} = 0.25 \text{mJ}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *For a vertical mass-spring system, measuring displacement from the equilibrium position means gravitational potential energy is already accounted for. The total energy is still *`E_{T} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} \left(x_{0}\right)^{2}`* where *$x_{0}$* is measured from equilibrium.*

parts.problemMd: Define the term *damping*.
parts.solutionMd:
Damping is...

- The reduction in the <u>energy</u> and <u>amplitude</u> of oscillations;** [1 mark]**
- Due to the <u>resistive forces</u> acting on the oscillating system; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain how damping affects the amplitude of an oscillating object.
parts.solutionMd:
Damping affects the amplitude of an oscillating object because...

- The <u>resistive forces</u> (such as friction or air resistance) act to <u>oppose the motion</u> of the oscillator;** [1 mark]**
- <u>Energy is transferred away</u> from the oscillating system; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the amplitude decreases; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *When answering an 'explain' question, make sure you use either 'because', 'due to' or 'therefore' in your answer to ensure you fully answer the question.*

> *Another way to phrase this answer would be:*

> *Damping reduces the amplitude of an oscillation [1 mark] due to the resistive force opposing the motion of the oscillator [1 mark] which transfer energy away from the system [1 mark].*

> *The trick with revising something like this is to find one or two examples which make sense to you, and just learn those. You will never need a long list in an exam.*

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the vertical oscillations of the mass–spring system shown in Fig. 1.1.

![6-3-s-q--q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-3-damped-and-forced-oscillations-resonance/assets/001-6-3-s-q-q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The system is suspended from one end of a thread passing over a pulley. The other end of the thread is tied to a weight. The system is shown in Fig. 1.1 with the mass at the equilibrium position, denoted by the fiducial mark. The spring constant is the same for each spring.

The table below shows the measurements recorded by the student over the course of 5 repeats of the experiment.

**Table 1.1**

| **Time for 40 oscillations of the mass-spring system / s** |   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 45.8 | 44.6 | 45.6 | 45.8 | 45.2 |

Determine the natural frequency of the mass-spring system and the percentage uncertainty in the data. Hence quote the natural frequency with its uncertainty to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the mean time period, *T*:

- Sum of times = 45.8 + 44.6 + 45.6 + 45.8 + 45.2 = 227
- Mean time for 40 oscillations, 40*T* =$\frac{227}{5}$ = 45.4 s
- Mean time period, *T* =$\frac{45.4}{40}$ = 1.135 s **[1 mark]**

Calculate the natural frequency:

- There is no driving force, so the natural frequency is $f_{0}$  =$\frac{1}{T}$
- Natural frequency, $f_{0}$ = $\frac{1}{1.135}$  = 0.881 Hz **[1 mark]**

Determine the percentage uncertainty in the data:

- For a set of data, the uncertainty = ± half of the range
- Uncertainty in data, Δ(40*T*) = $\frac{45.8-44.6}{2}$ = 0.6 s
- Percentage uncertainty = $\frac{\Delta ( 40 T ) }{40 T}$ × 100%
- Percentage uncertainty = $\frac{0.6}{45.4}$ × 100% = 1.3 % **[1 mark]**

Calculate the uncertainty in natural frequency and quote the final answer to 3 s.f:

- $\frac{\Deltaf_{0}}{f_{0}}$ =$\frac{\DeltaT}{T}$
- Δ$f_{0}$ = $f_{0}$  ×$\frac{\DeltaT}{T}$
- Uncertainty in natural frequency, Δ$f_{0}$ = 0.881 × $\frac{0.6}{45.4}$ = 0.012 Hz
- Therefore, $f_{0}$ = 0.881 ± 0.012 Hz (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It is easy to get confused when combining uncertainties in formulae, especially when we have the reciprocal of period here.*

> *In this equation:*

$\mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{time}}$

> *the percentage uncertainty of speed is simply the sum of the percentage uncertainties of distance and time.*

> *For the equation in this question:*

$f=\frac{1}{T}$

> *we are combining the percentage uncertainty of time period and the number 1. Obviously, the number 1 has no uncertainty so the percentage uncertainty of frequency is just 0 + the percentage uncertainty of period - this is why we can say:*

$\frac{Δf}{f}=\frac{ΔT}{T}$

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the new resonant frequency:

parts.problemMd:
A bar magnet is suspended on a spring as shown in Fig. 1.1. A pole of the magnet is located near to one end of a solenoid.

![6-3-s-q--q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-3-damped-and-forced-oscillations-resonance/assets/006-6-3-s-q-q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The observations made are summarised in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Supply** | **Observation** |
|---|---|
| Direct current (d.c.) | 1. The magnet moves vertically |
| Alternating current (a.c.) | 2. The magnet oscillates |
| 3. When the frequency of the alternating current (a.c) is changed, the amplitude of vibration of the magnet is associated with the applied frequency |   |

Explain these observations.
parts.solutionMd:
Why the magnet moves vertically when subjected to a direct current:

Any **two** from:

- When a d.c. supply is switched on, the solenoid produces a magnetic field; **[1 mark]**
- (Depending on the orientation of the bar magnet,) the magnetic field either attracts or repels the magnet; **[1 mark]**
- The magnetic field causes the magnet to move either towards or away from the solenoid; **[1 mark]**

Why the magnet oscillates when subjected to an alternating current:

Any **two** from:

- When a.c. passes through the solenoid, an <u>alternating</u> magnetic field is produced; **[1 mark]**
- The alternating magnetic field alternately attracts and repels the magnet; **[1 mark]**
- The alternating magnetic field causes the magnet to periodically move towards and away from the solenoid, hence oscillations occur; **[1 mark]**

Why the amplitude is associated with the applied frequency:

Any **two** from:

- The magnet undergoes <u>forced oscillations</u> as a result of the a.c. passing through the solenoid; **[1 mark]**
- The amplitude varies with the applied frequency of the driving oscillations; **[1 mark]**
- Frequency of magnet oscillations originate from the frequency of the alternating current supply; **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
An electric field does 3.6 × 10<sup>–17</sup> J of work on the negative ion to accelerate it through a distance of 75 mm.

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the electric force acting on the negative ion:

List the known quantities:

- Work done on the ion, *W* = 3.6 × 10<sup>–17</sup> J
- Displacement (in the direction of the force), *d* = 75 mm = 75 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m

Use the equation for work done to calculate force:

- Work done:  $W=Fd\RightarrowF=\frac{W}{d}$ **[1 mark]**
- Electric force:  $F=\frac{3.6\times10^{-17}}{75\times10^{-3}}$ = 4.8 × 10<sup>–16</sup> N<sup>  </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An electric field does 3.6 × 10^–17^ J of work on the negative ion to accelerate it through a distance of 75 mm. Show that the electric force acting on the negative ion is 4.8 × 10^–16^ N.

The magnitude of the electric field strength is 1.5 × 10<sup>3</sup> N C<sup>−1</sup>.

(i) Calculate the charge on the ion.

[2]

(ii) Deduce the number of electrons gained by the atom.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the charge on the ion:

List the known quantities:

- Electric force, $F$ = 4.8 × 10<sup>–16</sup> N (from part c)
- Electric field strength, $E$ = 1.5 × 10<sup>3</sup> N C<sup>−1</sup>

Use the equation for electric force on a charge:

- Electric force on a charge:  $F=qE\Rightarrowq=\frac{F}{E}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $q=\frac{4.8\times10^{-16}}{1.5\times10^{3}}$
- Charge on ion:  $q$ = (−)3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C **[1 mark]**

(ii) Deduce the number of electrons gained by the atom:

- Elementary charge, e = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C (from data page)
- The charge on one electron is 1e
- Therefore, the atom gained = $\frac{3.2\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}$ = 2 electrons; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration of the electron is:

List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength, *E* = 2.5 pN C<sup>–1</sup> =  2.5 × 10<sup>–12</sup> N C<sup>–1</sup>

From the formulae page:

- Rest mass of electron, *m*<sub>e</sub> = 9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup> kg
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

State the equations for the electric force:

- $F=qE=ma$

Rearrange for the acceleration, *a*:

- $a=\frac{qE}{m}$ ** [1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $a = \frac{ ( 1.60 \times 10^{ - } 19 ) \times ( 2.5 \times 10^{ - } 12 ) }{9.11 \times 10^{ - } 31}$ ** [1 mark]**
- $a=0.439=0.44ms^{-2}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

Fig 1.1 shows an electron in a uniform electric field. State the direction in which the electron will accelerate in the field and explain why this happens. The direction in which the electron accelerates is to the right.
The strength of the electric field is 2.5 pN C^–1^. Calculate the acceleration of the electron through the field. From the formulae page: Rest mass of electron, m_e = 9.11 × 10^–31 kg; Elementary charge, e = 1.60 × 10^–19 C. F = qE = ma; a = qE/m; a = 0.44 m s^–2.

Explain how the acceleration changes if a proton is accelerated instead.
parts.solutionMd:
If a proton is accelerated instead:

- The size of the acceleration would be smaller / lower **AND **it would be to the <u>left</u> / the opposite direction (to the electron's acceleration); **[1 mark]**
- Because the magnitude of charge is the same, but the mass is larger; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *We can see this from the equation *$a=\frac{qE}{m}$* in part (b). Since **E** and **q** are the same (it's the same field, and protons and electrons and electrons have the same magnitude of charge) then as **m** increases, **a** decreases. The mass of a proton is on the data page in your exam, and it's value is much higher than a mass of an electron!*

> *However, don't forget that they have **opposite** charges. Since acceleration is a vector, you must also mention the proton's **direction**.*

parts.problemMd:
The metal plates are 50 mm apart. When the switch is closed, the plates are charged by a 200 V dc supply, as shown in Fig 1.2.

![7-4-s-q--q3c-easy-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-2-uniform-electric-fields/assets/003-7-4-s-q-q3c-easy-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Calculate the electric field strength between the plates when the switch is closed.

State an appropriate unit for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the electric field strength between the plates:

List the known quantities:

- Potential difference between the plates, *V* = 200 V
- Separation between the plates, *d* = 50 mm = 50 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m

Use the equation for electric field strength:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{V}{d}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $E=\frac{200}{50\times10^{-3}}$* *
- Evaluate: * *$E$ = 4000 **[1 mark]**
- Unit:  V m<sup>–1 </sup>**OR**** **N C<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *There are two ways of calculating electric field strength, but it is important to understand the difference between them. *

> *The equation:*

$E=\frac{V}{d}$

> *is used to calculate the electric field strength between **parallel plates**, where **V** is the potential difference between the plates and **d** is the separation of the plates. This is a uniform field *

> *The equation: *

> $E=\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r^{2}}$*  *

> *is used to calculate the electric field strength around a **point charge**, where **Q** is the charge which produces the electric field and **r** is the distance between the charge producing the electric field to the point where the electric field strength is being calculated. This is a radial (a type of non-uniform) field.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A uniform electric field is produced between two charged parallel plates, A and B. A positively charged alpha particle enters the electric field and deflects, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

State and explain the effect on the deflection of the alpha particle when

(i) the potential difference applied between A and B is increased

[2]

(ii) the separation of A and B is increased.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Increasing the potential difference between the plates causes:

- A greater electric field strength / force (on the alpha particle); **[1 mark]**
- (Hence) a greater deflection; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Increasing the separation between the plates causes:

- A smaller electric field strength / force (on the alpha particle); **[1 mark]**
- (Hence) a smaller deflection; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *The stronger the electric field strength between the two parallel plates, the more a charged particle will deflect. The equation used to calculate the electric field strength, **E**, between two parallel charged plates is:*

$E=\frac{V}{d}$

> *where **V** is the voltage across the plates and **d** is the separation distance. *

> *From this equation, we can see that the electric field strength is inversely proportional to the distance between the plates *$( E \text{proportional} to \frac{1}{d} )$*. Therefore, if the distance between the charged plates **increases**, the electric field strength will **decrease**.*

The alpha particle is replaced by a beta particle. The separation of the plates and the potential difference applied across them is kept the same.

State and explain **two** properties of alpha and beta particles that can affect the amount these particles deflect in an electric field.
parts.solutionMd:
The properties of alpha and beta particles that can cause differences in deflections are:

**Final answer:** **Any two ****pairs from:**

- Charge; **[1 mark]**
- Opposite charges deflect in opposite directions **OR **the greater the charge, the greater the deflection **OR** alpha deflects more than beta due to greater charge; **[1 mark]**

- Mass; **[1 mark]**
- The greater the mass, the smaller the deflection **OR** alpha deflects less than beta due to larger mass; **[1 mark]**

- Speed; **[1 mark]**
- The greater the speed, the smaller the deflection; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The faster a charged particle enters the electric field, the smaller the deflection. This is because it will spend **less** **time** in the electric field. *

> *The **smaller** the potential difference applied between the charged parallel plates, the smaller the electric field strength. This is because electric field strength and potential difference are directly proportional *$( E = \frac{V}{d} )$*.*

> *This means that less force will be acting on a charged particle due to the electric field (since *$F=qE$*), and therefore less deflection.*

parts.problemMd: State Coulomb’s law.
parts.solutionMd:
Coulomb’s law states:

- The (electric) force between <u>two point charges</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Many definitions in A–level physics involve describing an equation in words. Remember that Coulomb’s law is equal to*

$F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$

> *Therefore, *$F\proptoQ_{1}Q_{2}$* (force is proportional to the product of the **two **charges) and *$F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$*  (force is inversely proportional to the square of their separation)*

parts.solutionMd:
A similarity between the force fields is:

- (Electric and gravitational) <u>forces</u> both follow an inverse square law with distance / $F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$; **[1 mark] ** **OR**

parts.problemMd:

An aluminium nucleus contains 13 protons.

The alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus are separated by a distance of 2.0 nm.

Calculate the electric force between the alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the electric force between the alpha and aluminium nuclei:

List the known quantities

- Distance between nuclei, *r* = 2.0 nm = 2.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from the data page)
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C (from the data page)
- Charge on alpha particle, *Q*<sub>*1*</sub> = 2*e* = 2 × (1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) C
- Charge on aluminium nucleus, *Q*<sub>*2*</sub> = 13*e* = 13 × (1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) C

Use Coulomb's law to calculate the electric force:

- Coulomb's law:  $F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $F = \frac{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) \times 2 \times 13 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{ - } 19 ) ^{2} }{( 2.0 \times 10^{ - } 9 ) ^{2} }$ **[1 mark]**
- Electric force:  $F$ = 1.5 × 10<sup>–9</sup> N **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
The answers in (a) give evidence for the existence of the strong nuclear force because:

- The force of <u>repulsion</u> is (much) greater than the force of <u>attraction</u>; **[1 mark]**

- To hold the nucleus together; **[1 mark]**

> *You can see from the numbers in part (a), **F*<sub>*E*</sub>* = 65 N (the force of **repulsion **between the protons) whilst **F*<sub>*G *</sub>*= 5.3 × 10*<sup>*–35*</sup>* N ) (the force of **attraction** between the protons). It wouldn't be enough to just say **F*<sub>*E*</sub>* > **F*<sub>*G*</sub>*, you must relate your answer to attractive and repulsive forces. *

> *Without the strong nuclear force, we wouldn't have nuclei (and therefore wouldn't exist!) since the electrostatic repulsion between protons would mean they could never be close together. Since neutrons are neutral (no charge) there are no electrostatic forces between them.*

parts.problemMd:
Two charged objects X and Y are made to circle a point O. X and Y are at a distance, *d* = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m and they have equal masses, where *m* = 1.7 × 10<sup>−9</sup> kg as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The objects carry an equal but opposite charge, where the magnitude *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C.

![dae17afb-852e-4b5a-8723-1796e5ba2bd7-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-3-electric-force-between-point-charges/assets/001-dae17afb-852e-4b5a-8723-1796e5ba2bd7-1.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the acceleration of X and Y.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Distance, *d* = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m
- Mass*, m* = 1.7 × 10<sup>−9</sup> kg
- Charge, *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Gravitational constant, *G* = 6.67 × 10<sup>−11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>−2</sup>
- Permittivity of free space, *ε*<sub>*o*</sub> = 8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup> C<sup>2</sup> N<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−2</sup>

Deduce an expression for the resultant force:

- X and Y are in a circular motion around O
- The forces which hold the particle in motion are gravity and the Coulomb force
- Resultant centripetal force, $F_{R}=F_{g}+F_{c}$

  - Where *F*<sub>*R*</sub> = resultant force, *F*<sub>*g*</sub> = force due to gravity, *F*<sub>*c*</sub> = Coulomb force

Find *F*<sub>*g*</sub>, the force due to gravity:

- $F_{g}=G\frac{Mm}{r^{2}}$
- Therefore $F_{g}=(6.67\times10^{-11})\times\frac{(1.7\times10^{-9})^{2}}{(1.8\times10^{-8})^{2}}=5.950\times10^{-13}N$ **[1 mark]**

Find *F*<sub>*c*</sub>, the Coulomb force by combining the equations for Coulomb's law and Coulomb's constant:

- $F_{c}=\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Therefore $F_{c}=\frac{(3.2\times10^{-19})^{2}}{4π\times(8.85\times10^{-12})\times(1.8\times10^{-8})^{2}}=2.842\times10^{-12}N$ **[1 mark]**

Add the forces to find the resultant and use *F = ma* to find acceleration:

- $F_{R}=ma$
- Therefore, $a=\frac{(F_{g}+F_{c})}{m}$
- Therefore $a=\frac{(5.950\times10^{-13})+(2.842\times10^{-12})}{(1.7\times10^{-9})}=2.022\times10^{-3}$
- *a* = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup> (2 s.f.); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In many situations gravity can be taken as negligible, however in this situation the particles are close enough together that gravity plays a part.*

> *An alternative method to find the time period would use the equation  *$F_{R}=mω^{2}r$*, which introduces one extra step but still ends at the same place and same answer.*

> *Once the force has been found, acceleration can be obtained from circular motion equations.*

> *Finally, the last equation can be found two ways, either by deriving as suggested in the solution above, or, using quick dimensional analysis as a reminder. Notice that angular velocity is measured in 'per seconds', therefore time period must be, in effect, 'per angular velocity'.*

parts.problemMd: State the formula for the electric field strength $E$ at the surface of the sphere and state the meaning of any other symbols used.
parts.solutionMd:
The formula for electric field strength at the surface of the sphere is:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The formula for electric field strength at the surface of the sphere is: E = Q/(4πε₀r²) Where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space, Q is the charge on the sphere, and r is the radius of the sphere.

The field strength at the surface of sphere A is 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>, and the field strength at the surface of sphere B is 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>.

The magnitude of the charge stored on the surface of sphere B is 7.5 µC.

(i) Show that the radius of sphere B is about 7 cm.

[2]

(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the charge stored on the surface of sphere A. Assume both spheres have an equal radius.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength at surface of A = 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Electric field strength at surface of B = 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Charge on surface of sphere B = 7.5 µC = 7.5 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from data page)

(i) Calculate the radius of sphere B:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Rearrange:  $r^{2}=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}E}\Rightarrowr=\sqrt{\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}E}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $r_{B} = \sqrt{ \frac{( 8.99 \\times 10^{9 ) \\times ( 7.5 \\times 10^{-6} } )}{1.3 \\times 10^{3}} }$
- Radius of B:  $r_{B}$ = 7.2 cm ≈ 7 cm **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the charge stored on the surface of sphere A:

- If the spheres have the same radius, then $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ = constant for both A and B
- Therefore, $\frac{E_{A}}{E_{B}}=\frac{Q_{A}}{Q_{B}}$
- The ratio of the field strengths is $\frac{E_{A}}{E_{B}}=\frac{2.6\times10^{3}}{1.3\times10^{3}}=2$ **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, $\frac{E_{A}}{E_{B}}=\frac{Q_{A}}{Q_{B}}=2$
- So, the charge on the surface of A is $Q_{A}=7.5\times2=15\mathrm{μC}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Notice that the field strength has been given in V cm*<sup>*–1*</sup>*, and the answer to (i) is required in cm. Look out for units in questions like this so you don't waste time converting units when you don't need to! *

> *In part (ii), if you are confident using ratios, you will be able to obtain the relationship between field strength and charge quickly and this can save a lot of time compared to carrying out two sets of calculations!*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Sphere X is a small conducting sphere that carries a charge of +2.0 × 10^−9^ C. This charge may be assumed to act as a point charge situated at the centre of sphere X. Coulomb constant, 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10^9 m F^–1. At 10 cm = 0.1 m: E = (8.99 × 10^9)(2.0 × 10^−9)/0.1^2 = 1800 V m^–1 (1.8 kV m^–1).

Sphere X is placed at a distance of 20 cm from sphere Y, which is identical to sphere X but carries a negative charge.

At the midpoint between the spheres X and Y:

(i) Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength

[2]

(ii) State the direction of the electric field.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength at the midpoint:

List the known quantities:

- Charge on sphere X, $Q_{X}$ = +2.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Charge on sphere Y, $Q_{Y}$ = –2.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Midpoint between spheres, $r$ = 10 cm
- Electric field strength at 10 cm = 1800 V m<sup>–1</sup> (from part b)

Add the field strengths to find the value at the midpoint:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Field at midpoint, $E=E_{X}+E_{Y}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E$ = 2 × 1800 = 3600 V m<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) The direction of the electric field at the midpoint is

- Towards sphere Y; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This is a simple question when you realise that the midpoint is 10 cm from both spheres, and they both have the same charge, so you simply need to use the value of field strength from the previous sub-part and multiply it by 2 to find the combined field strength due to both charges*

> *The easiest mistake to make with this question is to subtract E*<sub>*Y*</sub>* from E*<sub>*X*</sub>* as it carries a negative charge. However, remember that an electric field is understood by describing it as a region where a **positive charge** will be moved. Therefore, both charges would move a positive charge to the right (towards Y), hence the values add up and the overall field is **stronger**.*

- At the midpoint, the magnitude of the electric fields are equal and the directions are opposite **OR** at the midpoint, the overall electric field is $E=E_{X}-E_{X}=0$; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This question follows logically from the previous part, as now both spheres have the **same charge** and **repel **each other, so it makes sense that there must be a point between them where the electric field cancels out*

> *Remember that an electric field describes a region where a **positive charge** will be moved. Therefore, at the midpoint, both charges would move a positive charge to the right, but one would move it towards the midpoint and one would move it away from the midpoint, hence the values cancel out by the same amount*

parts.solutionMd:
The electric field strength the α-particle experiences is:

List the known quantities:

- Atomic number of the gold nucleus = 79
- Distance of closest approach, *r* = 0.75 × 10<sup>–14</sup> m

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>** OR **$\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

Determine the equation for the electric field strength of the gold nucleus, *E*:

- $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$

Determine *Q*, the charge of the gold nucleus:

- $Q = 79 e = 79 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{ - } 19 ) = 1.264 \times 10^{ - } 17 \mathrm{C}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the electric field equation:

- $E = \frac{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) \times ( 1.264 \times 10^{ - } 17 ) }{ ( 0.75 \times 10^{ - } 14 ) ^{2} }$ **[1 mark]**

> *Remember that the charge of a nucleus is just the total charge of the protons. Each proton has a charge, **e**, the elementary charge (the same charge as an electron, which makes atoms neutral). **Extract:**

An α-particle is moving directly towards a stationary gold nucleus (₇₉¹⁹⁷Au). The α-particle and the gold nucleus may be considered to be solid spheres with the charge and mass concentrated at the centre of each sphere. The α-particle approaches to 0.75 × 10⁻¹⁴ m from the gold nucleus where it is momentarily stationary. Calculate the electric field strength the α-particle experiences at the point.
E = 2.02 × 10²¹ V m⁻¹ (electric field strength due to gold nucleus, from part a)

Show that the gold nucleus experiences an electric field strength that is roughly 40 times less than the α–particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The gold nucleus experiences an electric field strength roughly 40 times less than the α–particle because:

List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength due to gold nucleus, *E*<sub>Au</sub> = 2.020153 × 10<sup>21</sup> V m<sup>–1</sup> (from part a)
- Distance of closest approach, *r* = 0.75 × 10<sup>–14</sup> m

From the formulae page:

- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

Determine the charge of the α–particle:

- An α–particle has 2 protons and 2 neutrons (helium nucleus)
- Therefore, it's charge *Q* = 2*e ***[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric field strength experienced by the gold nucleus (from the α–particle):

- $E_{\alpha } = \frac{2 e}{4 \mathrm{\pi } ϵ_{0} r^{2}} = \frac{( 8.99 \\times 10^{9 ) \\times 2 \\times ( 1.60 \\times 10^{-19} } )}{( 0.75 \\times 10^{- 14} )^{2}}$
- $E_{α}=5.11\times10^{19}Vm^{-1}$

Determine the ratio of the electric field strengths:

- $\frac{E_{Au}}{E_{α}} = \frac{2.02\times10^{21}}{5.11\times10^{19}}$ = 39.5 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *You must remember that the composition of an α-particle, which is the same as a helium nucleus (*${}_{2}^{4}{He}$*) is 2 protons and 2 neutrons.*

> *Remember **Q** in the electric field strength equation is the charge that is producing the field. The α-particle experiences the field of the gold nucleus, and vice versa. Since the α-particle has much less charge, it is expected that it will produce a much smaller electric field strength.*

parts.problemMd:
Two charges are separated by a distance of 23 cm, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![18-2-3c-m-point-charge-and-elec-field-sq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/005-18-2-3c-m-point-charge-and-elec-field-sq-cie-a-l.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the distance, in mm, from the −22.1 μC to the point between the two charges, where the resultant electric potential is zero:

List the known quantities:

- Separation, *r *= 23 cm = 0.23 m
- Charge 1, *Q*<sub>*1*</sub> = −22.1 μC =  −22.1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C
- Charge 2, *Q*<sub>*2*</sub> = +5.4 μC = 5.4 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C
- $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>−1</sup>

Draw a diagram of the situation:

![ddc09216-64df-473f-aa57-7fcb4f7bdc63](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/006-ddc09216-64df-473f-aa57-7fcb4f7bdc63.jpeg)

Use the equation for the electric potential to obtain an expression for the electric potential when it is zero:

- $V=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r}$
- Potential due to −22.1 μC charge is: $\frac{ ( - 22.1 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) x}$
- Potential due to +5.4 μC charge is: $\frac{ ( + 5.4 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) ( 0.23 - x ) }$
- So, $\frac{ ( - 22.1 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) x} + \frac{ ( + 5.4 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) ( 0.23 - x ) } = 0$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to obtain a value for *x*:

- $\frac{ ( - 22.1 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ x} = \frac{ ( - 5.4 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ ( 0.23 - x ) }$
- $( - 22.1 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) ( 0.23 - x ) = ( - 5.4 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) x$
- $( - 5.083 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) + ( 22.1 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) x = ( - 5.4 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) x$
- $( - 5.083 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) = ( - 2.75 \times 10^{ - } 5 ) x$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $x = \frac{ ( - 5.083 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) }{ ( - 2.75 \times 10^{ - } 5 ) } = 0.184 \mathrm{m} = 184 mm$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Electric potential is a scalar quantity, so the sum of the **resultant electric potential = 0**. In the method shown above the quantities from the question are substituted into the equation for electric potential. You could **rearrange and substitute at the end** too, sometimes it is easier to see a rearrangement with **numbers**. *

parts.problemMd:
Before the discovery of quarks, scientists speculated that the subatomic particles might be made up of smaller particles.

If an electron was made up of three smaller, identical particles with charge *q *which are brought in from an infinite distance to the vertices of an equilateral triangle, it would have the arrangement shown in Fig. 1.2.

![7-5-s-q--q3b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/014-7-5-s-q-q3b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Show that the work done in forming an electron consisting of three identical particles, as shown in Fig. 1.2, is:

$ΔW=\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{e^{2}}{3r}$

Where:

- The distance *r* is the radius of an electron which is 2.82 fm
- *e* is the charge of an electron
- $ε_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Length of side of equilateral triangle, *r* = 2.82 fm = 2.82 × 10<sup>-15</sup> m

From data sheet:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>-12</sup> F m<sup>-1</sup>
- Magnitude of the charge of an electron, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C

Determine size of charge of each particle, *q*:

- *q *= $\frac{1}{3}$*e ***[1 mark]**

Work done bringing second electron into the triangle, $\DeltaW_{2}$ :

- Work done, ∆*W* = *q*∆*V*
- Electric potential, *V* = $\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$
- ∆*V =*$V_{2}-V_{\infty}$* *– where $V_{2}$ is the electric potential at the second vertex due to the existing electron
- $\DeltaW_{2}$= $1 \frac{1}{3} e \\times ( \frac{1 \frac{1}{3} e}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{\epsilon }_{0} r} - 0 )$
- $\DeltaW_{2}$ = $\frac{\frac{e^{2}}{9}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric potential at the third vertex due to the other two electrons, $V_{3}$:

- $V_{3}$= 2 ×$\frac{q}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $V_{3}$ = $\frac{\frac{2}{3}e}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Work done bringing third electron into the triangle, $\DeltaW_{3}$:

- $\DeltaW_{3}$ = *q*($V_{3}-V_{\infty}$)
- $\DeltaW_{3}$ =$1 \frac{1}{3} e \\times ( \frac{ \frac{2}{3} e}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \mathrm{\epsilon }_{0} r} - 0 )$
- $\DeltaW_{3}$ =$\frac{\frac{2}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate total work done in forming the electron:

- $\DeltaW$ =  $\DeltaW_{2}+\DeltaW_{3}$
- $\DeltaW$ =  $\frac{\frac{1}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}+\frac{\frac{2}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{\frac{3}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{3e^{2}}{9r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{e^{2}}{3r}$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *To form the electron, we take each of the three charges from infinity and place them in the corners of the triangle.  When the first electron is brought from infinity to its position there is **no work done** as there are **no other charges**. *

> *When the second electron is brought from infinity into its position it has to do work against the repulsive force of the first electron. *

> *When the third electron is brought from infinity into its position it has to do work against the repulsive force of both the first and second electrons.*

A parallel plate capacitor X of capacitance 300 μF is fully charged to a potential difference of 8 V.

A parallel plate capacitor Y is placed in series with the parallel plate capacitor X. Capacitor Y has a capacitance of 200 µF.

Calculate the combined capacitance of capacitors X and Y in this arrangement.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Capacitance of capacitor X, *C*<sub>*X*</sub>* *= 300 µF
- Capacitance of capacitor Y, *C*<sub>*Y*</sub>* *= 200 µF

State the relationship between the capacitance of capacitors in series:

- $\frac{1}{C_{T}}=\frac{1}{C_{X}}+\frac{1}{C_{Y}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation:

- $\frac{1}{C_{T}}=\frac{1}{300}+\frac{1}{200}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to make total capacitance, *C*<sub>*T*</sub>  the subject:

- $\frac{1}{C_{T}}=\frac{1}{120}$
- $120=C_{T}$
- So, $C_{T}=120$ µF** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Three capacitors, each of capacitance 27 μF, are connected as shown in Fig. 1.1. [Fig 1.1: one 27 μF capacitor in series with a parallel combination of two 27 μF capacitors, between points P and Q]. From part (a): Capacitance of each capacitor, C = 27 × 10^−6 F; Capacitance across the parallel combination, C_P = 54 × 10^−6 F; total series capacitance = 18 μF.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the maximum safe potential difference that can be applied between points P and Q:

List the known quantities:

- Max p.d. across each capacitor = 4 V
- Capacitance of each capacitor, *C *= 27 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F (From part (a))
- Capacitance across the parallel combination, *C*<sub>*P*</sub> = 54 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F (From part (a))

Calculate the safe p.d. across the parallel combination:

- For components in series, the charge across each component is the same

  - Consider the single capacitor as component 1 and the parallel combination as component 2 in the circuit
  - Hence, *Q*<sub>*1*</sub> = *Q*<sub>*2*</sub>
- The total charge from P to Q = charge across the single capacitor

  - $Q_{1}=C_{1}V_{max}$
  - $Q_{1} = ( 27 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) \times 4$
  - $Q_{1}=1.08\times10^{-4}C$
- So, the p.d. across the parallel combination is:

  - `V _ 2 = Q _ 2 / C _ P = (( 1.08 x 10 ^ negative 4 ))/(( 54 x 10 ^ negative 6 )) = 2 V` **[1 mark]**

Calculate the p.d. across the series combination:

- p.d. in series combination = p.d. in parallel + p.d. across single
- p.d. in series combination = 2 + 4 = 6 V **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A healthy debate between two physics students concerns the equations for the energy stored by a capacitor.

A transcript of the debate is given below:** **

Student A: “The energy stored *E *by a capacitor is proportional to the potential difference *V*, because *E* = $\frac{1}{2}$*QV*.”

Student B: “Actually, the energy stored *E *by a capacitor is proportional to the *square* of the potential difference, *V*<sup>2</sup>, because *E *=$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>2</sup>.”

State and explain whether Student A or Student B is correct regarding the energy stored by a capacitor.

The equation for capacitance is: *C* = $\frac{Q}{V}$
parts.solutionMd:
State which student is correct:

- Student B is correct; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- When a capacitor is charging / discharging, *Q* <u>is not constant</u> **[1 mark]**
- Capacitance *C* is constant; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, it cannot be said that *E* ∝ *V ***OR** therefore it is only true that *E* ∝ *V*<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It’s important to note the distinction between the two equations for energy stored by a capacitor:*

> *E** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*QV** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>*2*</sup>*. *

> *As the capacitor charges, the potential difference across the capacitor plates **V** increases, such that the energy stored by the capacitor **E** increases. *

> *However, during this process, the charge stored **Q** is **also changing **– i.e., it is not constant. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that **E** ∝ **V** because **Q** is not constant. *

> *Whereas the equation **E** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>*2*</sup>* shows that **E** ∝ **V*<sup>*2*</sup>* for a **constant capacitance** **C**. Therefore, in this case, **Student B** is correct.*

parts.problemMd:
Dennis disconnects the circuit and increases the e.m.f. of the power supply by 50%.

He states that by doing this, the charge stored in the capacitor will increase by 50% and the energy stored in the capacitor will increase by 125%.

Justify Dennis’s statement with suitable calculations.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities algebraically:

- The initial potential difference across the capacitor, *V*
- The capacitance of the capacitor = *C*
- The initial charge stored by the capacitor,* Q = CV*
- The initial energy stored by the capacitor, *E = *$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>2</sup>

Write an expression for the new charge stored *Q’* at the new potential difference *V’*:

- *Q’* = *C × V’*

Write an expression for the new charge stored in terms of the old charge stored, *Q*:

- The new potential difference is 50% greater than the old potential difference, so *V’ *= 1.5V
- *Q’ = C × *(1.5*V*) = 1.5*CV = *1.5Q **[1 mark]**

Conclusion about charge stored:

- Dennis is correct / justified about the increase in charge stored **OR** this is an increase of 50% in charge stored; **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the new energy stored *E’* at the new potential difference *V’*:

- *E’* = ½ ×*C × *$V'^{2}$* *

Write an expression for the new energy stored in terms of the old potential difference, *V*:

- *E’* = ½ × *C × *(1.5*V*)<sup>2</sup>
- *E’* = ½ × *C × *2.25*V*<sup>2</sup> = 2.25 × ($\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>2</sup>) = 2.25 *E ***[1 mark]**

Conclusion about energy stored:

- Dennis is correct/justified about the increase in energy stored / this is an increase of 125% in energy stored (because it has increased from 100% to 225%); **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The technique used in this question – writing ‘new’ quantities in terms of ‘old’ quantities – is very commonly examined. It is powerful because you can directly see how different quantities change in response to proportional increases/decreases. *

> *Make sure you are comfortable with writing two equations in the form ‘old’ and ‘new’, identifying clearly which quantities have changed and which stay constant. For example, if the capacitance **C** stays constant, but the charge stored **Q** and the potential difference **V** changes, then:*

![7-6-s-q--3c--ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/19-capacitance/19-2-energy-stored-in-a-capacitor/assets/011-7-6-s-q-3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *New quantities might have risen by some percentage, like 25%, so for example: *

> *V’ = **1.25**V*

parts.problemMd:
The resistor, *R * in the experiment is fixed at a resistance of 100 Ω and the capacitor, *C  *has a capacitance of 25 μF and is discharging.

Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Resistance of resistor, *R *= 100 Ω
- Capacitance of capacitor, *C *= 25 μF

Convert the capacitance from μF to F:

- The metric multiplier micro μ means × 10<sup>-6</sup>
- So, 25 μF = 25 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the time constant equation to calculate the time constant, *τ*:

- Recall the time constant equation: *τ *= *RC ***[1 mark]**
- *τ *= 100 × (25 × 10<sup>−6</sup>) = 2.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Time constant, *τ  *= 0.24 ms
- Capacitance, *C*  = 78 × 10<sup>–9</sup> F

Convert the time constant from ms to s:

- 1 ms = 1 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s
- 0.24 ms = 0.24 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the time constant equation for the resistance, *R*:

- Recall the time constant equation: *τ* = *RC*
- $R=\frac{τ}{C}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Capacitance, *C* = 400 μF = 400 × 10<sup>–6</sup> F
- Resistance, *R* = 5 kΩ = 5000 Ω

Convert the units for capacitance from μF to F:

- μF = × 10<sup>–6</sup> F
- So, 400 μF = 400 × 10<sup>–6</sup> F **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

After becoming fully charged, a capacitor C is then discharged via a two-way switch, T, through a resistor R of resistance 5 kΩ. The capacitance of the capacitor when fully charged is 400 μF. This is shown in Fig. 1.1. Fig. 1.1. Calculate the time constant of the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1.

All other components are kept the same.

State and explain the effect this has on the time constant of the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1**.**
parts.solutionMd:
The effect on the time constant of the circuit will be:

- The time constant increases <u>by a factor of ten</u>; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- This is because the time constant is (directly) <u>proportional to</u> the resistance; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Being able to spot proportionalities and describe them is a crucial skill for A Level physics. *

> *Since the time constant  *$τ$*= **RC**, where **R**  is the resistance and **C** is the capacitance, then you should be able to see that *$τ$* ∝ **R**, if **C** is kept constant. This is the case in this question: but notice that the question specifies the resistance increases by **a factor of ten.** This is a cue to you to be as **quantitative** (numerical) in your answer as well. The time constant must therefore also increase by the same factor, because they are proportional. *

> *In this instance, simply saying ‘the time constant will increase’ **would not gain credit** as a full explanation. *

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The capacitor is connected to a 12.0 V power supply and two resistors P and Q are shown in Fig. 1.2. The resistance of P is 28 kΩ and the resistance of Q is 280 kΩ. The switch can be in either position A or position B. The switch is in position A so that the capacitor is fully charged. Use Fig. 1.1 to estimate the energy E stored in the capacitor.
The switch is now moved to position B. Show that the time constant of the discharge circuit is 4.2 s.

The fully charged capacitor in **(a) **stores energy $E$.

Determine the time $t$* *taken for the stored energy to decrease from $E$* *to $\frac{E}{4}$.

$t$* *= ......................................... s
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the time *t*aken for the stored energy to decrease from $E$* *to $\frac{E}{4}$:

List the known quantities:

- Time constant, $τ=4.2s$

Consider the relationship between *E *and *V*:

- Energy stored: $E=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$
- (Since $C$ is constant) $E\proptoV^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Obtain the value of *V *using the relationship:

- $\frac{E_{0}}{4}\propto\frac{V_{0}^{2}}{4}$
- $\sqrt{\frac{V_{0}^{2}}{4}}=\frac{V_{0}}{2}$

Use the capacitor discharge equation for *V*:

- $V=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$** [1 mark]**
- $\frac{V_{0}}{2}=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{4.2}}$
- $ln ( \frac{1}{2} ) = - \frac{t}{4.2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $t=4.2\times\mathrm{ln}2$
- $t=2.9s$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You must use the relationship *$E\proptoV^{2}$* because *$E=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$*. **C **is constant** because this is the **capacitance** of this capacitor. *

A second identical capacitor is connected in series with the first capacitor.

State and explain the change, if any, to the time constant of the discharge circuit.
parts.solutionMd:
When a second identical capacitor is connected in series to the first capacitor:

- The total capacitance of the circuit halves; **[1 mark]**
- The time constant also halves;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *For two identical capacitors in series, the total capacitance is equal to half of the value of each one, therefore:*

- *For one capacitor: **C*<sub>*T*</sub>* = **C*
- *For two capacitors (in series): **C*<sub>*T*</sub>* = ½**C*

> *The time constant is given by **τ** = **RC**, therefore:*

- *For one capacitor: **τ** = **RC*
- *For two capacitors (in series): **τ** = ½**RC*

parts.problemMd:
A 590 nF capacitor is charged fully from a 20 V battery. At time *t = *0 the capacitor begins to discharge through a resistor. When *t* = 15 s the energy remaining in the capacitor is one eighth of the energy it stored at 20 V.

Show that the potential difference across the capacitor when *t *= 15 s is around 7 V.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the potential difference across the capacitor:

List the known quantities:

- Initial voltage, $V_{1}$ = 20 V
- Final energy stored, $W_{2} = \frac{1}{8} W_{1}$

Recall the equation for the energy stored in a capacitor:

- $W = \frac{1}{2} C V^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the relation between energy stored and voltage:

- Energy stored:  $W \propto V^{2}$  **or ** $\frac{W_{2}}{W_{1}}$ =`\left(\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\right)^{2}` **[1 mark]**

Calculate the final voltage $V_{2}$ after *t* = 15 s:

- `\frac{W_{2}}{W_{1}} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\right)^{2}`
- $\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{8}}$
- $V_{2}$ =  $\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}} V_{1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{8}} \times 20 = 5 \sqrt{2}$ = 7.071 = 7.1 V (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- Decreasing the time-base will stretch the signal horizontally; **[1 mark]**
- This will increase the <u>resolution</u> of time measurements; **[1 mark]**

State how a greater resolution will affect the uncertainty in the measurement:

- A greater resolution will <u>reduce</u> (percentage) <u>*uncertainty*</u> in measurements of time **AND** this will <u>improve</u> the <u>accuracy</u> of determining the <u>time constan</u>t from the oscilloscope; **[1 mark]**

> *Decreasing** the time base means each square represents a smaller period of time. This is like 'zooming in' on the time line. If the time base is 0.5 ms, then the screen shows 5 ms. If the time base is 0.1 ms, the screen shows 1 ms and therefore is a greater **resolution**.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Pacemakers are devices used to deliver short electrical pulses to a patient who is suffering from a cardiac arrest. Fig. 1.1 shows a circuit that is used in such a pacemaker. The capacitor has a capacitance of 20 μF and is connected to a resistor of 220 kΩ. This is connected to a power supply of emf 4.0 kV, but upon changing a two-way switch, it forms a circuit with heart tissue. This has a resistance of 400 Ω.

Show that, when charging from 0 C, the time taken for the charge stored in the capacitor to reach 5.0 mC is approximately 0.3 s.

The equation for the charging of a capacitor is:

$x = x_{0} ( 1 - e^{ - } \frac{t}{R C} )$

where $x_{0}$ represents the maximum value of a given quantity.
parts.solutionMd:
List  the known quantities:

- Charge, *Q *= 5.0 mC = 5.0 × 10<sup>–3</sup> C
- Time, *t* = 0.3 s
- Maximum voltage, $V_{0}$= 4 kV = 4000 V
- Capacitance *C *= 20 μF = 20 × 10<sup>–6</sup> F

Calculate the time constant of the charging circuit:

- $τ = R C$
- $\text{tau} = ( 220 \times 10 ^{3} ) \times ( 20 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) = 4.4 \mathrm{s}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum charge:

- The maximum charge $Q_{0} = C V_{0}$
- $Q_{0}$= (20 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) × 4000 = 0.08 C **[1 mark]**

Rearrange charge equation for time, *t*:

- The charge stored on a charging capacitor, *Q*, is given by `Q = Q_{0} \left(1 - e^{- \frac{t}{R C}}\right)`
- $\frac{Q}{Q_{0}} = 1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$
- $e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} = 1 - \frac{Q}{Q_{0}}$
- $\ln ( e^{- \frac{t}{R C}} ) = \ln ( 1 - \frac{Q}{Q} _{0} )$
- $- \frac{t}{R C} = \ln ( 1 - \frac{Q}{Q} _{0} )$
- $t = - R C \ln ( 1 - \frac{Q}{Q} _{0} )$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute values into equation time *t* equation:

- $t = - 4.4 \times ln ( 1 - \frac{5.0 \times 10^{ - } 3}{0.08} )$ = 0.28 s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
State equation for the voltage *V* of a discharging capacitor:

- $V=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$

Write equations for the initial energy $E_{0}$ and final energy *E *stored in a discharging capacitor:

- Initial energy stored $E_{0}$*=*$\frac{1}{2}$* C*$( V_{0} ) ^{2}$ **AND**
- Final energy stored *E = *$\frac{1}{2}$*C*(*V*)<sup>2</sup> =$\frac{1}{2}$*C*($V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$)<sup>2 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Take the ratio of the two equations and simplify fully:

- $\frac{E}{E_{0}}$= $\frac{ \text{begin display style} \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} e^{ - } \text{begin display style} \frac{t}{R C} ) ^{2} }{ \text{begin display style} \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} ) ^{2} }$

Simplify equations fully:

- $\frac{E}{E_{0}}$= $\frac{\frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} ) ^{2} e^{ - } \frac{2 t}{R C}}{\frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} ) ^{2} }$  = $e^{-\frac{2t}{RC}}$ **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Remember when raising a power in an exponential expression, the new power is found by **multiplying** the two powers together. E.g  (x*<sup>*a*</sup>*)*<sup>*b*</sup>* = x*<sup>*ab*</sup>* therefore for exponentials, (e*<sup>*x*</sup>*)*<sup>*2*</sup>* = e*<sup>*2x*</sup>*.*

parts.solutionMd:
The angle which would result in the largest force being exerted on the conductor is:

- *θ* = 90° **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *The equation to calculate the size of the force, **F**, on the conductor is: *

> *         F** = **BIL** sin**(θ**) *

> *The magnetic flux density of the magnetic field, **B**, current flowing through the conductor, **I**, and the length of the conductor, **L**, are all constants. **θ** is the angle between the conductor and the **B** field. *

> *To achieve the largest value for the force acting on the conductor, **F**, sin** θ** need to be as large as possible. The largest value which sin **θ** can have is 1. *

> *To calculate the size of the angle **θ** you need to find the inverse sine of 1.** *

> *         θ** = sin*<sup>*–1*</sup>*(1) = 90 *

> *This means that when the conductor is at 90° (**perpendicular**) to the **B** field, the force exerted on it will be largest.*

Calculate the force acting on the conductor.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the force acting on the conductor:

List the known quantities and convert to SI units:

- Length of conductor, *L* = 1.2 m
- Current flowing in conductor, *I *= 0.85 A
- Magnetic flux density of B field, *B* = 70 mT = 70 × 10<sup>–3</sup> T
- Angle between conductor and B field, *θ* = 30<sup>o</sup>

Calculate the force acting on the conductor using the magnetic force equation:

- $F=BIL\mathrm{sin}θ$
- $F=(70\times10^{--3})\times0.85\times1.2\times\mathrm{sin}(30)$ **[1 mark]**
- *F* = 0.0357 = 0.036 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This is a topic where there will be some very small numbers (such as the mT in this question) and very large ones. Make sure you always replace prefixes with the correct power of ten before you start calculating.*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a wire of length 15 cm and mass 30 g which has a current of 2.0 A flowing through it. When the wire is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field it 'floats' in equilibrium in the magnetic field.

![q3c-figure-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-2-force-on-a-current-carrying-conductor/assets/007-q3c-figure-1.png)

Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the wire when it is carrying current.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the wire when it is carrying current:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the wire, *m* = 30 g = 0.03 kg
- Acceleration of free fall,* g* = 9.81 m s<sup>–2</sup> (from the data page)

For a wire 'floating' in equilibrium in a magnetic field:

- The magnetic force *F* = weight of the wire *W*

Calculate the weight of the wire, W:

- $W=mg=0.03\times9.81$
- *W* = 0.2943 = 0.29 N **[1 mark]**

Determine the size of the force holding the wire in equilibrium:

- When the wire is in equilibrium,* F *= 0.29 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Using Fleming’s left–hand rule you can determine that the force acting on the wire due to the magnetic field acts **upwards**.*

> *As we are told that the wire ‘floats’ in equilibrium (i.e. it is not moving), then the **downwards** force of the weight must equal the **upwards** force produced by the magnetic field.*

![4fc8adae-01f8-46c7-94d5-73f87759d6bd](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-2-force-on-a-current-carrying-conductor/assets/008-4fc8adae-01f8-46c7-94d5-73f87759d6bd.jpeg)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows a wire of length 15 cm and mass 30 g which has a current of 2.0 A flowing through it. When the wire is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field it 'floats' in equilibrium in the magnetic field. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the wire when it is carrying current.
For a wire 'floating' in equilibrium in a magnetic field: The magnetic force F = weight of the wire W. W = m g = 0.03 × 9.81 = 0.2943 N. When the wire is in equilibrium, F = 0.29 N.

Calculate the magnetic flux density required to keep the wire ‘floating’ in equilibrium.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnetic flux density:

List the known quantities:

- Force acting on wire due to magnetic field, *F *= 0.2943 N (from part c)
- Current flowing through wire, *I *= 2.0 A (from part c)
- Length of wire in magnetic field, *L* = 15 cm = 0.15 m (from part c)

Recall the magnetic force equation and rearrange for *B*:

- $F=BIL\mathrm{sin}θ$
- The wire and field are perpendicular, hence, *sin θ* = 1
- $F=BIL\RightarrowB=\frac{F}{IL}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the magnetic flux density, *B*:

- $B=\frac{0.2943}{2.0\times0.15}$
- *B* = 0.98 T **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The section of wire shown in the diagram has a length of 85 mm, a diameter of 1.1 mm, and a current of 0.42 A.

Copper contains 8.4 × 10<sup>28</sup> free electrons per cubic metre.

Show that there are about 7 × 10<sup>21</sup> free electrons in this section of the wire.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that there are about 7 × 10<sup>21</sup> free electrons in this section of the wire:

List the known quantities:

- Electron density of copper = 8.4 × 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>−3</sup>
- Length of section, *L* = 85 mm = 85 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m
- Diameter of wire, *d* = 1.1 mm = 1.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m

Calculate the volume of the section of the wire:

- Volume of a cylinder:  $V = π r^{2} L$ (area of a circle × length)
- $V = \mathrm{\pi } \\times ( \frac{1.1 \\times 10^{- 3} }{2} )^{2} \\times ( 85 \\times 10^{- 3} ) = 8.078 \\times 10^{- 8} \mathrm{m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of free electrons in the section of wire:

- Number of free electrons = electron density × volume **[1 mark]**
- Number of free electrons = `\left(8 . 4 \times 10^{28}\right) \times \left(8 . 078 \times 10^{- 8}\right) = 6 . 8 \times 10^{21} = 7 \times 10^{21}` **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *When you have a 'show that' question, remember that you must finish with the value given in the question. This will usually involve rounding to less significant figures that you ordinarily would.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The section of wire shown in the diagram has a length of 85 mm, a diameter of 1.1 mm, and a current of 0.42 A.
Number of free electrons in the section of wire = 6.8 × 10^21 (from part c, shown to be about 7 × 10^21).

The average magnetic force acting on one electron is 5.5 × 10<sup>−24</sup> N.

Use your answer from part (c) to determine the magnetic flux density of the magnetic field.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the magnetic flux density:

List the known quantities:

- Force on each electron, *F* = 5.5 × 10<sup>−24</sup> N
- Number of free electrons in the section of wire, *n* = 6.8 × 10<sup>21</sup> (from part c)
- Current, $I$ = 0.42 A
- Length of wire section, *L* = 85 mm = 85 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m

Recall the magnetic flux density equation and rearrange for flux density, B:

- $F=BIL\RightarrowB=\frac{F}{IL}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the net force acting on the wire:

- In the section of wire, *n* electrons each experience a force *F*
- Therefore, the net force is $n F = ( 6.8 \times 10^{21} ) \times ( 5.5 \times 10^{ - } 24 )$

Substitute in the known values to calculate *B*:

- $B = \frac{ ( 6.8 \times 10^{21} ) \times ( 5.5 \times 10^{ - } 24 ) }{0.42 \times ( 85 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) }$** [1 mark]**
- $B = 1.0 \mathrm{T} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

(ii) An electron enters the magnetic field at point A, as shown in Fig. 1.3.

On Fig. 1.3, draw

**1.**  an arrow on the electron to show the direction of the force

**2.**  the path of the electron through the magnetic field

![q4b-figure-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/012-q4b-figure-1.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The magnetic field is acting:

- Into the page; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The force and motion of the electron are as follows:

**1.** The force on the electron

![4b-mark-scheme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/013-4b-mark-scheme.png)

- Arrow perpendicular to electron beam; **[1 mark]**
- Pointing downwards; **[1 mark]**

**2.** The motion of the electron

![4d-mark-scheme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/014-4d-mark-scheme.png)

- Moves in a circular arc; **[1 mark]**
- Leaves the field pointing downwards; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *We can use Fleming’s left–hand rule to determine the direction of the force acting on the electron, however, as we have an isolated charge the second finger gives the direction of the **velocity** of a **positive** charge.*

> *As we have a **negatively-charged** electron we reverse the direction of the velocity*

- *The second finger (motion) will point to the left (since the electron, or negative charge, is moving to the right)*
- *The first finger (field) points into the page*
- *Hence the thumb (force) will point downwards*

> *When the electron is in the magnetic field the force acting on it will be perpendicular to the direction in which it is moving. This causes the electron to move in a **circular path**.*

> *The force exerted on the electron from the magnetic field will point towards the centre of the circular path, hence in this example, the circular arc is directed downwards*

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Use the equations from **(c)** to derive the equation for radius:

- Magnetic force on a charge:  $F=Bqv$
- Centripetal force:  $F=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$

Equate the two expressions of force:

- Equate:  $Bqv=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ **[1 mark]**
- Rearrange:  $r=\frac{mv^{2}}{Bqv}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation from part (i):

- $r=\frac{mv}{Bq}$
- $r = \frac{ ( 9.11 \times 10^{ - } 31 ) \times ( 3.0 \times 10^{6} ) }{ ( 3.2 \times 10^{ - } 3 ) \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{ - } 19 ) }$ **[1 mark]**
- $r$ = 5.3 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A thin slice of conducting material has its faces PQRS and VWXY normal to a uniform magnetic field of flux density *B*, as shown in Fig. 6.1.

![q6-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/006-q6-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 6.1**

Electrons enter the slice at right angles to face SRXY.

A potential difference, the Hall voltage *V*<sub>H</sub>, is produced between two faces of the slice.

(i) Use letters from Fig. 6.1 to identify the two faces between which the Hall voltage is produced.

.......................................... and .......................................... [1]

(ii) State and explain which of the two faces named in** (a)(i)** is the more positive.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Consider the position of the magnetic field in relation to the current:

- The hall voltage states that the magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the current

Therefore the two faces between which the Hall voltage is produced are:

- PSVY <u>and</u> QRWX; **[1 mark]**

![file-000-50](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/007-file-000-50.png)

(ii) Consider the deflection of an electron in the field:

- An electron moving in the magnetic field will be deflected towards face QRXW; **[1 mark]**
- Hence, the negative electrons will build up and create an overall surplus negative charge
- (On the other face PSVY, there will be a surplus of positive charge) so PSVY is more positive; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *In part (i) **draw** lines on the **diagram **to identify the faces perpendicular to the current and parallel to the magnetic field*

  - *Don't be fooled by** PQRS** this face is **parallel **to the current*

- *In part (ii) consider Fleming's Left-Hand Rule:*

  - *The magnetic field is represented by the first finger and acts down the page*
  - *The current is represented by the second finger and acts across the page to the right in the opposite direction to the electron flow*
  - *The thumb represents the subsequent motion of the electrons which will move into the page and toward face QRWX*

parts.problemMd:
A proton of mass *m* and electric charge *q* enters a region of magnetic field at point P and exits at point Q, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The speed of the proton at P is *v. *The path followed by the proton is a quarter of a circle.

![q1_magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/001-q1-magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents-ib-sl-p.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State whether the speed *v* is the same, more than, or less than, the speed of the proton at Q. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The speed of the proton is:

- The <u>same</u> (at P and Q); **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- The magnetic force is always at right angles / perpendicular to the velocity; **[1 mark]**

**EITHER**

- The velocity (of the proton) changes only in direction; **[1 mark]**
- The speed / magnitude of the velocity (of the proton) does not change; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force (i.e. the radius of the circular path);
- The radius does not change, so, no work is done (by the magnetic force on the charge); **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the kinetic energy, and hence speed (of the proton) does not change; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *To get full marks in this question you must either consider one of two explanations 1. vectors, or 2. energy*

> *Explanation 1 (vectors) is arguably the easier route as you only need to consider the difference between velocity and speed in circular motion*

> *Explanation 2 (energy) is a little more involved, but thinking in terms of energy might suit the way your brain works better, so go for this one if it makes more sense to you. Here we need to consider the work done on the charge while it is in the magnetic field. We're only interested in the displacement in the **direction** of the force. Since the path of the proton is circular, the force is directed towards the centre of the circle, so a change in displacement would be equivalent to a change in **radius**. Always link this back to the kinetic energy, since the work done is simply equal to the **change** in kinetic energy. If no work is done, then there is no change in kinetic energy i.e. it remains constant.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A proton of mass *m* and electric charge *q* enters a region of magnetic field at point P and exits at point Q, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The speed of the proton at P is *v.* The path followed by the proton is a quarter of a circle.

Show that the radius of the circular path is given by

$R=\frac{mv}{qB}$

where *B* is the magnetic flux density.
parts.solutionMd:
State the equations for centripetal force and the magnetic force on a moving charge:

- Centripetal force: * *$F=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$
- Force on a moving charge:  $F=qvB\mathrm{sin}θ$

Determine the value of sin *θ*:

- The proton is moving at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field, so *θ* = 90⁰
- So, sin 90° = 1, hence $F=qvB$ **[1 mark]**

Equate the magnetic and centripetal forces:

- Since the magnetic force is the force that keeps the proton moving in a circle, this is equal to its centripetal force
- $F=\frac{mv^{2}}{R}=qvB$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make radius *R* the subject and simplify:

- $mv^{2}=RqvB$
- $\frac{mv^{2}}{qvB}=R$
- $\frac{m v^{ \cancel{2} } }{q \cancel{v} B} = R$
- $R=\frac{mv}{qB}$* ***[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This is a very common derivation that you will be expected to know. *

parts.solutionMd:
Show that the radius of the path is 16 cm:

List the known quantities:

- Magnetic flux density, *B* = 0.21 T

From the data page:

- Rest mass of proton, *m*<sub>*p*</sub> = 1.67 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg

Substitute and calculate the value of *R*:

- So, *R *= 0.159 m = 0.16 m = 16 cm **[1 mark]**** **

If you are stuck on where to start, have a look at the previous subparts. These are more often than not linked and guiding you through the question!*

![q3b_magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/004-q3b-magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents-ib-sl-.png)

An electron enters the region between the plates with a speed of 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>and experiences zero net force as it travels through to the other side.

(i) State the direction of the magnetic field

[1]

(ii) Determine the magnitude of the magnetic field.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State the direction of the magnetic field:

![q3b-magnetic-effects-of-electric-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/005-q3b-magnetic-effects-of-electric-ma.png)

- For the net force to be zero, the magnetic force F<sub>B</sub> must act in the opposite direction to the electric force F<sub>E</sub>
- The negatively charged electron will be attracted to the positively charged (top) plate
- Therefore, the magnetic force will be directed downwards / towards the negative (bottom) plate; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the magnitude of the magnetic field:

List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength, *E* = 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N C<sup>–1</sup>
- Speed of electron, *v *= 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>

Recall the equation for the force on a charge in an electric field:

- Electric force: * *$E=\frac{F_{E}}{q}\RightarrowF_{E}=Eq$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric force on the electron:

- *F*<sub>E</sub>* *= (2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup>) × (1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup>)
- *F*<sub>E</sub>* *= 4.16 × 10<sup>–16</sup> N **[1 mark]**
- The magnitude of the magnetic and electric forces are the same, i.e. *F*<sub>B</sub> = *F*<sub>E</sub>

Recall the equation for the force on a moving charge in a magnetic field:

- Magnetic force:  $F_{B}=qvB\mathrm{sin}θ$
- The motion of the electron and the magnetic field are perpendicular, so sin 90° = 1
- Therefore, $F_{B}=qvB$* ***[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation and calculate magnetic flux density, *B*:

- $F_{B}=qvB\RightarrowB=\frac{F_{B}}{qv}$
- $B=\frac{4.16\times10^{-16}}{(1.6\times10^{-19})\times(3.0\times10^{5})}=8.7\times10^{-3}T$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]*** *

> *The tricky part of this question is realising that the quantity given 2.6 × 10*<sup>*3*</sup>* N C*<sup>*–1*</sup>* is the equivalent to *$\frac{F}{q}$* for the electric field. Look first at the units N C*<sup>*–1*</sup>*, so it must be *$\frac{\mathrm{Force}}{\mathrm{Charge}}$*.*

**Fig. 1.1**

It is suggested that *E* is related to *x* by the relationship

$E=IZe^{-kx}$

where *I* is the current in coil P, and *k* and *Z* are constants.

Plan a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between *E* and *x*.

Draw a diagram showing the arrangement of your equipment.

Explain how the results could be used to determine values for *k* and *Z*.

In your plan you should include:

•    the procedure to be followed

•    the measurements to be taken

•    the analysis of the data
