parts.solutionMd:
Plan a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between *E* and *x*. Draw a diagram showing the arrangement of your equipment. Explain how the results could be used to determine values for *k* and *Z*.

**Each point from the list can score ****one mark**** up to a ****maximum of 15 marks**** (****but read the guidance below in blue****):**

***Defining the problem:***

- *x *is the independent variable and *E *is the dependent variable **OR**** **vary *x *and measure *E*; **[1 mark]**
- The r.m.s current $I_{rms}$ / peak current $I_{0}$* *in coil P is the <u>control variable;</u> **[1 mark]**

***Methods of data collection:***

- A diagram of the apparatus that includes labels for coils P, Q and distance *x* **AND** coils P and Q supported by a stand; **[1 mark]**

- Circuit diagram 1: an a.c. power supply / signal generator connected to coil P in series with an ammeter **AND**
- Circuit diagram 2: a voltmeter / CRO connected to coil Q; **[1 mark]**

- A method to determine *x *e.g. use a ruler to measure the distance *x *between the coils; **[1 mark]**
- A method to measure *x *from the <u>centre</u> of the two coils e.g. measure the width of each coil and divide by 2, then add to the separation of the coils; **[1 mark]**

***Method of analysis:***

- Plot a graph of ln *E* against x; **[1 mark]**
- The gradient of the graph is −*k*; **[1 mark]**
- The y-intercept = ln *IZ*  **or ** $Z = e^{y} \text{short dash} i n t e r c e p \frac{t}{I}$; **[1 mark]**

***Additional detail including safety procedures:***

**Final answer:** **Any ****six ****from:**

- Do not touch the <u>hot</u> coil / use gloves to position the <u>hot</u> coil; **[1 mark]**
- Use a large current / a large number of turns / an iron core to produce a large magnetic field / induced e.m.f; **[1 mark]**
- Use a high frequency a.c. to produce a large induced e.m.f; **[1 mark]**
- Keep the number of <u>turns</u> on each coil <u>constant</u> / frequency of the a.c. <u>constant</u>; **[1 mark]**
- A method to check that the current is constant** **e.g. use a variable resistor to keep the ammeter reading constant; **[1 mark]**
- Take repeat measurements of *x *for <u>different</u> parts of the coil <u>and</u> take the average; **[1 mark]**
- A method to position the ruler horizontally to measure *x *as described e.g. use a spirit level; **[1 mark]**
- A method to keep the coils parallel e.g. adjust coil Q until the maximum reading is obtained; **[1 mark]**
- Taking logs of the given equation leads to ln *E* = −*k*x + ln (*IZ*); **[1 mark]**
- This relationship is valid if a straight line is produced when the graph of ln *E* against *x* is plotted; **[1 mark]**

**An example of an answer which would score 15 marks is:**** **

<u>Method</u>

1. Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram below **[1] [2]**. Use a ruler to measure the horizontal distance *x *between the two coils **[3]**.
2. The distance *x* must be measured from the centre of coil P to the centre of coil Q. This centre can be located by measuring the width of both coils, dividing by 2 and then *x* can be obtained by adding these half widths to the separation of the coils **[4]**. A spirit level should be used with a ruler to ensure *x *is measured horizontally** ****[5]****.**
3. The independent variable is* x *and the dependent variable is *E* **[6]**. The current in coil P, the number of turns on each coil and the frequency of the a.c. must be kept constant throughout **[7]**.
4. For different values of *x*, repeat measurements of *x *should be taken at different points on the coil and then calculate an average **[8]**.
5. Connect coil P to a high frequency a.c. to induce a large e.m.f which will in turn, generate a large magnetic field **[9]**** **and induce a current in coil Q.
6. To ensure the coils are parallel, adjust coil Q until the maximum reading is obtained **[10]**

![em-induction-experiment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-4-magnetic-fields-due-to-currents/assets/010-em-induction-experiment.png)

<u>Analysis:</u>

1. Plot a graph using the mean values of ln *E* against *x ***[11]**
2. Taking logs of the equation $E=IZe^{-kx}$ leads to $\mathrm{ln}E=-kx+\mathrm{ln}IZ$ **[12]**.** **This relationship is valid if a straight line is produced when the graph of ln *E* against *x* is plotted **[13]****.**
3. Comparing this to the equation of a straight line, y = mx + c

  - Gradient = −*k *
  - y-intercept = ln *IZ*
4. Determine a value for *k* using *k* = −gradient and *Z* using $Z = e^{y} \text{short dash} i n t e r c e p \frac{t}{I}$ **[14]**.

<u>Safety considerations:</u>

- The coils will get very hot, so gloves should be worn during handling **[15]**

parts.problemMd:
State Faraday's Law

(i) in words

[2]

(ii) as an equation, defining all the quantities.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states:

- The (magnitude of the) induced e.m.f. is (directly) proportional to the rate; **[1 mark]**
- of change of magnetic flux linkage; **[1 mark]** ** **

(ii) Faraday's law is defined by the equation

- $\text{epsilon} = \frac{\Delta ( N \text{capital phi} ) }{\Delta t}$ **[1 mark]**
- Where $ε$ = induced e.m.f., $\Delta ( N \text{capital phi} )$ = change in magnetic flux linkage and $\Deltat$ = time interval of change; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It’s crucial that you remember an emf is only induced if there is a **change** in magnetic flux linkage. *

> *How quickly this quantity changes (i.e., the **rate **of change of magnetic flux linkage) determines the magnitude of the induced emf. *

parts.problemMd:

Use the words below to complete the description of Lenz's law

| **attracts ** | **opposes** | **density** |
|---|---|---|
| **direction** | **linkage** | **magnitude** |

The _________ of an induced emf is always set up in a way such that it  ________ the change in magnetic flux ___________ that causes it.
parts.solutionMd:
The correct sentence is:

- The **direction** of an induced emf; **[1 mark]**
- is always set up in a way such that it **opposes**; **[1 mark]**
- the change in magnetic flux **linkage** that causes it; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks] **

> *Stating Lenz’s law in words comes up quite often in examinations, make sure you can describe it in terms of the **direction** of the induced emf*

> *The induced emf is always set up in such a way that the effect is to try and **stop**, or **oppose**, whatever is inducing it. This is a consequence of **conservation of energy** (i.e., electromagnetic energy cannot be created for free!).   *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(ii) Faraday's law is defined by the equation \$\$\epsilon = \frac{\Delta \left(N \Phi\right)}{\Delta t}\$\$ Where \$\$\epsilon\$\$ = induced e.m.f., \$\$\Delta \left(N \Phi\right)\$\$ = change in magnetic flux linkage and \$\$\Delta t\$\$ = time interval of change

Rewrite the equation you wrote in **(a)(ii)** to include Lenz's law.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation including Lenz's law is:

- $\text{epsilon} = - \frac{\Delta ( N \text{capital phi} ) }{\Delta t}$
- Minus sign included; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Lenz’s law says the **direction** of the induced emf is set up to oppose the change causing it, which is encapsulated by the negative sign in the equation.*

> *This is similar to vectors, for example, if vector **a** and vector **b** are related by **a** = – **b**, this means they point in opposite directions. In this sense, the vectors ‘**oppose**’ each other, just like the induced emf **ε** opposes the changing flux linkage. *

> *If the magnet reverses from the coil, there **is** a change in magnetic flux linkage in the **opposite** direction to that initially observed in **Fig. 1.1b** – therefore the deflection on the voltmeter is in the opposite direction as the current is in the opposite direction.*

> *Notice the question says the magnet is removed **faster** than it entered, therefore, the **rate of change** of magnetic flux linkage is greater which means a larger induced e.m.f. and current (and larger deflection), as required by Faraday’s law.*

parts.solutionMd:
Recall Faraday’s Law and Lenz’s Law:

- Faraday’s Law states that the induced emf is <u>proportional</u> to the <u>rate</u> of change of magnetic flux linkage **AND**
- Lenz’s law states that the induced emf is set up in such a way that it <u>opposes</u> the change causing it; **[1 mark] **

Comment on the correct application of Faraday’s law:

- The student has correctly indicated an induced emf in the coil; **[1 mark]**

  - This is shown by the ammeter deflection
- The induced emf creates a south pole at the top of the coil / north pole at the bottom of the coil as the magnet approaches it; **[1 mark]**

Comment on the correct application of Lenz’s law:

- The student has correctly indicated a reversal of emf as <u>indicated by a reversed current on the ammeter</u>; **[1 mark]**

Comment on the corrections required using Faraday’s Law:

- The emf induced in the opposite direction should be greater than the initial induced emf **OR**
- The student's reversed deflection on the ammeter should be larger than the initial deflection; **[1 mark]**

Comment on the corrections required using Lenz’s Law:

- (As the magnet passes the centre of the coil) the induced emf should create a <u>south pole</u> at the bottom of the coil / a north pole at the top of the coil as the magnet falls through **OR**
- The direction of current round the coil should reverse once the magnet has passed through (in order to oppose the motion); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *Contexts in which you apply Faraday’s Law and Lenz’s Law tend to have a lot of subtleties and are regularly examined, so make sure you carefully consider what happens at each stage of the magnet’s descent. *

parts.problemMd:
As part of an introductory lesson on electromagnetic induction, a physics teacher plans a series of experiments for her students to carry out.** **

In experiment 1, two metal rings A and B are dropped from the same height between two magnets, as shown in Fig. 1.1. They are identical, apart from a small slit cut in B as shown.

Apply Faraday’s law:

- Faraday’s law states that in a conductor, an emf is induced proportional to the rate of change of flux (linkage)
- As A and B descend, the flux linkage through both of them changes so an emf is induced in them both; **[1 mark]**
- Because A is a complete ring, the emf in it drives a current; **[1 mark]**

Apply Lenz’s law:

- Len’s law states that the induced emf is set up in a direction so as to oppose the change that caused it
- The emf is induced <u>in the same direction</u> in both A and B **AND** there is an <u>upward force on A</u> due to the induced current inside it; **[1 mark]**

Describe the motion of A and B:

- Both A and B <u>accelerate</u> (downward); **[1 mark]**

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- But A accelerates at a slower rate / the acceleration of A is less than B; **[1 mark]**
- The resultant force on A is smaller than B; **[1 mark]**
- Forces correctly labelled on a sketch as shown below (implying a smaller resultant force on A); **[1 mark]**

![7-9-s-q--q4a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-5-electromagnetic-induction/assets/018-7-9-s-q-q4a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**[Total: 5 marks]**** **

> *Any question involving a metal conductor in motion through a magnetic field should immediately trigger a reminder to you to state and apply both Faraday’s law and Lenz’s law. *

> *The crucial thing you should remember is that an emf is **always** induced if flux linkage changes, but a current is only driven to flow by that emf if the conductor is part of a **complete circuit. **This question interrogates that very fact: only one ring contains a flowing current, which then results in an upward force on it (the magnetic fields interact), opposing its weight force.*

parts.solutionMd:
Sketch the flux linkage-time graph:

- A <u>straight line</u> with <u>positive gradient</u> showing increasing flux linkage between $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ ;<sub> </sub>**[1 mark]**
- A <u>straight line</u> with <u>zero gradient</u> showing constant flux linkage between $t_{2}$ and $t_{3}$ ;<sub> </sub>**[1 mark]**
- A <u>straight line</u> with <u>negative gradient</u> showing decreasing flux linkage between $t_{3}$ and $t_{4}$ ;<sub> </sub>**[1 mark]**
- The gradient between *t*<sub>1</sub> and *t*<sub>2 </sub>should be the same magnitude as that between $t_{3}$ and $t_{4}$ ;<sub> </sub>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Linking the gradient of a flux linkage-time graph to the induced emf is very common in exams.*

- *Faraday’s law states the induced emf is the rate of change of flux linkage (i.e. the gradient of a flux linkage graph)*
- *Lenz' law states that the emf opposes the change inducing it*
- *This means the gradient of a flux linkage-time graph represents the **negative** magnitude of induced emf *

> *So, if emf is constant and **negative **then the gradient of the flux linkage graph is constant and **positive**.*

> *Some questions require you to determine the shape of the induced emf from a flux linkage graph (using the gradient). Others, like this one, give you the induced emf graph and require you to work ‘backwards’ to figure out the shape of the flux linkage-time graph. This is more tricky.*

parts.problemMd:
A generator produces an alternating voltage which can be described by the equation

$V = 150 \sin ( 200 \mathrm{\pi } t )$

where *V* is measured in volts and *t* is in seconds.

For this alternating voltage, determine

(i) the peak voltage,

[1]

(ii) the r.m.s. voltage,

[1]

(iii) the frequency.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Alternating voltage: $V = 150 \sin ( 200 \mathrm{\pi } t )$

(i) Determine the peak voltage:

- Alternating voltage:  $V=V_{0}\mathrm{sin}ωt$
- Hence, peak voltage, $V_{0}$ = 150 V** [1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the r.m.s. voltage:

- r.m.s. voltage:  $V_{rms}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
- r.m.s. voltage:  $V_{rms}=\frac{150}{\sqrt{2}}$ = 106 V** [1 mark]**

(iii) Determine the frequency:

- From $V=V_{0}\mathrm{sin}ωt$:  $ω=200π$
- Frequency:  $ω=2πf\Rightarrowf=\frac{ω}{2π}$
- Frequency:  $f=\frac{200π}{2π}$ = 100 Hz** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A generator produces an alternating voltage which can be described by the equation V = 150 sin(200πt) where V is measured in volts and t is in seconds. The peak voltage V₀ = 150 V and the r.m.s. voltage Vrms = 150/√2 = 106 V.

The alternating voltage is supplied across a 100 Ω resistor.

Calculate

(i) the peak current and hence the r.m.s. current in the resistor,

[2]

(ii) the mean power dissipated in the resistor,

[2]

(iii) the peak power dissipated in the resistor.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Peak voltage, $V_{0}$ = 150 V (from **(b)**)
- r.m.s. voltage, $V_{rms}$ = 106 V (from **(b)**)
- Resistance, R = 100 Ω

(i) Calculate the peak and r.m.s. current in the resistor:

- Peak current:  $V_{0}=I_{0}R\RightarrowI_{0}=\frac{V_{0}}{R}$
- Peak current:  $I_{0}=\frac{150}{100}$ = 1.5 A **[1 mark]**
- r.m.s. current:  $I_{rms}=\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
- r.m.s. current:  $I_{rms}=\frac{1.5}{\sqrt{2}}$ = 1.06 A **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the mean power dissipated in the resistor

- Mean power:  $\langle P = V_{r} m s I_{r} m s \rangle$
- Mean power:  $\langle P = 106 \\times 1.06 \rangle$ **[1 mark]**
- Mean power:  $\langle P = 112 \mathrm{W} \rangle$ **[1 mark]**

(iii) Calculate the peak power dissipated in the resistor:

- Peak power:  $\langle P_{0} = 2 \\times P \rangle$
- Peak power:  $P_{0}=2\times112$ **[1 mark]**
- Peak power:  $P_{0}=224W$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the correct capacitor to use for smoothing the output:

List the known quantities:

- Resistance, *R* = 3.6 k Ω = 3600 Ω
- Time interval between adjacent peaks, *t* = 40 ms = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s (from the graph)

- Capacitor 2, *C*<sub>*2*</sub> = 60 µF = 60 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F

Calculate the time constants for both capacitors:

- Time constant:  $T=RC$
- Capacitor 1:  $T_{1}=3600\times(360\times10^{-9})=1.3\times10^{-3}s$
- Capacitor 2:  $T_{2}=3600\times(60\times10^{-6})=0.216s$

Compare the time constants of the capacitors with the time between peaks:

- The time constant of capacitor 1, *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 1.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s, is <u>less than</u> the time interval, *t* = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s; **[1 mark]**

The circuit in Fig. 1.1 is then modified by two students. One student adds a single capacitor, as shown in Fig. 1.3. The other adds two capacitors in series, as shown in Fig. 1.4.

Compare the effects of each modification on the graph you drew on Fig. 1.2, when both circuits are completed to form full-wave rectifiers. Explain any differences.
parts.solutionMd:
Comparing the effects of each capacitor configuration on the output signal:

- The single capacitor <u>smooths</u> the peaks in the output voltage; **[1 mark]**
- The two capacitors <u>smooth</u> the peaks <u>less than</u> the single capacitor; **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) there are larger fluctuations / ripples in the output voltage with the two capacitors; **[1 mark]**

Explain the difference:

- Because capacitors in series have a <u>lower capacitance</u>; **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) the time constant is smaller; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Recall that capacitors in series have a combined capacitance according to the following equation:*

$\frac{1}{C_{tot}}=\frac{1}{C_{1}}+\frac{1}{C_{2}}$

> *This means total capacitance is less than the individual capacitance of either capacitor, i.e. adding capacitors in series reduces total capacitance. This means the time constant is smaller, so the capacitor system discharges faster and the output voltage dips more in between input peaks. *

[2]
parts.solutionMd:

(ii) To find the force applied to the spaceship:

parts.problemMd:
A heated filament and anode are placed in a vacuum, as shown in Fig 1.1. The anode has a gap through which electrons can pass.

![22-1-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-1-energy-and-momentum-of-a-photon/assets/001-22-1-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig 1.1**

A potential difference of 15 V is applied across the filament and anode.

An electron is then emitted from the heated filament with a speed of 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate its initial kinetic energy in electronvolts.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the kinetic energy in eV:

List the known quantities:

- Electron mass, *m*<sub>*e*</sub>  = 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg
- Speed of electron, *v*  = 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C

Calculate the kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> , in joules:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$
- $E_{k} = \frac{1}{2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{ - } 31 \times ( 1.5 \times 10^{6} ) ^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=1.02\times10^{-18}J$

Convert this to eV:

- $1 \mathrm{J} = ( \frac{1}{1.60 \times 10^{ - } 19} ) eV$
- $E_{k}=1.02\times10^{-18}J=\frac{1.02\times10^{-18}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=6.4\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *It can be easy to become confused when converting between eV and J. Just remember, you can only either divide or multiply by a factor of 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*.*

> *Going from J to eV, your value should increase a lot (so divide by the very small number, 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*).*

> *Going from eV to J, your value should decrease a lot (so multiply by the very small number, 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*).*

parts.problemMd:
Photon energy and photon momentum are related by the equation:

*E*<sup>*2*</sup> = (*pc)*<sup>*2*</sup> + (*mc*<sup>*2*</sup>)<sup>2</sup>

Derive from this equation the equation $p=\frac{h}{λ}$ for calculating the momentum of a photon.
parts.solutionMd:
Consider the mass of a photon, *m*:

- The mass of a photon *m *= 0
- So, *E*<sup>*2*</sup> = (*pc)*<sup>*2 *</sup>
- and *E *= *pc ***[1 mark]**

Substitute the equation for photon energy in terms of wavelength:

- $E=\frac{hc}{λ}$

parts.problemMd:
A laser sitting at rest on wheels that are free to move produces 5.00 × 10<sup>27</sup> photons. Each photon has a frequency 3.95 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.

Calculate the magnitude of the momentum in producing these photons on the laser.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Number of photons, *n *= 5.00 × 10<sup>27</sup>
- Frequency of each photon, *f *= 3.95 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz
- Planck's constant, *h *= 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s
- Speed of light in free-space, *c *= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Obtain an equation in terms of the momentum of *n *photons:

- $p=n\frac{hf}{c}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to calculate the momentum of *n *photons:

- $p = ( 5.00 \times 10^{27} ) \times \frac{ ( 6.63 \times 10^{ - } 34 ) \times ( 3.95 \times 10^{14} ) }{ ( 3.00 \times 10^{8} ) }$
- $p=4.365$ kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

**AND**

- This is equivalent to the backwards momentum of the laser; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> $p=\frac{hf}{c}$* is the equation for the momentum of **one** photon, multiply it by the number of photons to get the total momentum. Momentum is conserved, so the forward momentum of the photons is equal to the backwards momentum of the recoiling laser. This is a closed system, as the laser is free to move.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A certain metal with a work function of 2.2 eV is selected to create two parallel plates. These are connected in a circuit to a sensitive ammeter and a power source, such that a uniform electric field of 140 N C^–1^ exists between them. Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 255 nm is incident on plate B, such that photoelectrons are emitted from B and move towards A. The ammeter detects a photocurrent in the circuit.

Show that the maximum possible speed of the photoelectrons as they reach plate A is approximately 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Wavelength, *λ *= 255 nm = 255 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Distance between the plates, *d* = 25 mm = 25 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Electric field strength, *E* = 140 N C<sup>–1</sup>
- Work function,*ϕ* = 2.2 eV = 2.2 × (1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) = 3.5 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J

From the data sheet:

- Speed of light in a vacuum, *c = *3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Planck’s constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup> J s
- Magnitude of the charge of electron, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C
- Electron rest mass, $m_{e}$ = 9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup> kg

Calculate the energy available from incident light:

- *hf* = *h* × $\frac{c}{λ}$ = (6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × $( \frac{3 \\times 10^{8}{255 \\times 10^{-9} } } )$ = 7.8 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons released to the surface:

- *hf = ϕ* + $KE_{max}$ so $KE_{max}$ = *hf* – *ϕ*
- $KE_{max}$= (7.8 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) – (3.5 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) = 4.3 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the potential difference between the plates, *V*:

- The uniform electric field strength between parallel plates *E =*$\frac{V}{d}$
- The potential difference *V* = *E × d = *140 × (25 × 10<sup>­-3</sup>) = 3.5 V **[1 mark]**

Calculate the kinetic energy transferred due to the potential difference between the plates:

- The potential difference between the plates, *V* = $\frac{W}{e}$
- The work done on the photoelectrons contributes to their KE, so *W* = *KE* = *e × V*
- *KE* = (1.6 × 10<sup>­–19</sup>) × 3.5 = 5.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons reaching plate **A**:

- Total maximum $KE_{total}$  = $KE_{max}$ from incident photons + *KE* transferred from the potential difference
- Total maximum $KE_{total}$ = (4.3 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) + (5.6 × 10<sup>­–19</sup>) = 9.9 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum speed of photoelectrons:

- $KE_{total}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$*m*$( v_{m} a x ) ^{2}$
- 9.9 × 10<sup>–19  </sup>= $\frac{1}{2}$ × (9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup>) × $( v_{m} a x ) ^{2}$
- 19.8 × 10<sup>–19</sup> = (9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup>) × $( v_{m} a x ) ^{2}$
- $( v_{m} a x ) ^{2}$ = 2.17 × 10<sup>12</sup>
- $v_{max}$= $\sqrt{2.17\times10^{12}}$ = 1.474 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>= 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>(2 s. f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**** **

> *For the final mark, it doesn’t matter whether you substitute the values in before rearranging (as done in this mark scheme) or rearrange for  *$v_{max}$*before substituting, as long as you get the correct final answer.*

| 2.5 | 2.8 |
| 3.5 | 2.1 |

**Table 1.1**

Discuss whether the data in Table 1.1 is consistent with the de Broglie equation:

$λ=\frac{h}{mv}$
parts.solutionMd:
State the proportionality between wavelength and velocity:

- The de Broglie equation suggests that the wavelength *λ *is <u>inversely proportional</u> to the electron velocity *v*; **[1 mark]**
- If the wavelength is inversely proportional to velocity, then *λv = *constant, or $λ_{1}v_{1}$= $λ_{2}v_{2}$

Calculate the constant of proportionality:

- From the first row of Table 1.1, *λv = *(4.9 × 10<sup>–11</sup>) × (1.4 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 6.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup>
- From the second row of Table 1.1, *λv = *(2.8 × 10<sup>–11</sup>) × (2.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 7.0 × 10<sup>–4</sup>
- From the third row of Table 1.1, *λv = *(2.1 × 10<sup>–11</sup>) × (3.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 7.4 × 10<sup>–4</sup>
- All values correctly calculated; **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- The results support the de Broglie equation because the constant of proportionality between pairs of values for *λ* and *v*  is approximately equal (to 1 significant figure); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Demonstrating whether results from a table (or graph) are consistent with an equation are a common hard question in A-level Physics that is a similar method every time.*

- *If two variables are **proportional** to each other e.g. **a ∝  b** , then the fraction  *$\frac{a}{b}$* = constant*
- *You must then find the value of *$\frac{a}{b}$* for each value in the table, or graph, and see if the values are approximately equal (even just to 1 decimal place) *

- *If two variables are **inversely proportional** to each other e.g. **a ∝ *$\frac{1}{b}$* **, then **ab **= constant*
- *You must then find the value of **ab **for each value in the table, or graph, and see if the values are approximately equal (even just to 1 decimal place)*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An experiment to investigate how the de Broglie wavelength λ of an electron varies with its velocity v is carried out.

Discuss whether the data in Table 1.1 is consistent with the de Broglie equation: λ = h/(mv)

The experiment required electrons to travel at very high speeds. To achieve this, they were first accelerated through a very high voltage, *V*.

Show that the de Broglie wavelength *λ * of these electrons is related to the accelerating voltage *V*  by the expression:

*                     λ *∝ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$
parts.solutionMd:
Consider energy transfers for the electron:

- The energy transferred (or work done) *W* on a particle with charge *q* as it moves across a potential difference *V *is given by *W* = *qV*
- For an electron, *q* = *e* so the energy transferred by a potential difference is given by *eV*
- The energy is transferred is to the electron’s kinetic energy, $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- Therefore, $eV=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$<sup> </sup>**[1 mark]**

Substitute the de Broglie wavelength:

- de Broglie wavelength *λ* = $\frac{h}{mv}$, therefore *v* = $\frac{h}{λm}$
- Therefore, *eV  = *$\frac{1}{2}$*m*$( \frac{h}{ \lambda m} ) ^{2}$*= *$\frac{1}{2}$*m*$( \frac{h ^{2} }{ \lambda ^{2} m ^{2} } )$* *= $\frac{h^{2}}{2mλ^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Deduce the proportionality between *λ *and *V*:

- *eV * = $\frac{h^{2}}{2mλ^{2}}$
- *λ*<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{h^{2}}{2meV}$
- *λ =  h *$\sqrt{\frac{1}{2meV}}$* *therefore *λ *∝ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$ **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The Planck constant *h* is an important fundamental constant in quantum physics.

Determine the S.I. base units for *h*.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the S.I. base units for *h*:

- The units of *h* are usually stated as J s
- A Joule is defined as the energy required to exert a force of 1 N over 1 m, J → Nm
- Therefore the units of *h* can be given as N m s
- A Newton is defined as the force required to give a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s<sup>−2</sup>, N → kg m s<sup>−2</sup>
- Therefore the units of *h* can be given as kg m s<sup>−2</sup> m s **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, base unit = kg m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The key with dimensional analysis questions is to think about the definitions of the different non-base units, or related equations. Linking joules and newton metres can be done with the equation work done = force × distance, for example.*

parts.problemMd:
A researcher is investigating the de Broglie wavelength of charged particles. The charged particles are accelerated through a potential difference *V*.  The de Broglie wavelength *λ* of these particles is then determined by the researcher. Each particle has mass *m* and charge *q*.

Show that the de Broglie wavelength λ is given by the expression:

$λ^{2}=\frac{h^{2}}{2mq}\times\frac{1}{V}$
parts.solutionMd:
To show that the de Broglie wavelength $λ$ is given by the expression $λ^{2}=\frac{h^{2}}{2mq}\times\frac{1}{V}$:

Recall the de Broglie equation and square it:

- $λ=\frac{h}{mv}$ where *v* is the velocity of the particle
- $λ^{2}=\frac{h^{2}}{m^{2}v^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall that the particles are accelerated to a velocity *v*  by a potential:

- Kinetic energy, $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- Electrical potential energy, $E_{P}=qV$

  - Energy is transferred from the electrical potential energy store to the kinetic energy store
- $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=qV$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange this equation to give an expression for *v*<sup>2</sup> :

- $v^{2}=\frac{2qV}{m}$

Substitute this into the squared de Broglie equation:

- $\lambda ^{2} = \frac{h ^{2} }{m ^{2} ( \frac{2 q V}{m} ) }$

**AND**

- $λ^{2}=\frac{h^{2}}{2mqV}$ (this is the required equation) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Any time you see a 'show that' question like this, you are going to be assessed on how you present your algebra as well as whether you can reach the required expression. Don't skip steps! You can even annotate your working with what you are doing at each step, e.g. 'cancelling out the mass term in the denominator'. *

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the wavelength of radiation emitted when an electron falls from level *n* = 4 to the ground state in the hypothetical atom:

List the known quantities:

- Speed of light in free space, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Planck constant, *h *= 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s
- Electron energy at *n *= 4, *E*<sub>*4*</sub> = −7.65 eV
- Electron energy at *n *= 1, *E*<sub>*1*</sub> = −122.4 eV

Calculate the change in energy in J:

- $\DeltaE=E_{4}-E_{1}$
- $\Delta E = - 7.65 - ( - 122.4 ) = 114.75 eV$
- $\Delta E = 114. 75 \times ( 1.602 \times 10^{ - } 19 ) = 1.84 \times 10^{ - } 17 \mathrm{J}$ **[1 mark]**

Use Planck's equation to calculate the frequency of the emitted photon:

- $\DeltaE=hf$
- $f=\frac{\DeltaE}{h}=\frac{1.84\times10^{-17}}{6.63\times10^{-34}}$
- $f=2.78\times10^{16}\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the wave equation to calculate the wavelength of the radiation emitted during the change of state:

- $c=fλ$
- $λ=\frac{c}{f}=\frac{3\times10^{8}}{2.78\times10^{16}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $λ=1.08\times10^{-8}m$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

Calculate the kinetic energy of the ionised electron:

parts.problemMd:
An atom has a ground state energy of −8.80 eV. The complete line emission spectra for this atom is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![22-3-3b-m-emission-spectra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/003-22-3-3b-m-emission-spectra.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Sketch a diagram of the possible energy levels for the atomic line spectra shown in Fig 1.1. Label each energy level with the value of its energy.
parts.solutionMd:
Sketch a diagram of the possible energy levels for the atomic line spectra shown in Fig 1.1:

List the known quantities:

- Ground state energy of the atom = −8.80 eV
- Speed of light in free space, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Planck constant, *h *= 6.63 × 10<sup>−34 </sup>J s
- Shortest wavelength photon emitted, *λ*<sub>*a*</sub> = 267 nm = 267 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Middle wavelength photon emitted,  *λ*<sub>*b*</sub> = 325 nm = 325 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Longest wavelength photon emitted, *λ*<sub>*c*</sub> = 1500 nm = 1500 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m

Use the photoelectric equation to calculate the energy of *λ*<sub>*c*</sub>:

- $E=hf=\frac{hc}{λ}$
- $E_{c} = \frac{ ( 6.63 \times 10^{ - } 34 ) \times ( 3 \times 10^{8} ) }{1500 \times 10^{ - } 9} = 1.33 \times 10^{ - } 19 \mathrm{J}$
- In eV, this is $\frac{1.33\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=0.83\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the first energy level, n = 2:

- Ground state energy level n = 1, *E *= −8.8 eV
- First energy level = ground state + energy emitted in transition for *λ*<sub>*c*</sub>
- First energy level = −8.8 + 0.83 = −7.97 eV **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy of *λ*<sub>*b*</sub>:

- $E_{b} = \frac{ ( 6.63 \times 10^{ - } 34 ) \times ( 3 \times 10^{8} ) }{325 \times 10^{ - } 9} = 6.12 \times 10^{ - } 19 \mathrm{J}$
- In eV, this is $\frac{6.12\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=3.83\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the second energy level, n = 3:

- Second energy level = first energy level + energy emitted in transition for *λ*<sub>*b*</sub>
- Second energy level = −7.97 + 3.83 = −4.14 eV **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy of *λ*<sub>*a*</sub>:

- $E_{a} = \frac{ ( 6.63 \times 10^{ - } 34 ) \times ( 3 \times 10^{8} ) }{267 \times 10^{ - } 9} = 7.46 \times 10^{ - } 19 \mathrm{J}$
- In eV, this is $\frac{7.46\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=4.66\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Check your calculations at the end by calculating the value of the transition from n = 1 to n = 3:

- Ground state energy + energy of *λ*<sub>*a*</sub> = energy level at n = 3 = −8.8 + 4.66 = −4.14 eV
- This is equal to the two transition energies *λ*<sub>*b*</sub> + *λ*<sub>*c*</sub> = 3.83 + 0.83 = 4.66 eV

parts.problemMd:
Unstable nuclei can decay in a variety of ways.

Electron capture is one such process, during which the nucleus ‘captures’ an orbiting inner-shell electron. The resulting nucleus has one less proton and one more neutron. Sometimes this process is accompanied by the emission of a characteristic X-ray photon, as illustrated in Fig. 1.1.

![2-5-s-q--q1a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/010-2-5-s-q-q1a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Explain why an X-ray photon is produced in this process and suggest why it is called ‘characteristic’.
parts.solutionMd:
X-ray photon emission:

- An <u>outer electron</u> / electron in a <u>higher energy state</u> replaces the missing electron (which has been absorbed by the nucleus); **[1 mark]**
- This transition to a <u>lower energy state</u> releases an X-ray photon **OR** the electron <u>de-excites</u> and energy is released in the form of an X-ray photon; **[1 mark]**

Characteristic X-ray photon:

- The X-ray photon is characteristic because its energy is <u>equal to the difference in energy levels</u> (of the transiting electron); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Notice the very specific language around higher and lower energy and energy states, and the understanding that a photon is emitted whenever an electron moves from a higher to lower energy state/level. Remember to be really clear about the fact that the photon energy is exactly equal to the difference in energy levels.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Electron capture is one such process, during which the nucleus 'captures' an orbiting inner-shell electron. The resulting nucleus has one less proton and one more neutron. Sometimes this process is accompanied by the emission of a characteristic X-ray photon, as illustrated in Fig. 1.1.

The Auger Effect is a process that sometimes accompanies that illustrated in Fig. 1.1. This process involves the emission of an electron – called an Auger electron – from the atom when a core electron is removed, leaving a vacancy. This is illustrated in Fig. 1.2.

![2-5-s-q--q1b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/011-2-5-s-q-q1b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

This emission occurs if sufficient X-ray energy is transferred to outer shell electrons during the process.

Show that the speed of a typical Auger electron is around 22% of the speed of light, stating any assumptions you make in your calculation.

(Typical X-ray wavelength is ~ 10<sup>–10 </sup>m).
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- X-ray photon wavelength, *λ* = 1 × 10<sup>-10</sup> m

From data page:

- Planck constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup> J s
- Speed of light in free space, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Rest mass of an electron, *m = *9*.*11 × 10<sup>–31</sup> kg

Calculate the frequency of a typical X-ray photon:

- Wave speed, *c = fλ*
- 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> = *f* × (1 × 10<sup>–10</sup>)
- *f = *3 × 10<sup>18</sup> Hz **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy of a typical X-ray photon:

- *E = hf*
- *E* = (6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × 3 × 10<sup>18</sup> = 1.99 × 10<sup>–15</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the speed of the Auger electron:

- If the energy of the photon is absorbed as kinetic energy of the Auger electron, then *E = hf = *$\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>2</sup>
- 1.99 × 10<sup>–15</sup> = 0.5 × (9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup>) × *v*<sup>2</sup>
- *v  = *$\sqrt{\frac{2\times1.99\times10^{-15}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}}$*=* 6*.*6 × 10<sup>7</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Speed as a fraction of *c*:

- $\frac{6.6\times10^{7}}{3\times10^{8}}$ × 100 = 22% the speed of light; **[1 mark]**

Assumption:

- This calculation assumes that all the energy from the X-ray photon is absorbed by the electron

**OR**

- There is a 1:1 interaction between photons and electrons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Auger electrons tend to have very high energies. At such high energies, their wave-like nature can be used to investigate the structure of crystalline solids.

When a beam of high-energy electrons is sent through a regularly spaced array of crystal atoms, they form a diffraction pattern of concentric bright and dark rings on a fluorescent screen, as shown in Fig. 1.3.

![2-5-s-q--q1c-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/012-2-5-s-q-q1c-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

It can be shown that the angle of electron-diffraction *θ*  is related to the diameter of an atomic nucleus *d*  by the equation

sin *θ  *= 1.22$\frac{λ}{d}$

Suggest what the term *λ *in the equation represents and describe how the observed diffraction pattern will vary in response to it.
parts.solutionMd:
State the meaning of the *λ *term:

- *λ *represents the <u>de Broglie</u> wavelength of the electrons; **[1 mark]**

Describe the proportionality to the diffraction angle:

- If the de Broglie wavelength increases / decreases, <u>then sin </u><u>*θ *</u><u>increases / decreases</u> and therefore the diffraction angle *θ *increases / decreases; **[1 mark]**

Describe how the diffraction pattern is affected by varying *λ*:

- If the diffraction angle *θ  *increases then the concentric rings get further apart / the diffraction pattern spreads out

**OR**

- If the diffraction angle *θ *decreases then the concentric rings get closer together / the diffraction pattern narrows; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *It’s a really common mistake to say that “**θ **is proportional to **λ” **in the equation sin **θ **= 1.22*$\frac{λ}{d}$* . This is not mathematically true: be careful to note that **sin **θ  **is proportional to **λ**. In other words, a graph of sin **θ **against **λ **would be a straight line through the origin, but a graph of **θ **against **λ **would not be. However, as sin **θ  **increases, **θ  **increases** **(up to 90°).*

> *Avoid saying just ‘wavelength’ and be specific about the ‘de Broglie wavelength’.*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the complete line emission spectrum for another particular atom.

![2-5-s-q--q2b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/006-2-5-s-q-q2b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

This atom has a ground state energy of  –10.0 eV.

Sketch a diagram of the possible energy levels for the atomic line spectrum shown in Fig. 1.1.

Label each energy level with the value of its energy.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Ground state energy of the atom = –10.0 eV

From the data page:

- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C
- Planck constant, *h*  = 6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup> J s
- Speed of light in free space, *c*  = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>

An energy level diagram that would score 6 marks should look like:

![2-5-s-q--q2b-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/007-2-5-s-q-q2b-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

- Correct gap sizes and positions; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy of the photon corresponding to the 1400 nm line:

- For the line at 1400 nm, this corresponds to an emitted photon wavelength of 1400 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- The energy of this photon *E* = *hf* = *h × *$\frac{c}{λ}$*= *(6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × $( \frac{3 \\times 10^{8}{1400 \\times 10^{-9} } } )$ = 1.42 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J
- In electronvolts, this energy is $\frac{1.42\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}$= 0.9 eV **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy of the photon corresponding to the 300 nm line:

- For the line at 300 nm, this corresponds to an emitted photon wavelength of 300 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m

- The energy of this photon *E* = *hf* = *h × *$\frac{c}{λ}$*= *(6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × $( \frac{3 \\times 10^{8}{300 \\times 10^{-9} } } )$ = 6.63 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J
- In electronvolts, this energy is $\frac{6.63\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}$ = 4.1 eV **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy of the photon corresponding to the 250 nm line:

- For the line at 250 nm, this corresponds to an emitted photon wavelength of 250 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m

- The energy of this photon *E* = *hf* = *h × *$\frac{c}{λ}$*= *(6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × $( \frac{3 \\times 10^{8}{250 \\times 10^{-9} } } )$ = 7.96 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J
- In electronvolts, this energy is $\frac{7.96\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}$= 5.0 eV **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy levels:

- Since the ground state energy of the atom is –10.0 eV, then the largest energy photon is emitted by a transition between the biggest energy gap
- The largest energy photon is 5.0 eV, corresponding to the line at 250 nm

  - This means there is an energy level at (–10.0 + 5.0) = –5.0 eV **[1 mark]**
- From Fig. 1.1, there is another line close to 250 nm at 300 nm

  - This corresponds to a photon with energy 4.1 eV
- Therefore, there is an energy level creating a gap similar in size to that between –10.0 eV and –5.0 eV, with a gap of 4.1 eV

  - Therefore, there is an energy level at (–5.0 – 4.1) = –9.1 eV **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]*** *

> *A general tip for all exam questions is to minimise rounding before your final answer. This is especially important here, as the ground state energy level is only given to 1 decimal place, but the energy calculations require multiple steps. *

> *It’s also worthwhile to do a sense-check when figuring out energy levels: here, you should sketch the photons corresponding to each energy gap to ensure that everything checks out as expected:*

![2-5-s-q--q2b-answer1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/008-2-5-s-q-q2b-answer1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *You may have drawn a separate energy level for each line on the emission spectrum. However, you must spot that this is the **complete** spectrum. If there were 3 energy levels above the ground state, we would see 6 lines on the spectrum to account for all the transitions between all the energy levels. Don't forget that de-excitation transitions occur between **all **energy levels. *

parts.problemMd: Explain the significance of an electron at an energy level of 0 eV.
parts.solutionMd:
Link 0 eV to ionisation:

- If an electron exists at an energy level 0 eV, this means the atom has become ionised; **[1 mark]**

Explain the process of ionisation:

- Enough <u>energy has been transferred</u> to the electron such that it is able to escape the atom; **[1 mark]**
- And it is no longer bounded by the (electrostatic force from the) nucleus; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Since the electron levels get smaller (more negative) as they reach the ground state, they are increasing (less negative) as they get further away from the ground state. This is until they reach 0 eV, at which point they are at such a high level that they are no longer bound by the atom, and are ionised.*

![2-5-s-q--q2c-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-4-energy-levels-in-atoms-and-line-spectra/assets/009-2-5-s-q-q2c-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

parts.problemMd: Define *atomic mass unit*.
parts.solutionMd:
The atomic mass unit is defined as:

- A twelfth / $\frac{1}{12}$ of the mass; **[1 mark]**
- Of a (neutral) atom of carbon-12; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This is the precise definition of the atomic mass unit - make sure you learn it in terms of how it relates to carbon-12. It is equal to 1.66 × 10*<sup>*−27*</sup>* kg, which is roughly equal to a proton or neutron, hence, this is what you will need to use in calculation questions.*

parts.problemMd:
The unified atomic mass unit *u* is roughly equal to 1.66 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg which is the mass of one nucleon.

Calculate the mass, in kg, of a nucleus of uranium−238. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the mass of a nucleus of uranium−238:

List the known quantities:

- Mass number of uranium−238 = 238
- Atomic mass unit, u = 1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg

Determine the mass of uranium−238 in kg:

- Mass of uranium−238 = 238 u = (1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) × 238 **[1 mark]**
- Mass of uranium−238 = 3.95318 × 10<sup>−25</sup> kg **[1 mark]**
- Mass of uranium−238 = 3.95 × 10<sup>−25</sup> kg (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Exam questions commonly ask you to "estimate" the mass of a nuclide, but don't let this throw you off, as this is simply referring to the fact that the atomic mass unit is **approximately** equal to its total mass in a.m.u.*

The unified atomic mass unit u is roughly equal to 1.66 × 10^−27 kg which is the mass of one nucleon. Calculate the mass, in kg, of a nucleus of uranium−238. Mass of uranium−238 = 3.95 × 10^−25 kg (3 s.f.)
Einstein's Theory of Relativity showed that mass could be converted into energy, and energy into mass. This is summarised by the following equation ΔE = Δmc² where E represents Energy (joules/J), m represents Mass (kilograms/kg), c represents Speed of light (m s^−1).

Calculate the energy released, in J, if all of the mass in the nucleus of uranium−238 were converted into energy.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the energy released by a nucleus of uranium-238

List the known quantities:

- Mass of uranium−238 nucleus, Δ*m* = 3.95 × 10<sup>−25</sup> kg (from **(b)**)
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Substitute the known values into the equation:

- Mass-energy equivalence:  $\DeltaE=\Deltamc^{2}$
- $\Delta E = ( 3.95 \times 10^{ - } 25 ) \times ( 3.00 \times 10^{8} ) ^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
State the meaning of the terms

(i) binding energy,

[1]

(ii) mass defect.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Binding energy is defined as:

- The energy needed / required to <u>separate the nucleons</u> of a nucleus **OR **the energy released when a <u>nucleus is formed</u> from its nucleons; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Mass defect is defined as:

- The <u>difference</u> between the <u>mass</u> of a nucleus, and the <u>sum of the masses</u> of the nucleons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Remember that a nucleus's binding energy is required to **combine** the individual protons and neutrons into the nucleus. As a result, some of the mass of the protons and neutrons is sacrificed and converted into energy (using **E** = **mc*<sup>*2*</sup>*). This loss of mass is the mass defect.*

> *However, when defining binding energy and mass defect in the exam, use the keywords and stick to the definitions outlined above to ensure you get the marks. It is ok to say 'neutrons and protons' instead of nucleons, but you need to be specific: for example, saying 'constituent parts' isn't enough to get you the marks.*

parts.problemMd:
The nuclear rest mass $m_{total}$ of oxygen−16 $ (  {}_{8}^{16}\mathrm{O}  ) $ is 15.994914 u.

The following equation describes the relationship between mass defect $\Deltam$* *and the mass of the constituents of a nucleus

$Δm=Zm_{p}+Nm_{n}-m_{total}$

(i) State the meaning of the terms $Zm_{p}$ and $Nm_{n}$.

[2]

(ii) Calculate the mass defect of oxygen−16.

$m_{p}$ = 1.007276 u

$m_{n}$ = 1.008665 u

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The meaning of the terms is:

- $Z$ = proton number / number of protons **AND** $m_{p}$ = proton rest mass **OR**
- $Zm_{p}$ = total mass of the protons in the nucleus; **[1 mark]**
- $N$ = number of neutrons **AND** $m_{n}$ = neutron rest mass **OR**
- $Nm_{n}$ = total mass of the neutrons in the nucleus; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the mass defect of oxygen−16:

List the known quantities:

- Nuclear rest mass of oxygen−16 $ (  {}_{8}^{16}\mathrm{O}  ) $ = 15.994914 u
- Proton rest mass,* m*<sub>*p*</sub>* *= 1.007276 u
- Neutron rest mass,* m*<sub>*n*</sub>* *= 1.008665 u

Determine the numbers of protons and neutrons in oxygen−16

- From ${}_{8}^{16}\mathrm{O}$:
- Number of protons, $Z$ = 8 **AND**
- Number of protons, $N$ = 16 − 8 = 8 **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values into the equation:

- $\Deltam=Zm_{p}+Nm_{n}-m_{total}$
- $\Delta m = ( 8 \times 1.007276 \mathrm{u} ) + ( 8 \times 1.008665 \mathrm{u} ) - 15.994914 \mathrm{u}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\Deltam=0.132614u$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The equation *$Δm=Zm_{p}+Nm_{n}-m_{total}$* is **not** in the data booklet, but you do need to know how to calculate Δ**m**.*

> *You may prefer to memorise the equation, but the best approach is to remember that the mass defect is the **sum of the individual rest masses**, minus the **total rest mass of the nucleus** in question.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calculate the mass defect of oxygen−16: Δm = (8 × 1.007276 u) + (8 × 1.008665 u) − 15.994914 u = 0.132614 u

Use the mass defect from **(b)** to show that the total binding energy of a nucleus of oxygen−16 is about 2 × 10<sup>−11</sup> J.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the total binding energy of a nucleus of oxygen−16 is about 2 × 10<sup>−11</sup> J:

List the known quantities:

- Mass defect of oxygen−16, Δ*m* = 0.132614 u (from **(b)**)
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Atomic mass unit, *u* = 1.66 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg

Substitute the known values into the mass-energy equivalence equation to calculate Δ*E*:

- Mass-energy equivalence $\DeltaE=\Deltamc^{2}$
- Mass defect (in kg):  $\Deltam$ = (0.132614) × (1.66 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) **[1 mark]**
- Binding energy:  $\DeltaE$ = (0.132614) × (1.66 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) × (3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 1.981 × 10<sup>−11</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *In this topic, you are working with lots of decimal places and lots of scientific notation. This has the potential for calculation errors to creep in, especially under the pressure of the exam.*

> *It is best practice to double-check every number you input into your calculator so that you can catch any such errors as you are working. Due diligence like this will save you time and ensures you don't make any silly mistakes.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Use the mass defect from (b) to show that the total binding energy of a nucleus of oxygen−16 is about 2 × 10^−11 J.
Binding energy: ΔE = 1.981 × 10^−11 J

Determine the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of oxygen−16.
parts.solutionMd:
The binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of oxygen-16 is:

List the known quantities:

- Binding energy of oxygen−16, $\DeltaE$ = 1.981 × 10<sup>−11</sup> J (from **(c)**)
- Number of nucleons in oxygen−16 = 16
- 1 eV = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J

Determine the binding energy per nucleon:

- Binding energy per nucleon = $\frac{\mathrm{Binding} \mathrm{energy}}{\mathrm{Number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{nucleons}}$
- Binding energy per nucleon = $\frac{ ( 1.981 \times 10^{ - } 11 ) }{16}$ **[1 mark]**
- Binding energy per nucleon = $1.238\times10^{-12}J$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the energy into MeV:

- Binding energy per nucleon = $\frac{1.238\times10^{-12}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Binding energy per nucleon = 7 737 500 = 7.74 MeV **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The binding energy per nucleon is the **total** binding energy **divided** by the nucleon number. In this case, since the nucleon number is 16, the binding energy per nucleon is found by **dividing** the total binding energy by 16.*

parts.problemMd:
In terms of the forces acting within the nucleus, explain why:

(i) fusion occurs for nuclides with low nucleon numbers.

[2]

(ii) fission occurs for nuclides with high nucleon numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Fusion occurs for nuclides with low nucleon numbers because:

- Attractive strong nuclear forces between nucleons dominate; **[1 mark]**
- Over repulsive electrostatic forces between protons; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Fission occurs for nuclides with high nucleon numbers because:

- Repulsive electrostatic forces between protons (begin to) dominate; **[1 mark]**
- These forces (tend to) break apart the nucleus; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Nuclei with low nucleon numbers tend to have a lower binding energy per nucleon, hence, they are generally less stable.*

> *This means the lightest elements have weaker electrostatic forces and are the most likely to undergo **fusion**.*

> *For nuclei with high nucleon numbers, the general binding energy per nucleon is high and gradually decreases with increasing nucleon number.*

> *This means the heaviest elements are the most unstable and likely to undergo **fission**.*

parts.problemMd:

Complete the sentences by circling the correct word.

In fusion, the mass of the nucleus that is created is slightly **more / less **than the total mass of the original nuclei and the daughter nucleus is **more / less** stable.

In fission, an unstable nucleus is converted into more stable nuclei with a **larger / smaller** total mass. In both cases, this difference in mass, the mass defect, is equal to the binding energy that is released.

**Fission / Fusion **releases much more energy per kg than **fission / fusion**. The greater the increase in binding energy, the **more / less** energy is released.
parts.solutionMd:
The correct sentences are as follows:

**One**** mark for each correct sentence:**

- In fusion, the mass of the nucleus that is created is slightly **less **than the total mass of the original nuclei and the daughter nucleus is **more** stable; **[1 mark]**
- In fission, an unstable nucleus is converted into more stable nuclei with a **smaller **total mass; **[1 mark]**
- In both cases, this difference in mass, the mass defect, is equal to the binding energy that is released.
- **Fusion** releases much more energy per kg than **fission****;** **[1 mark]**
- The greater the increase in binding energy, the **more** energy is released; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

One nuclear reaction that can take place in a nuclear reactor may be represented, in part, by the equation shown below.

parts.solutionMd:
Complete the equation `U _ 92 ^ 235 + n _ 0 ^ 1 -> with _ on top Mo _ 42 ^ 95 + La _ 57 ^ 139 + 2 n _ 0 ^ 1 + ................ + energy`:

Balance the nucleon numbers in the equation:

- 235 + 1 = 95 + 139 + 2 + A
- A = 236 − 95 − 139 − 2 = 0

Balance the proton numbers in the equation:

- 92 + 0 = 42 + 57 + 0 + Z
- Z = 92 − 42 − 57 = −7

The missing term in the equation in nuclide notation is:

- $7   {}_{- 1}^{0}\mathrm{e}$** [1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that the energy equivalent to 1.00 u is 934 MeV:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, $m$ = 1.00 u = 1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg
- Speed of light in free space, $c$ = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Use the mass-energy equivalence equation to calculate the energy, $E$ in J:

- $E=mc^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E = ( 1.661 \times 10^{ - } 27 ) \times ( 3 \times 10^{8} ) ^{2} = 1.495 \times 10^{ - } 10 \mathrm{J}$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the energy from J to MeV:

- $E=\frac{1.495\times10^{-10}}{1.6\times10^{-13}}=934\mathrm{MeV}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of lanthanum-139 $ (  {}_{57}^{139}\mathrm{La}  ) $:

List the known quantities:

- Nucleon number = 139
- Number of protons = 57
- Number of neutrons = 139 − 57 = 82
- Rest mass of a neutron, $m_{n}$ = 1.00863u
- Rest mass of a proton, $m_{p}$ = 1.00728u
- Mass of ${}_{57}^{139}\mathrm{ } La$ = 138.955u

Calculate the mass defect, $\Deltam$ of ${}_{57}^{139}\mathrm{La}$:

- $\Deltam=82m_{n}+57m_{p}-massofnuclide$
- $\Delta m = ( 82 \times 1.00863 ) u + ( 57 \times 1.00728 ) u - 138.955 u$
- $\Deltam=1.16762u$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the binding energy per nucleon:

- Binding energy = 1.16762 × 934 MeV = 1090 MeV **[1 mark]**
- Binding energy per nucleon = $\frac{bindingenergy}{nucleonnumber}$
- Binding energy per nucleon = $\frac{1.16762\times934}{139}=7.84\mathrm{MeV}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Memorise** the conversions between:*

  - *J and eV*
  - *u and kg*
- *Read** the **question carefully** to apply the correct conversions*

parts.problemMd:
A nuclear fission reaction occurs that has the following equation

${}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}    +    {}_{92}^{235}\mathrm{U}    \rightarrow    {}_{38}^{90}\mathrm{Sr}    +    {}_{54}^{143}\mathrm{Xe}    +    x {}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}$

(i) Determine, for this nuclear reaction, the value of $x$.

[1]

(ii) Data for the binding energy per nucleon of some nuclei are given in Table 1.2.

Use the data to calculate the energy, in MeV, released in this reaction.

**Table 1.2**

|   | **binding energy per nucleon / MeV** |
|---|---|
| ${}_{92}^{235}U$ | 7.59 |
| ${}_{38}^{90}\mathrm{Sr}$ | 8.70 |
| ${}_{54}^{143}\mathrm{Xe}$ | 8.20 |

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The value of $x$ is:

- ${}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}    +    {}_{92}^{235}\mathrm{U}    \rightarrow    {}_{38}^{90}\mathrm{Sr}    +    {}_{54}^{143}\mathrm{Xe}    +    x {}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}$
- Number of nucleons on LHS:  1 + 235 = 236
- Number of nucleons on RHS:  90 + 143 + $x$ = 233 + $x$
- Hence, $x$ = 236 − 233 = 3 **[1 mark]** ** **

(ii)** **Calculate the energy change that takes place in this reaction.

List the known quantities:

- Binding energy per nucleon of U-235, $E_{U}$ = 7.59 MeV
- Binding energy per nucleon of Sr-90, $E_{S}$ = 8.70 MeV
- Binding energy per nucleon of Xe-143, $E_{X}$ = 8.20 MeV

The amount of energy released during the fission reaction:

- Energy released:  $\Delta E = ( 90 E_{S} + 143 E_{X} ) - 235 E_{U}$
- Energy released:  $\DeltaE$ = (90 × 8.70) + (143 × 8.20) − (235 × 7.59) **[1 mark]**
- Energy released: * *$\DeltaE$* = *172 MeV **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Under the right conditions, a hydrogen-2 `H ^ 2` nucleus can fuse with a hydrogen-1 `H ^ 1` to make a helium-3 `He ^ 3` nucleus. The values of binding energy per nucleon for these nuclei are shown in Table 1.3.

|---|---|

(i) Write down the nuclear equation for this reaction.

(ii) Explain why the binding energy per nucleon of hydrogen-1 is zero.

parts.solutionMd:

- $\mathrm{H} pre^{2} + \mathrm{H} pre^{1} \rightarrow \text{He} pre^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The binding energy per nucleon of hydrogen-1 is zero because:

- Hydrogen-1 is a single proton, so it is not bound to any other nucleons / it cannot release energy (by separation); **[1 mark]**

(iii)** **Calculate the energy released in this reaction:

List the known quantities:

- Binding energy per nucleon of hydrogen-2, $E_{H}$ = 0.864 MeV
- Binding energy per nucleon of helium-3, $E_{He}$ = 2.235 MeV

The amount of energy released during the fission reaction:

- Energy released:  $\DeltaE=3E_{He}-2E_{H}$

Energy released: ΔE = (90 × 8.70) + (143 × 8.20) − (235 × 7.59) = 172 MeV (energy released in the fission reaction of uranium-235)

When two hydrogen-2 nuclei fuse into a helium-4 nucleus, 3.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup> J of energy is released. This reaction is shown below

$\mathrm{H} pre^{2} + \mathrm{H} pre^{2} \rightarrow \text{He} pre^{4}$

Show that the fusion of 1 kg of two hydrogen-2 nuclei releases about 8 times more energy per kg than the fission of 1 kg of uranium-235.

The masses of hydrogen-2 and uranium-235 are shown in Table 1.4.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the energy per kg for the fission and fusion reactions:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of <sup>2</sup>H = 2.013553 *u*
- Mass of <sup>235</sup>U = 235.0439 *u*
- Atomic mass unit, *u* = 1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg
- Energy available from fusion of <sup>2</sup>H = 3.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup> J
- Energy available from fission of <sup>235</sup>U = 172 MeV (from **(b)**)

Calculate the energy available per 1 kg of hydrogen-2:

- Mass of <u>two</u> <sup>2</sup>H nuclei = 2 × 2.013553 u
- Number of <sup>2</sup>H nuclei in 1 kg = $\frac{1 kg}{2 \times 2.013553 \times ( 1.66 \times 10^{ - } 27 ) }$ = 1.496 × 10<sup>26</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Energy per kg = (1.496 × 10<sup>26</sup>) × (3.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup>) = 5.39 × 10<sup>14</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy available per 1 kg of uranium-235:

- Mass of <u>one</u> <sup>235</sup>U nucleus = 235.0439 u
- Number of <sup>235</sup>U nuclei in 1 kg = $\frac{1 kg}{235.0439 \times ( 1.66 \times 10^{ - } 27 ) }$ = 2.562 × 10<sup>24</sup>
- Convert energy to J:  172 MeV = (172 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × (1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup>)
- Energy per kg = (2.562 × 10<sup>24</sup>) × (172 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × (1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup>) = 7.05 × 10<sup>13</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Compare the two values for energy released per kg:

- Ratio:  $\frac{energyperkgfromfusion}{energyperkgfromfission}=\frac{5.39\times10^{14}}{7.05\times10^{13}}$ = 7.65 ≈ 8 **[1 mark]**
- Hence, hydrogen fusion provides about 8 times more energy per kg than uranium fission

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
If deuterium $ (  {}_{1}^{2}\mathrm{H}  ) $ nuclei undergo fusion, a possible reaction is

${}_{1}^{2}\mathrm{H}    +    {}_{1}^{2}\mathrm{H}    \rightarrow    {}_{1}^{3}\mathrm{H}    +    {}_{1}^{1}\mathrm{H}$

The masses of the nuclei involved in the reaction are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **mass / u** |
|---|---|
| ${}_{1}^{1}H$ | 1.0078 |
| ${}_{1}^{2}H$ | 2.0135 |
| ${}_{1}^{3}H$ | 3.0160 |

(i) Explain what is meant by nuclear fusion.

[1]

(ii) Determine the energy released, in J, when 3.00 mol of deuterium undergoes this fusion reaction.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Fusion is defined as:

- When two nuclei combine to form a (single) nucleus; **[1 mark]**

(ii)** **Determine the energy released when 3.00 mol of deuterium reacts:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of hydrogen-1, $m_{1}$ = 1.0078 *u*
- Mass of hydrogen-2, $m_{2}$ = 2.0135 *u*
- Mass of hydrogen-3, $m_{3}$ = 3.0160 *u*
- Atomic mass unit, *u* = 1.66 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg
- Speed of light, $c$ = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Avogadro constant, $N_{A}$ = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

Determine the mass defect:

- Mass defect:  $\Delta m = 2 m_{2} - ( m_{3} + m_{1} )$
- $\Deltam$ = [(2 × 2.0135) – (3.0160 + 1.0078)] *u*
- $\Deltam$ = 0.0032 u **[1 mark]**

Use mass-energy equivalence to determine the energy released:

- Mass-energy equivalence:  $\DeltaE=\Deltamc^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\DeltaE$ = 0.0032 × (1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup>) × (3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup>)<sup>2</sup>
- $\DeltaE$ = 4.78 × 10<sup>–13</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Determine the energy released when 3.00 mol of deuterium reacts:

- 3.00 mol of deuterium forms 1.50 mol of hydrogen-3 **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the number of hydrogen-3 nuclei = 1.50 mol × $N_{A}$
- Total energy = 1.50 × (6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>) × (4.78 × 10<sup>–13</sup>)
- Total energy = 4.32 × 10<sup>11</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
During a particular fission process, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a slow-moving neutron to form uranium-236. This initiates the fission reaction, creating a krypton-92 nucleus and a barium-141 nucleus, among other fission products.

Fig. 1.1 shows the relationship between the binding energy per nucleon and the mass number for various nuclides.

![8-4-s-q--q2a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/23-nuclear-physics/23-1-mass-defect-and-nuclear-binding-energy/assets/010-8-4-s-q-q2a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Using Fig. 1.1, calculate the energy released during this fission process.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the energy released during this fission process:

- Fission reaction:  $\mathrm{U} pre_{ } pre^{235} + \mathrm{n} pre_{ } pre^{1} \rightarrow \mathrm{U} pre_{ } pre^{236} \rightarrow \text{Ba} pre_{ } pre^{141} + \text{Kr} pre_{ } pre^{92}$

![8-4-s-q--q2a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/23-nuclear-physics/23-1-mass-defect-and-nuclear-binding-energy/assets/011-8-4-s-q-q2a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

- Binding energy per nucleon of U-235 (or U-236), Ba-141 and Kr-92 correctly read from the graph; **[1 mark]**

  - Binding energy per nucleon (U-235/U-236) = 7.0 MeV
  - Binding energy per nucleon (Ba-141) = 7.8 MeV
  - Binding energy per nucleon (Kr-92) = 8.2 MeV

Calculate the binding energy of the products and reactants:

- Binding energy = binding energy per nucleon × nucleon number
- Binding energy of reacting nuclei (U-235 **or** U-236) = (7.0 × 235) = 1645 MeV (or 1652 MeV if U-236 used)
- Binding energy of product nuclei (Ba-141 + Kr-92) = (7.8 × 141) + (8.2 × 92) = 1854.2 MeV

Calculate the difference in energy between products and reactants:

- Energy released in one fission = binding energy of product nuclei – binding energy of reacting nuclei
- Energy released in one fission = (1854.2 – 1645) MeV **[1 mark]**
- Energy released in one fission = 209 MeV (or 202 MeV if U-236 used) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that the binding energy = binding energy per nucleon × nucleon number (or mass number)!*

During a particular fission process, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a slow-moving neutron to form uranium-236. This initiates the fission reaction, creating a krypton-92 nucleus and a barium-141 nucleus, among other fission products. Using Fig. 1.1, calculate the energy released during this fission process.

parts.solutionMd:
Identify the other fission products:

- The other fission products in this process are <u>three</u> neutrons; **[1 mark]**
- This is because neutrons are produced in fission

  - The total mass number of the reactants is 236 (Uranium)
  - The total mass number of the products is 141 (Barium) + 92 (Krypton) = 233
  - The missing number of neutrons is 236 – 233 = 3

Justify why they can be discounted:

parts.problemMd:
A different fission process occurs. Fission of uranium-235 is triggered again by the absorption of a slow-moving neutron. Gamma-ray photons of wavelength 2.5 × 10<sup>–12</sup> m are released. The process is described by the equation below:

`U _ 92 ^ 235 + n _ 0 ^ 1 -> Te _ 52 ^ 138 + Zr _ 40 ^ 98 + gamma`

In this process, 90% of the energy released is carried away as kinetic energy of the two daughter nuclei.

Show that approximately 32 gamma-ray photons are released in this process.

Mass of ${}_{92}^{235}U$ = 235.0439u

Mass of ${}_{52}^{138}\mathrm{Te}$ = 137.9603u

Mass of ${}_{40}^{98}\mathrm{Zr}$ = 97.9197u

Mass of ${}_{0}^{1}n $ = 1.0087u

You may use the fact that 1 u is the equivalent of 931.5 MeV c<sup>–2</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that approximately 32 gamma-ray photons are released in this process:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of ${}_{92}^{235}\mathrm{U}  $= 235.0439u
- Mass of ${}_{52}^{138}\mathrm{Te}$ = 137.9603u
- Mass of ${}_{40}^{98}\mathrm{Zr}$ = 97.9197u
- Mass of ${}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}$ = 1.0087u
- Wavelength of $γ$ photons emitted = 2.5 × 10<sup>–12</sup> m
- % of energy released as kinetic energy of ${}_{52}^{138}\mathrm{Te}$ and ${}_{40}^{98}\mathrm{Zr}$ = 90%
- Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 931.5 MeV c<sup>–2</sup>
- 1 eV = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J
- Planck’s constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s (from data page)
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup> (from data page)

Calculate the mass defect between the reactants and the products:

- Mass of reactants = 235.0439 + 1.0087 = 236.0526 u
- Mass of products = 137.9603 + 97.9197 = 235.88 u
- Mass defect:  Δ*m* = 236.0526 – 235.88 = 0.1726 u **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total energy released as gamma photons:

- The energy released in the fission process is the energy equivalent of the mass difference
- Total energy released:  Δ*E* = Δ*mc*<sup>2</sup>
- Total energy released:  Δ*E* = 0.1726 × 931.5 MeV c<sup>–2</sup> × c<sup>2</sup>
- Total energy released:  Δ*E* = 0.1726 × (931.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × (1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) = 2.57 × 10<sup>–11</sup> J **[1 mark]**
- If 90% of the energy is the kinetic energy of the daughter nuclei, then the remaining 10% is in the form of gamma photons
- Energy released as photons:  Δ*E* = 0.10 × (2.57 × 10<sup>–11</sup>) = 2.57 × 10<sup>–12</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the frequency of the photons:

- Energy of one photon:  $E=hf=\frac{hc}{λ}$
- Energy of one photon:  $E = \frac{ ( 6.63 \times 10^{ - } 34 ) ( 3.00 \times 10^{8} ) }{2.5 \times 10^{ - } 12}$ = 7.956 × 10<sup>–14</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total number of photons:

- Number of photons = $\frac{energyreleasedasphotons}{energyofonephoton}$
- Number of photons = $\frac{2.57\times10^{-12}}{7.956\times10^{-14}}$ = 32.3 ≈ 32** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Note that this draws on photon energy from the quantum physics topic. To convert the mass difference in atomic units into energy, convert into MeV, then eV, then J  *

> *1 u →  931.5 MeV → 931.5 × 10*<sup>*6*</sup>* eV → 931.5 × 10*<sup>*6*</sup>* × (1.6 × 10*<sup>*–19*</sup>*) J*

A different fission process occurs. Fission of uranium-235 is triggered again by the absorption of a slow-moving neutron. Gamma-ray photons of wavelength 2.5 × 10^–12^ m are released. The process is described by the equation below: \$\$\_{92}^{235}U + \_{0}^{1}n \rightarrow \_{52}^{138}Te + \_{40}^{98}Zr + \gamma\$\$ In this process, 90% of the energy released is carried away as kinetic energy of the two daughter nuclei. Mass of \$\$\_{52}^{138}Te\$\$ = 137.9603u; Mass of \$\$\_{40}^{98}Zr\$\$ = 97.9197u

Assuming the uranium nucleus is initially at rest, show that the ${}_{40}^{98}\mathrm{Zr}$ nucleus is emitted with a speed about 1.4 times larger than the ${}_{52}^{138}\mathrm{Te}$ nucleus.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that Zr-98 is emitted with a speed about 1.4 times larger than Te-138:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of Zr-98, $m_{Zr}$ = 97.9197u
- Mass of Te-138, $m_{Te}$ = 137.9603u
- Initial velocity of nuclei = 0
- Final velocity of Zr-98 = $v_{Zr}$
- Final velocity of Te-138 = $v_{Te}$

Apply conservation of momentum to the two nuclei:

- Momentum: $p=mv$
- By conservation of momentum, the two nuclei move away in opposite directions
- So, $m_{Zr}v_{Zr}-m_{Te}v_{Te}=0\Rightarrowm_{Zr}v_{Zr}=m_{Te}v_{Te}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the ratio of speeds using the ratio of masses:

- Ratio of speed:  $\frac{v_{Zr}}{v_{Te}}=\frac{m_{Te}}{m_{Zr}}=\frac{137.9603u}{97.9197u}$ = 1.41 ≈ 1.4 **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, $v_{Zr}\approx1.4v_{Te}$

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The negative sign shows that the particles move in opposite directions, but you are being asked about their speed, i.e. comparing the **magnitudes** of these velocities.*

parts.problemMd:
When a uranium–235 nucleus undergoes fission, one possible reaction is:

${}_{92}^{235}\mathrm{U}    +    {}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}    \rightarrow    {}_{54}^{139}\mathrm{Xe}    +    {}_{38}^{95}\mathrm{Sr}    +    2 {}_{0}^{1}\mathrm{n}    +    energy$

The binding energy per nucleon *E* is given in Table 1.1 below:

**Table 1.1**

| **nuclide** | ***E***** / MeV** |
|---|---|
| ${}_{38}^{95}{Sr}$ | 8.74 |
| ${}_{54}^{139}{Xe}$ | 8.39 |
| ${}_{92}^{235}U$ | 7.60 |

A nuclear reactor, operating at 27% efficiency, outputs 1500 MW. It uses enriched fuel containing 2% uranium–235 and 98% uranium–238.

Estimate the total mass of original fuel required per year in the nuclear reactor (assume the molar mass of uranium-235 is 0.235 kg/mol).
parts.solutionMd:
Estimate the total mass of original fuel required per year:

List the known quantities:

- Binding energy per nucleon of U-235 = 7.60 MeV / nucleon
- Binding energy per nucleon of Xe-139 = 8.39 MeV / nucleon
- Binding energy per nucleon of Sr-95 = 8.74 MeV / nucleon
- Power output, *P*<sub>out</sub> = 1500 MW
- Efficiency = 27% = 0.27
- Molar mass of U-235 = 0.235 kg mol<sup>–1</sup>
- Avogadro’s constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub>* *= 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> (from the data page)
- 1 eV = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J
- Time, *t* = 1 year = (60 × 60 × 24 × 365) = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s

Calculate the total energy released by the fission reaction:

- Energy released = difference in binding energy of the products and reactants
- Binding energy of the reactants (U-235) = 7.60 × 235 = 1786 MeV
- Binding energy of the products (Sr-95 + Xe-139) = (8.74 × 95) + (8.39 × 139) = 1996.5 MeV
- Energy released per fission = 1996.5 – 1786 = 210.5 MeV **[1 mark]**

Calculate the supplied energy per year:

- Efficiency = $\frac{usefulenergyoutput}{totalenergyinput}$
- The energy output in a year = $P_{out}t$ = (1500 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × (3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup>) = 4.73 × 10<sup>16</sup> J
- Therefore, the energy supplied in a year = $\frac{4.73\times10^{16}}{0.27}$ = 1.75 × 10<sup>17</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of uranium−235 nuclei in 1 kg of fuel:

- Amount (moles) of U-235:  $n=\frac{mass}{molarmass}=\frac{N}{N_{A}}$
- Number of U-235 nuclei per kg:  *N* = $( 6.02 \times 10^{23} ) \times \frac{1 kg}{0.235}$ = 2.56 × 10<sup>24</sup> **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy released per kilogram of fuel:

- In every kg of fuel, 2% contains the energy released from U-235 fission
- So, energy released per kg of U-235 = 0.02 × energy released per fission (in J) × *N*
- Energy released per kg of U-235 = 0.02 × (210.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>)(1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) × (2.56 × 10<sup>24</sup>) = 1.72 × 10<sup>12</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Estimate the mass of original fuel required per year:

- Mass required per year = $\frac{energysuppliedperyear}{energyreleasedperkg}=\frac{1.75\times10^{17}}{1.72\times10^{12}}=1.02\times10^{5}\mathrm{kg}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Often the data given at the start of a question provides a hint as to the approach you should take.*

> *In the question above, the molar mass of uranium–235 is given: this should act as a hint that you will likely need to the Avogadro’s constant to calculate a mass and/or number of particles.  *

> *The power is given in units of **watts** which is the energy per **second**. This is how you know you need to multiply this value by 60 × 60 × 24 × 365 to get the amount of energy per **year**.*

parts.problemMd:
Radioactive decay is often described as a spontaneous and random process.

State what is meant by

(i) radioactive decay

[2]

(ii) a spontaneous process

[2]

(iii) a random process

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Radioactive decay is defined as:

- The emission of a radioactive particle (alpha, beta or gamma); **[1 mark]**
- From a <u>nucleus</u>; **[1 mark]**

(ii) A spontaneous process is defined as:

- A decay which is unaffected by environmental changes; **[1 mark]**
- Such as temperature / pressure / chemical conditions; **[1 mark]**

(iii) A random process is defined as:

- The constant probability that a nucleus will decay (per unit time); **[1 mark]**
- (Because) it cannot be predicted which particular nucleus will decay next; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

[2]

(ii) Calculate the decay constant, in s<sup>−1</sup>, of lead-209.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Decay constant is defined as:

**EITHER**

- The probability of decay (of a nucleus) / the fraction of the number of nuclei in a sample that decay; **[1 mark]**
- Per unit time; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- $\lambda = - ( \frac{d N}{d t} ) \frac{1}{N}$; **[1 mark]**
- Where $- ( \frac{d N}{d t} )$ is the rate of decay of nuclei and *N* is the number of nuclei in the sample; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the initial activity of the sample of polonium-213.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the initial activity of the sample of polonium-213:

List the known quantities:

- Activity after 7 hours, *A* = 12 kBq = 12 × 10<sup>3</sup> Bq
- Time, *t* = 7 hours = 7 × 60 × 60 = 25 200 s
- Decay constant of lead-209, $λ=5.83\times10^{-5}s^{-1}$(from **(b)**)

Calculate the initial activity using the exponential decay equation:

- Exponential decay:  $A=A_{0}e^{-λt}\RightarrowA_{0}=\frac{A}{e^{-λt}}$
- $A_{0} = \frac{12 \times 10 ^{3} }{e^{ - } ( 5.83 \times 10^{ - } 5 ) \times ( 25 200 ) }$ **[1 mark]**
