(i) State the relation between the activity A of a sample of a radioactive isotope containing N atoms and the decay constant λ of the isotope.

[1]

(ii) Determine the number of lead-209 nuclei in the sample initially.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State the relationship between *A*, *N* and *λ*:

- $A=λN$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the number of lead-209 nuclei in this sample

List the known quantities:

- Decay constant, $λ=5.83\times10^{-5}s^{-1}$ (from **(b)**)

Calculate the initial number of lead nuclei:

- $N_{0}=8.94\times10^{8}=8.9\times10^{8}$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Units are extremely important throughout this question!*

> *When using the equation *$x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$*, it doesn't matter which unit of time you use for **λ **and **t** as long they have the **same units** (e.g. s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* and s or hr*<sup>*–1*</sup>* and hr)*

parts.problemMd:

(i)** **The student could demonstrate the spontaneous nature of radioactive decay by:

- To show that the rate of decay / activity does not change; **[1 mark]**

- Plotting a graph of count rate against time (using a data logger / computer software); **[1 mark]**
- To show the presence of fluctuations **OR** that the (decay) curve is not smooth; **[1 mark]**

**OR**** max ****one mark ****for:**

- (Random decay means) the time of decay (of a nucleus) cannot be predicted **OR** a nucleus has a constant probability (of decaying) in a given time; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A source of water is found to be contaminated with the radioactive isotope radium-228 $ (  {}_{88}^{228}\mathrm{Ra}  ) $.

This isotope of radium has a half-life of 5.75 years.

parts.solutionMd:
The half-life of radium-228 is:

- The time taken for the number of atoms / nuclei / activity of radium-228; **[1 mark]**
- To be reduced to one-half (of its initial value); **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- In 5.75 years, the number of atoms / nuclei / activity of radium-228; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the decay constant, in s<sup>–1</sup>, of radium-228.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the decay constant of radium-228:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of radium-228, $t_{1/2}$ = 5.75 years

Convert half-life into seconds:

- Half-life:  $t_{1/2}$ = 5.75 × (60 × 60 × 24 × 365) = 1.81 × 10<sup>8</sup> s **[1 mark]**

Determine the decay constant:

- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}$
- $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{1.81\times10^{8}}$ = 3.83 × 10<sup>−9</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

Half-life of radium-228, t_1/2 = 5.75 years
Decay constant: λ = ln 2 / t_1/2 = ln 2 / (1.81 × 10^8) = 3.83 × 10^−9 s^−1

A sample is taken of the contaminated water. The activity of radium-228 in a sample of 1.0 kg of water is found to be 20 mBq.

The mass of water in 1.0 mol is 18 g.

Calculate

(i) the number of radium-228 atoms in 1.0 kg of the contaminated water

[2]

(ii) the ratio

`(number of molecules of water in 1.0 kg of water)/(number of Ra ^ 228 atoms in 1.0 kg of water)`

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Decay constant of radium-228, *λ* = 3.83 × 10<sup>−9</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)
- Activity in 1.0 kg of water, *A* = 20 mBq = 0.020 Bq
- Avogadro's constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Mass of water in 1.0 mol, *m* = 18 g = 0.018 kg

(i) The number of radium-228 atoms in 1.0 kg of the contaminated water is:

- Activity:  $A=λN$
- Number of atoms in 1.0 kg of water:  $N=\frac{A}{λ}=\frac{0.020}{3.83\times10^{-9}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Number of atoms in 1.0 kg of water:  N = 5.22 × 10<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) The ratio of molecules of water to the number of radium-228 atoms is:

- Number of water molecules in 1.0 kg = $\frac{N_{A}}{m}=\frac{6.02\times10^{23}}{0.018}$ = 3.34 × 10<sup>25</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Ratio = `(number of molecules of water in 1.0 kg of water)/(number of Ra ^ 228 atoms in 1.0 kg of water)`
- Ratio = $\frac{3.34\times10^{25}}{5.22\times10^{6}}$ = 6.4 × 10<sup>18</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

The maximum safe limit for the activity of radium-228 in water has been set as 18.5 mBq kg<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the time, in days, for the activity of the contaminated water to be reduced to the safe limit.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the time for the activity to be reduced to the safe limit:

List the known quantities:

- Target activity, *A* = 18.5 mBq kg<sup>−1</sup>
- Initial activity, *A*<sub>*0*</sub> = 20 mBq kg<sup>−1</sup>
- Decay constant of radium-228, *λ* = 3.83 × 10<sup>−9</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)

Use the exponential decay equation for activity to determine the time:

- Exponential decay:  $A=A_{0}e^{-λt}$ **[1 mark]**
- `A / A _ 0 = e ^ negative lambda t <-> ln ( A / A _ 0 ) = - lambda t <-> t = - (ln ( A / A _ 0 ))/(lambda)`
- Time (in s):  $t = - \frac{ln ( \frac{18.5}{20} ) }{3.83 \times 10^{ - } 9}$ = 2.04 × 10<sup>7</sup> s **[1 mark]**
- Time (in days):  $t=\frac{2.04\times10^{7}}{60\times60\times24}$ = 236 days **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the fraction of undecayed nuclei *N *remaining* *relative to *N*<sub>*0*</sub> at time *t* = 1.25*T*.

List the known quantities:

- Half-life = *T*
- Time, *t* = 1.25*T*

Use the exponential decay equation:

- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{T}$
- Exponential decay:  $N=N_{0}e^{-λt}\Rightarrow\frac{N}{N_{0}}=e^{-λt}$
- $\frac{N}{N_{0}}=e^{-\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{T}\times1.25T}=e^{-1.25\times\mathrm{ln}2}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The radioisotope uranium-238 $ (  {}_{92}^{238}\mathrm{U}  ) $ decays through a decay chain to the radioisotope lead-206 $ (  {}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{Pb}  ) $, which is stable.

During the decay chain, 8 alpha particles are emitted, and X beta particles are emitted.

Calculate the value of X.
parts.solutionMd:
Recall the proton and mass number of alpha and beta particles:

- An alpha particle has 2 protons and 4 neutrons / ${}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{ \alpha }$ **AND** A beta particle is an electron / ${}_{- 1}^{0}\mathrm{ \beta }$ **[1 mark] **

Calculate the new proton and mass number after 8 alpha decays, labelling this unknown isotope as Y:

- 8 alpha decays means the proton number will decrease by 8 × 2 = 16 and the mass number will decrease by 8 × 4 = 32
- ${}_{92}^{238}\mathrm{U}    \rightarrow    {}_{76}^{206}\mathrm{Y}    +  8   {}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{ \alpha }$** [1 mark]**

Calculate the change in proton number from isotope Y to lead-206:

- ${}_{76}^{206}\mathrm{Y}$ to ${}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b$ means the proton number must increase by 6
- ${}_{76}^{206}\mathrm{Y}    \rightarrow    {}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{P} b    +    6 {}_{- 1}^{0}\mathrm{ \beta }$** [1 mark]**
- This means 6 beta particles are emitted: X = 6 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks] **

> *Notice that tackling this question hinges on knowing the proton and mass number of an alpha particle and a beta particle, even though stating this wasn’t explicitly asked in the question. *

> *Knowing the basic properties of radioactive decay – e.g. type, nature, penetration depth, etc. – is really crucial and you should be on the lookout to apply them in different contexts.*

parts.problemMd:
The half-life of uranium-238 is so long in comparison to any of the isotopes in its decay chain that we can assume the number of lead-206 nuclei, $N_{Pb}$ at any time is equal to the number of uranium-238 that have decayed.

The number of uranium-238 nuclei $N_{U}$ at time *t* is given by the equation:

$N_{U}=N_{0}e^{-λt}$

where $N_{0}$ is the number of uranium-238 nuclei at *t = *0.

Show that the ratio $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}$ is given by:

$\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=e^{λt}-1$
parts.solutionMd:
Write an expression for the initial number of uranium-238 nuclei:

- Initial number of uranium-238 nuclei = number of decayed nuclei + number of uranium-238 nuclei remaining
- $N_{0}=N_{Pb}+N_{U}$** ****[1 mark] **

Rearrange this expression for the number of lead-206 nuclei and divide both sides by $N_{U}$ to get an expression for the ratio required:

- $N_{Pb}=N_{0}-N_{U}$
- $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=\frac{N_{0}}{N_{U}}-\frac{N_{U}}{N_{U}}$  **[1 mark]**

Substitute the expression for $N_{U}$ and simplify the expression:

- $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=\frac{N_{0}}{N_{0}e^{-λt}}-1$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=\frac{1}{e^{-λt}}-1=e^{λt}-1$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Make sure you are comfortable interpreting the ‘exponential decay’ equation as the number of nuclei remaining in a sample. That way, you can always form an expression for the **initial number** of nuclei, in terms of a sum of the number of decayed nuclei and the number of nuclei remaining.*

parts.problemMd:
Enriched uranium fuel is a mixture of the fissionable uranium-235 with the more naturally abundant uranium-238. Mixtures of radioactive nuclides such as this are very common in the nuclear power industry.

Two samples of radioactive nuclides **X** and **Y** each have an activity of $A_{0}$ at *t* = 0. They are subsequently mixed together. The half-lives of **X **and **Y** are 16 and 8 years, respectively.

Show that the total activity of the mixture at time *t *= 48 years is equal to $\frac{9}{64}A_{0}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write an expression for the activity of each nuclide in terms of the number of half-lives completed:

- $A_{X} = A_{0} ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{N}$  and $A_{Y} = A_{0} ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{N}$ where *N* is the number of half-lives
- The amount of time elapsed, *t, *can be written as some multiple *N * of half-lives: $t=N\timest_{1/2}$

- Number of half-lives:* *$N=\frac{t}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}$ **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the activity of each nuclide in terms of the time elapsed:

- $A_{X} = A_{0} ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{\frac{48}{16}}$ **AND** $A_{Y} = A_{0} ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{\frac{48}{8}}$ **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the total activity *A  *of the mixture:

- $A=A_{X}+A_{Y}$
- $A = A_{0} ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{\frac{48}{16}} + A_{0} ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{\frac{48}{8}}$

Simplify the expression fully:

- $A = A_{0} [ ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{3} + ( \frac{1}{2} ) ^{6} ]$`= \left(\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{64}\right) = \frac{9}{64} A_{0}` **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You may have simply determined the number of half-lives of each isotope in 48 years by dividing 48 years by 8 and then 16, and halving each **A*<sub>*0 *</sub>*the appropriate number of times before combining. This method is equally correct, but you must clearly show and explain your reasoning with each step.*

parts.problemMd:
Rubidium (Rb) was found in samples of moon rock which were retrieved from the Apollo missions. The isotope ${}_{37}^{87}\mathrm{R} b$ is known to have a half-life of 4.90 × 10<sup>10</sup>years.

One of the moon rock samples contains 1.2 mg of ${}_{37}^{87}\mathrm{R} b$.

Show that the mass of ${}_{37}^{87}\mathrm{R} b$ that the rock sample contained when the moon was formed 4.47 ×10<sup>9 </sup>years ago was about 1.3 mg.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Half-life of ${}_{37}^{87}\mathrm{R} b$, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$= 4.90 × 10<sup>10 </sup>years
- Current mass of ${}_{37}^{87}\mathrm{R} b$, *m* = 1.2 mg = 1.2 × 10<sup>–3 </sup>g
- Time since the formation of the moon, *t* = 4.47 × 10<sup>9</sup> years** **

Calculate the decay constant  of the rubidium using the expression from the formula page:

- $λ=\frac{0.693}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}=\frac{0.693}{4.90\times10^{10}}$ = 1.41 × 10<sup>–11 </sup>year<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark] **

Use the decay equation from the formula page to calculate the mass *m* of ${}_{37}^{87}\mathrm{R} b$ present in the rock sample 4.47 × 10<sup>9 </sup>years ago:

- $x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$ so *m* =$m_{0}e^{-λt}$ (because mass *m* is proportional to number of nuclei $x$)
- (1.20 × 10<sup>–3</sup>) = $m_{0} e^{ - } ( 1.41 \times 10^{ - } 11 ) \times ( 4.47 \times 10^{9} )$ = 0.939 ×$m_{0}$
- $m_{0}$*= *$\frac{1.2\times10^{-3}}{0.939}$*=* 1.28 × 10<sup>–3</sup> g ~ 1.3 mg **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *All quantities such as number of radioactive nuclei, activity and mass of radioactive material decay exponentially and follow the equation *$x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$*. This is given on your formula page in your exam, but you must understand the quantities that **x** can represent.*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Though this question asks you to calculate the activity, you need to spot the tricky unit conversions throughout the question to gain full credit:*

parts.problemMd:
Radioactive carbon dating is a method for determining the age of samples containing organic material. This is a commonly used method for terrestrial objects.

Pieces of ancient wood found in a fireplace at an archaeological site can be dated by measuring the activity of carbon-14. A sample contains one carbon-14 atom per 8.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> carbon-12 atoms. In living wood, the concentration of carbon-14 atoms is greater at one carbon-14 atom per 3.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> carbon-12 atoms.

The half-life of carbon-14 is 1.8 × 10<sup>11</sup> s.

Explain why the concentration of carbon-14 is greater in living wood and calculate the age, in years, of the sample taken from the archaeological site.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain why the concentration of carbon-14 is greater in living wood:

- Carbon-14 is constantly absorbed / replaced in living wood; **[1 mark]**
- (In dead wood, it is not replaced, but) carbon-14 undergoes radioactive decay over time **AND** carbon-12 is <u>stable</u>; **[1 mark]**

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of carbon-14, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$= 1.8 × 10<sup>11</sup> s
- Initial ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 (in living wood) = 1/(3 × 10<sup>10</sup>)
- Final ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 (in the ancient wood) = 1/(8 × 10<sup>10</sup>)

Calculate the decay constant of carbon-14:

- $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{1.8\times10^{11}}$ = 3.9 × 10<sup>–12</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the elapsed time using the decay equation:

- $x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$ where $x$  represents the ratio of C-14
- $\frac{1}{8 \times 10^{10}} = \frac{1}{3 \times 10^{10}} e^{ - } ( 3.9 \times 10^{ - } 12 ) t$ **[1 mark]**
- Multiply both sides by 3 × 10<sup>10</sup> to obtain 0.375 = $e^{ - } ( 3.9 \times 10^{ - } 12 ) t$
- ln 0.375 = – (3.9 × 10<sup>–12</sup>) × t
- t = 2.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> s = 7900 years **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

Specific acoustic impedance is defined as:

- In the medium; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

parts.problemMd:

Describe the piezoelectric effect in terms of the energy transfers taking place when:

(i) a gas lighter ignites a flame using a small spark,

[1]

(ii) a motion sensor uses ultrasound waves to signal an automatic door to open,

[1]

(iii) an inkjet printer ejects ink from nozzles onto a sheet of paper,

[1]

parts.solutionMd:
(i) When a gas lighter ignites a flame using a small spark:

(iv) When a hearing aid receives sound:

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

[2]

parts.solutionMd:
(i) The transducer produces a short pulse of ultrasound by:

**Final answer:** **Any ****four**** from:**

- Connecting the <u>electrodes</u> to an alternating / high frequency emf / voltage / p.d.; **[1 mark]**
- The frequency of the alternating p.d. is equal to the resonant frequency of the crystal (which is above 20 kHz); **[1 mark]**
- (Hence) the <u>crystal</u> expands and contracts / vibrates at the same frequency as the alternating p.d.; **[1 mark]**
- The vibration produces ultrasound / pressure waves in the crystal / plastic membrane; **[1 mark]**
- The <u>backing material</u> damps the oscillations of the crystal / stops the vibration of crystal; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Ultrasound is incident on a boundary between two materials. Some of the ultrasound is reflected at the boundary and the rest is transmitted across the boundary.

The acoustic impedance of air is 4.29 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

The acoustic impedance of coupling gel is 1.48 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

The acoustic impedance of skin is 1.65 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the percentage of the ultrasound which would be transmitted into the skin when incident on

(i) an air−skin boundary,

[2]

(ii) a gel−skin boundary.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Acoustic impedance of air, $Z_{a}$ = 4.29 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of coupling gel, $Z_{g}$ = 1.48 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of skin, $Z_{s}$ = 1.65 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate the % transmitted into the skin for the air−skin boundary:

- Intensity reflection equation:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ s - Z _ a ) ^2 / ( Z _ s + Z _ a ) ^2 = ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 - 4.29 x 10 ^2 ) ^2 / ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 + 4.29 x 10 ^2 ) ^2`
- Fraction reflected:  $\frac{I_{R}}{I_{0}}$ = 0.99896 **[1 mark]**
- % transmitted = (1 − 0.99896) × 100% = 0.1% **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the % transmitted into the skin for the gel−skin boundary:

- `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ s - Z _ g ) ^2 / ( Z _ s + Z _ g ) ^2 = ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.48 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.48 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2`
- Fraction reflected:  $\frac{I_{R}}{I_{0}}$ = 2.9499 × 10<sup>–3</sup> **[1 mark]**
- % transmitted = (1 − 2.9499 × 10<sup>–3</sup>) × 100% = 99.7% **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Since the equation has the difference in acoustic impedance **squared**, it doesn't actually matter which boundary you use as **Z*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **Z*<sub>*2*</sub>* , as *$( Z_{2} - Z_{1} ) ^{2} = ( Z_{1} - Z_{2} ) ^{2}$*. Therefore, focus on making sure you've put in the correct numbers into your calculator and **squared** them too, as this is easy to forget!*

parts.problemMd:
Most modern ultrasound transducers are made from the piezoelectric material lead zirconate titanate (PZT).

Fig. 1.1 shows the effect on the structure of a crystal of PZT when an alternating potential difference is applied across it.

![24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-crystal-applied-p-d--cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/004-24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-crystal-applied-p.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

(i) Describe what happens at a molecular level when an alternating potential difference is applied across a PZT transducer to generate ultrasound.

You may draw on Fig. 1.1 to help with your answer.

[4]

(ii) Describe the conditions that will enable maximum energy conversion into ultrasound to occur.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) When an alternating potential difference (p.d.) is applied to a PZT transducer:

**Final answer:** **Any ****four**** from:**

- The positive / negative charges are attracted to the negative / positive terminal **OR** charges in the lattice (of the PZT crystal) separate; **[1 mark]**
- The movement of the central positive charge (along the central axis) causes the PZT crystal to deform / change shape / expand and contract; **[1 mark]**
- When the p.d. changes direction, the central positive charge moves in the opposite direction, causing the crystal to deform (in the opposite direction); **[1 mark]**
- The repeated crystal deformations lead to oscillations **OR** demonstrate on diagram e.g. $( 1 ) \rightarrow \text{with} e x p a n d i n g \text{on top} ( 2 ) \rightarrow \text{with} c o n t r a c t i n g \text{on top} ( 1 ) \rightarrow \text{with} e x p a n d i n g \text{on top} ( 3 ) \rightarrow \text{with} c o n t r a c t i n g \text{on top} ( 1 )$ **[1 mark]**
- The alternating p.d. causes the crystal to oscillate at the same frequency (as the applied field); **[1 mark]**
- The oscillations are transferred to the surrounding air molecules to produce ultrasound (if frequency >20 000 Hz); **[1 mark]** ![24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/005-24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma.png)

(ii) Maximum energy transfer occurs when:

- The frequency of the applied (alternating) p.d. is equal to the <u>natural frequency</u> of the PZT crystal / transducer; **[1 mark]**
- This causes resonance to occur; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *The diagram might look daunting at first, but the key part to notice is the **movement of the central ion** which has a net charge of +4e*

> *A simplified view is shown below:*

![24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/006-24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma1.png)

(ii) Explain why a B-scan would be better than an A-scan for imaging damaged tissue that surrounds the eye.

parts.solutionMd:
(i) An A-scan can be used to measure the thickness of a patient's eye lens by:

- Pulses of ultrasound are sent into the eye; **[1 mark]**
- The front and back of the lens reflect the pulses (which are displayed on an oscilloscope); **[1 mark]**
- The thickness of the lens is determined from the speed of ultrasound (in the medium) and the time; **[1 mark]**

(ii) A B-scan is better for imaging damaged tissue that surrounds the eye because:

- A-scans are one-directional, they can only be used to take measurements of the eye; **[1 mark]**
- B-scans produce 2 or 3-dimensional images, so they can be used to investigate the structures in / around the eye; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The paths of the ultrasound pulses are as follows:*

![24-1-1b-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-eye-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/008-24-1-1b-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-eye-ma.png)

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.3 shows an ultrasound A-scan trace from the scan of an eye.

![24-1-1c-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-pulse-oscilloscope-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/009-24-1-1c-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-pulse-oscilloscope-c.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

The speed of ultrasound in the eye is 1520 m s<sup>–1</sup> and the speed of ultrasound in the lens is 1670 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

Use Fig. 1.3 to calculate the thickness of

(i) the lens, in mm,

[2]

(ii) the eye, in cm.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the thickness of the eye lens:

List the known quantities:

- Speed of ultrasound in the eye, $c_{eye}$ = 1520 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Speed of ultrasound in the lens, $c_{lens}$ = 1670 m s<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate the thickness of the lens:

![24-1-1c-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-puls-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/010-24-1-1c-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-puls-ma.png)

- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave enters the lens at **L**<sub>**1**</sub> when *t* = 8.5 μs
- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave leaves the lens at  **L**<sub>**2**</sub> when *t* = 14 μs
- Time taken:  Δ*t *= 14 – 8.5 = 5.5 μs

Calculate the thickness of the lens:

- Lens thickness = $\frac{1}{2}c_{lens}\Deltat$ **[1 mark]**
- Lens thickness = $\frac{1}{2} \times 1670 \times ( 5.5 \times 10^{ - } 6 )$
- Lens thickness = 4.59 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m = 4.6 mm **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the thickness of the eye :

- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave enters the eye at A when *t* = 5.5 μs
- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave meets the back of the eye at B when *t* = 31.5 μs
- Time taken from **A** to **L**<sub>**1**</sub>:  Δ*t*<sub>A</sub>* *= 8.5 – 5.5 = 3.0 μs
- Time taken from **L**<sub>**2**</sub> to **B**:  Δ*t*<sub>B</sub>* *= 31.5 – 14 = 17.5 μs

Calculate the distances before and after the lens:

- Distance **A** → **L**<sub>**1**</sub> = $\frac{1}{2}c_{eye}\Deltat_{A}$
- Distance **A** → **L**<sub>**1**</sub> = $\frac{1}{2} \times 1520 \times ( 3.0 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) = 2.28 \times 10^{ - } 3 \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**
- Distance **L**<sub>**2**</sub> → **B** = $\frac{1}{2}c_{eye}\Deltat_{B}$
- Distance **L**<sub>**2**</sub> → **B** = $\frac{1}{2} \times 1520 \times ( 17.5 \times 10^{ - } 6 ) = 1.33 \times 10^{ - } 2 \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the thickness of the eye:

- Eye thickness = distance (**A** → **L**<sub>**1**</sub>) + lens thickness + distance (**L**<sub>**2**</sub> → **B**)
- Eye thickness = 0.23 + 0.46 + 1.33 = 2.02 cm **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Take some time to decipher the graph to make sure you understand it before diving into the calculations*

> *At each boundary between media, some of the energy of the ultrasound pulse is **reflected** back to the transducer and the rest is **transmitted. **The reflected pulses are what give rise to the spikes we see on the graph*

- *The first spike represents the ultrasound entering the cornea at boundary **A*
- *The next two spikes represent the boundaries **L*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **L*<sub>*2*</sub>*, which are the front and rear surfaces of the eye lens*
- *The final spike is where contact is made with the retina at boundary **B**, i.e. the back of the eye*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.3 shows an ultrasound A-scan trace from the scan of an eye. The speed of ultrasound in the eye is 1520 m s^–1^ and the speed of ultrasound in the lens is 1670 m s^–1^.

Calculate the thickness of the eye: Eye thickness = distance (A → L1) + lens thickness + distance (L2 → B) = 0.23 + 0.46 + 1.33 = 2.02 cm

The first spike represents the ultrasound entering the cornea at boundary A. The final spike is where contact is made with the retina at boundary B, i.e. the back of the eye.

The graph in Fig. 1.4 shows the attenuation of the intensity of ultrasound at a frequency of 3 MHz with depth.

![24-1-1d-h-24-1-h-attenuation-of-ultrasound-graph-3-mhz-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/011-24-1-1d-h-24-1-h-attenuation-of-ultrasound-graph.png)

**Fig. 1.4**

When carrying out the scan, a gel is applied between the transducer and eye to enable 100% transmission of the ultrasound into the eye.

Use the information in Table 1.1 and the graph in Fig. 1.4 to calculate the ratio of the intensity of the reflections from A and B, by the time the pulses come back to the receiver.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **acoustic impedance / kg m**<sup>**–2**</sup>** s**<sup>**–1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| eye | 1.52 × 10<sup>6</sup> |
| eye lens | 1.84 × 10<sup>6</sup> |
| surrounding tissue | 1.69 × 10<sup>6</sup> |
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the ratio of the intensity of the reflections from A and B:

List the known quantities:

- Acoustic impedance of the eye, $Z_{e}$ = 1.52 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of the lens, $Z_{l}$ = 1.84 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of the surrounding tissue, $Z_{t}$ = 1.69 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at each boundary:

- Intensity reflection coefficient:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- Eye-lens boundary:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.84 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.84 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 9.1 x 10 ^ negative 3` **[1 mark]**
- Eye-tissue boundary:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.69 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.69 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 2.8 x 10 ^ negative 3` **[1 mark]**

Determine the total energy lost by reflection between A and B:

- At each boundary, only a small fraction of energy is reflected
- Hence, transmitted energy at B = (0.9909 × 0.9909 × 0.9972) = 0.9791, so 0.021 of that is reflected
- It is reasonable to make the approximation 0.9791 ≈ 1.0
- So the same amount of energy is reflected at both A and B; **[1 mark]**

Determine the energy lost by attenuation:

- The decrease in intensity must be due to the attenuation of the signal only
- Total distance travelled = 2 × eye thickness = 4 cm

![NWtsA8zL_24-1-1d-h-24-1-h-attenuation-of-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/012-nwtsa8zl-24-1-1d-h-24-1-h-attenuation-of-ma.png)

- (From the graph) when depth = 4 cm, the intensity is reduced from 8 to 2, or $I_{0}\rightarrow\frac{I_{0}}{4}$
- Therefore, $\frac{I_{A}}{I_{B}}=4$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *At first, this question looks more complicated than it really is. When you realise that all the energy loss results from attenuation, rather than reflection, it simplifies the question greatly*

> *Remember that attenuation happens in both directions. It is reasonable to assume that attenuation occurs at the same rate in all tissues, so you don't need to determine attenuation in the lens and eye separately*

parts.problemMd:
An ultrasound investigation was used to identify a small volume of an unknown substance in a patient. It is suspected that this substance is either a cyst or a tumour.

During the ultrasound investigation, an ultrasound pulse of frequency 5 MHz is passed through soft tissue and then into the small volume of the unknown substance.

The ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity for the ultrasound pulse reflected at the boundary was found to be 7.54 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

Table 1.1 shows some information about the density and speed of ultrasound in soft tissue, cysts and tumours.

**Table 1.1**

| **material** | **density / kg m**<sup>**−3**</sup> | **ultrasound velocity / m s**<sup>**−1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| soft tissue | 1065 | 1530 |
| cyst | 1020 | 1570 |
| tumour | 990 | 1565 |

(i) Use the information in Table 1.1 to show that the unknown medium is a cyst.

[4]

(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later.

Determine the length of the cyst, in cm, to two significant figures.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the percentage of energy from the ultrasonic transducer that is reflected:

- Acoustic impedance:  $Z=ρc$
- Acoustic impedance of soft tissue:  $Z_{st}=1065\times1530=1.629\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of cyst:  $Z_{c}=1020\times1570=1.601\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of tumour:  $Z_{t}=990\times1565=1.549\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$ **1 mark for all Z values correct**

Use the intensity reflection coefficient equation:

- Intensity reflection coefficient:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- Cyst:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 7.5 x 10 ^ negative 5` **[1 mark]**
- Tumour:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 6.3 x 10 ^ negative 4` **[1 mark]**

Compare the ratios to the ratio given in the question to identify the medium:

- The intensity reflection coefficient given, $7.54\times10^{-5}$, is closer to the value for a cyst than a tumour **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the unknown medium is a cyst

(ii) Determine the length of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Time detected from front of cyst = 27.5 µs
- Time detected from rear of cyst = 43.2 µs
- Speed of ultrasound in cyst, *c* = 1570 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the length of the cyst:

- The difference in times is due to the longer signal passing through the cyst, then reflecting
- Length of cyst:  $d=\frac{1}{2}c\Deltat$
- $d = \frac{1}{2} \times 1570 \times ( 43.2 - 27.5 ) \times 10^{ - } 6$ **[1 mark]**
- $d=0.01232m=1.2\mathrm{cm}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *The time difference accounts for the time spent while the pulse travels through the cyst, and then back through it as it is reflected. Therefore, during half of this time, the pulse travels the length of the cyst, so we can simply find this length using the speed of the pulse and the time taken.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later. Determine the length of the cyst, in cm, to two significant figures. [Answer: Speed of ultrasound in cyst, c = 1570 m s^−1; Length of cyst: d = ½ c Δt = ½ × 1570 × (43.2 − 27.5) × 10^−6 = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm]

Fig. 1.1 shows a beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst.

The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue.

![24-1-3b-h-24-1-h-x-ray-intensity-cyst-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/003-24-1-3b-h-24-1-h-x-ray-intensity-cyst-cie-ial-sq.png)

**Fig. 1.1 **(not to scale)

The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup> for X-rays. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>.

You may assume that the attenuating behaviour of X-rays in matter is the same as that of ultrasound in matter.

The X-ray beam is switched on for a time *t*.

Determine the energy of the X-ray beam incident on the front surface of the cyst each second. State any assumptions you make.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the X-ray energy incident on the cyst each second:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation constant of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance travelled through the tissue, $x$ = 2.1 cm

Calculate the intensity of the X-ray beam at the cyst:

- Intensity of a beam in tissue:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- $I = ( 4.6 \times 10 ^{3} ) e^{ - } ( 0.85 \times 2.1 ) = 771.9 \mathrm{W} \mathrm{m} ^{ - } 2$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the cross-sectional area of the front surface of the cyst:

- Cross-sectional area of the cyst:  $A = \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } \\times ( \frac{0.012}{2} )^{2}$ = 1.13 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> **AND**
- Assumption: the front surface is circular; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the power and energy incident on the cyst:

- Intensity of a wave:  $I=\frac{P}{A}\RightarrowP=IA$
- Incident power:  $P = 771.9 \times ( 1.13 \times 10^{ - } 4 ) = 0.087 \mathrm{W}$
- Energy transferred each second:  $E=Pt=0.087J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You are not explicitly told the shape of the cyst. With the information, you must **assume** that its width is the same as its length. The fact that the question asks for assumptions is a big hint for this.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(a)(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later. Determine the length of the cyst, in cm. Length of cyst: d = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm.

(b) Fig. 1.1 shows a beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst. The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue. The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm^–1 for X-rays. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10^3 W m^–2. You may assume that the attenuating behaviour of X-rays in matter is the same as that of ultrasound in matter.

The ratio of the intensities of the emergent X-ray beams X and Y is determined to be

$\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$

(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst.

[3]

(ii) Describe the quality of the images that would be obtained from the ultrasound and the X-ray scans of the cyst, explaining your answers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation coefficient of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance between the tissue and cyst = 2.1 cm
- Total distance = 4.8 cm

Use the attenuation equation:

- X-ray attenuation:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- Final intensity of beam X:  $I_{X} = ( 4.6 \\times 10^{3} ) e^{- 0.85 \\times 4.8}$
- Final intensity of beam Y:  $I_{Y} = ( 4.6 \\times 10^{3} ) [ ( e^{- 0.85 \\times 2.1} ) ( e^{- 1.2 \mu } ) ( e^{- 0.85 \\times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 )} ) ]$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute into the ratio given in the question:

- Ratio of the emergent intensities:  $\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$
- Substitute:  $\frac{ ( 4.6 \times 10 ^{3} ) [ ( e^{ - } 0.85 \times 2.1 ) ( e^{ - } 1.2 mu ) ( e^{ - } 0.85 \times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 ) ) ] }{ ( 4.6 \times 10 ^{3} ) e^{ - } 0.85 \times 4.8} = 0.94$ **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $e^{0.85 ( 4.8 - 2.1 - 1.5 ) - 1.2 \mu } = 0.94 \Leftrightarrow e^{1.02 - 1.2 \mu } = 0.94$
- Take natural logs:  $1.02-1.2μ=\mathrm{ln}0.94\Rightarrowμ=\frac{1.02-\mathrm{ln}0.94}{1.2}$
- Attenuation coefficient of cyst:  $μ$ = 0.90 cm<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Describe and explain the quality of the images from the two scans:

For the X-ray image...

- The <u>attenuation coefficients</u> (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are too similar / have approximately the same value **AND**
- (Hence) no / poor contrast would be obtained between the cyst and surrounding tissue / cyst would not be distinguishable from the surrounding tissue; **[1 mark]**

For the ultrasound image...

- The <u>acoustic impedances</u> (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are similar / have approximately the same value **AND**
- (Hence) there will be little reflection so the cyst (boundary) would be poorly imaged; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The expression for the attenuation of beam Y may look intimidating, but all it is saying is that the beam is attenuated by 2.1 cm of tissue, 1.2 cm of cyst and 1.5 cm (4.8 cm − 1.2 cm − 2.1 cm) of more tissue.*

> *We can combine as many attenuations as we like simply by multiplying by another exponential factor. Just make sure to use the appropriate coefficient for each difference material.*

parts.problemMd:
The accelerating potential difference between the cathode and the anode of an X-ray tube is 75 kV.

(i) State the maximum energy, in eV, of the photons produced in the X-ray tube.

[1]

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The maximum energy of the X-rays is:

- Energy gained by electron = energy of photon
- (Hence) maximum photon energy = 75 keV **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the minimum wavelength of photons in the X-ray beam:

List the known quantities:

- Planck constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup> J s
- Charge on the electron, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the minimum wavelength using the photon energy equation:

- Energy of a photon:  $E=\frac{hc}{λ}$ **[1 mark]**
- $eV=\frac{hc}{λ}\Rightarrowλ=\frac{hc}{eV}$
- $\lambda = \frac{ ( 6.63 \times 10^{ - } 34 ) \times ( 3 \times 10^{8} ) }{ ( 1.6 \times 10^{ - } 19 ) \times ( 75 \times 10 ^{3} ) }$ **[1 mark]**
- $λ$ = 1.66 × 10<sup>–11</sup> m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Work done on a charge, **W** =** QV **where **Q** is the charge and **V** the potential difference. Since the charge of an electron is **e** this means that **W** = **E** (energy transferred) = **eV**.*

parts.problemMd: Describe the differences between CT scanning and X-ray imaging.
parts.solutionMd:
The differences between CT scanning and X-ray imaging are:

- An X-ray image is a single ‘shadow’ image / 2-D image (of the whole structure); **[1 mark]**
- A CT image is made up of many X-rays images of a (thin) slice (through a structure); **[1 mark]**
- At different angles / combined to make a 3-D image; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A parallel beam of X-rays is incident on a medium with a linear absorption coefficient *μ*.

State what is meant by the linear absorption coefficient.
parts.solutionMd:
The linear absorption coefficient is:

- $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$ **[1 mark]**
- Where $I_{0}$ is the intensity of the incident beam, $I$ is the intensity of the transmitted beam and $x$ = distance travelled through the material; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Make sure not just to state the equation, but explain each of the variables for full marks. You must be detailed in some equations e.g. just writing ‘**I **is the intensity’ will not get you the mark, because **two** beams are involved, so you must state the intensity of which one this is referring to.*

parts.problemMd: Describe the difference between sharpness and contrast in X-ray imaging.
parts.solutionMd:
The sharpness of an X-ray image describes:

- How well defined the edges of a structure / boundary are; **[1 mark]**

The contrast of an X-ray image describes:

- The difference in (the degree of) blackening between structures; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: State** two** causes of the loss of sharpness of an X-ray image.
parts.solutionMd:
Loss of sharpness happens due to:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** from:**

- Scattering of photons in tissue; **[1 mark]**
- Not using a parallel beam / collimator / lead grid; **[1 mark]**
- A large blurring effect / penumbra on shadow; **[1 mark]**
- Using a beam / an anode which is too wide; **[1 mark]**
- Not using a sensor / CCD with high enough resolution / small enough pixels; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
State

(i) what is meant by the hardness of an X-ray beam

[2]

(ii) how the hardness of the X-ray beam is controlled.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Hardness of an X-ray beam is:

- Its ability to penetrate (a material); **[1 mark]**
- The greater the hardness, the greater the penetration; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Hardness can be controlled by:

- Changing the anode voltage / electron energy; **[1 mark]**
- The higher the anode voltage / electron energy, the greater the penetration / hardness; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
(i) State what is meant by contrast in an X-ray image.

[1]

(ii) A parallel beam of X-ray radiation is incident, separately, on samples of bone and of muscle.

Data for the thickness *x* of the samples of bone and of muscle, together with the linear attenuation coefficients *μ* of the radiation in bone and in muscle, are given in Table 10.1.

**Table 10.1**

|   | ***x***** / cm** | ***μ***** / cm**<sup>**–1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| bone | 1.5 | 2.9 |
| muscle | 4.0 | 0.95 |

Calculate the ratio

$\frac{\mathrm{intensity} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{radiation} \mathrm{transmitted} \mathrm{through} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{bone}}{\mathrm{intensity} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{radiation} \mathrm{transmitted} \mathrm{through} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{muscle}}$.

ratio = ........................................ [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State what is meant by contrast in an X-ray image:

- Contrast means a <u>difference</u> in the amount of blackening in the image; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the ratio $\frac{\mathrm{intensity} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{radiation} \mathrm{transmitted} \mathrm{through} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{bone}}{\mathrm{intensity} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{radiation} \mathrm{transmitted} \mathrm{through} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{muscle}}$:

- $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$ **[1 mark]**
- $I_{b}=I_{0}e^{-2.9\times1.5}$
- $I_{m}=I_{0}e^{-0.95\times4}$
- `I _ b / I _ m = (I _ 0 e ^ negative 2.9 x 1.5 )/(I _ 0 e ^ negative 0.95 x 4 ) = ( e ^ negative 2.9 x 1.5 )/(e ^ negative 0.95 x 4 ) = 0.577 = 0.58 ( 2 s. f. )`** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
(i) Explain how X-rays are produced for use in medical diagnosis

[3]

(ii) Discuss **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of using CT scanning over X-ray imaging.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) X-rays are produced by:

- Accelerating electrons (through a high p.d.); **[1 mark]**
- Electrons are incident on a metal target; **[1 mark]**
- (When electrons hit the target) X-rays are produced as the electrons decelerate; **[1 mark]**

(ii) One advantage and disadvantage of using CT scanning is:

One advantage is:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- (CT scans produces) more detailed (3D) image which is better for diagnosis; **[1 mark]**
- (CT scans) can distinguish between different structures with similar attenuation coefficients as X-ray scans just detect a 'shadow'; **[1 mark]**

One disadvantage is:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- Patients are exposed to a higher dose of ionising radiation which could cause cancer / damage cells; **[1 mark]**
- Usually requires contrast media which can have negative / adverse side effects; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
An X-ray image is taken of the skull of a patient. Another patient has a CT scan taken of their entire head.

Describe how the image produced during CT scanning differs from the image produced by X-ray imaging.
parts.solutionMd:
The image produced during CT scanning differs from the image produced by X-ray imaging by:

**Final answer:** **Max ****four**** from:**

- An X-ray image is flat / 2D; **[1 mark]**
- CT scan takes many images of a section / slice at different angles; **[1 mark]**
- The images are combined to build up an image of a section / slice through the body; **[1 mark]**
- The process is repeated for different sections / slices; **[1 mark]**
- These images are combined together to build a 3D image; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Two patients arrive at a hospital. One patient is a child with a broken arm, the other is a pregnant woman coming in for a check-up for her unborn foetus.

Over the course of the diagnosis and treatment of the child’s broken arm, several images of the arm are required.

Similarly, to check the progress of a woman’s pregnancy, several images of the foetus are required.

For each scenario, suggest the most appropriate imaging technique to use and give **two** reasons for the choice.
parts.solutionMd:
For a broken arm, x-ray imaging is the most appropriate because:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** from:**

- X-ray imaging provides a good contrast between bone and the surrounding tissue; **[1 mark]**
- X-ray creates a sharp / high resolution image (compared to ultrasound); **[1 mark]**
- X-rays pass straight through soft tissue, whereas ultrasound does not; **[1 mark]**

For a fetal scan, ultrasound imaging is the most appropriate because:

**Final answer:** **Any**** two**** from:**

- Ultrasound is safer / non-ionising (for the mother and child); **[1 mark]**
- Ultrasound can detect changes in tissue type; **[1 mark]**
- Ultrasound transmission / detection allows imaging in real-time; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
An X-ray image showing the cross-section of the bone and muscle is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![24-1-3d-m-24-1-xray-bone-muscle-diagram-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-2-production-and-use-of-x-rays/assets/003-24-1-3d-m-24-1-xray-bone-muscle-diagram-cie-ial-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Parallel X-ray beams of intensity $I_{0}$ are incident on the muscle and bone as shown. The emergent beam after passing through muscle alone has an intensity of $I_{m}$ and an intensity of $I_{bm}$ after passing through the bone and the muscle.

(i) Determine, in terms of $I_{0}$, the intensities $I_{m}$ and $I_{bm}$ of the emergent X-rays.

The linear attenuation coefficient of bone is 2.90 cm<sup>−1</sup>

The linear attenuation coefficient of muscle of 0.95 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

[4]

(ii) Suggest why, on an X-ray plate, the contrast between bone and muscle is much greater than the contrast between fat and muscle.

The linear attenuation coefficient of fat is 0.90 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the intensities of the emergent X-rays:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation coefficient in bone, $μ_{b}$ = 2.90 cm<sup>−1</sup>
- Thickness of bone, $x_{b}$ = 2.0 cm
- Attenuation coefficient in muscle, $μ_{m}$ = 0.95 cm<sup>−1</sup>
- Thickness of muscle, $x_{m}$ = 5.0 cm

Determine the intensity of X-rays transmitted through muscle alone:

- Attenuation of X-rays:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$ **[1 mark]**
- Intensity transmitted through muscle alone:  $I_{m}=I_{0}e^{-μ_{m}x_{m}}$
- $I_{m}=I_{0}e^{-0.95\times5.0}=8.7\times10^{-3}I_{0}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the intensity of X-rays transmitted through muscle and bone:

- Intensity transmitted through bone:  $I_{b}=I_{0}e^{-μ_{b}x_{b}}$
- Intensity transmitted through muscle and bone:  $I_{b} m = I_{0} ( e^{ - } mu_{b} x_{b} ) \times ( e^{ - } mu_{m} \Delta x )$
- Where $\Deltax=x_{m}-x_{b}$ = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 cm
- $I_{b} m = I_{0} ( e^{ - } 2.90 \times 2.0 ) \times ( e^{ - } 0.95 \times 3.0 )$ **[1 mark]**
- $I_{bm}=1.8\times10^{-4}I_{0}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The contrast between bone and muscle is much greater than between fat and muscle because:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** from:**

- Contrast depends on the <u>difference</u> in attenuation; **[1 mark]**
- The difference between µ of muscle and fat is small (hence poor contrast); **[1 mark]**
- The difference between µ of bone and soft tissue / fat is large (hence good contrast); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *Remember in part (i) when the X-rays travel through the muscle and bone, it is travelling through 2.0 cm of bone but only 5.0 – 2.0 = **3.0 cm** of muscle.*

parts.problemMd:
The data in Table 1.1 shows how the attenuation coefficient *μ* depends on the energy of the X-rays in bone and muscle.

**Table 1.1**

| maximum X-ray energy / keV | $μ_{bone}$ / cm<sup>−1</sup> | $μ_{muscle}$ / cm<sup>−1</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 3.32 | 0.54 |
| 100 | 0.60 | 0.21 |
| 250 | 0.32 | 0.16 |
| 4000 | 0.087 | 0.049 |

Using the data in Table 1.1, state and explain which X-ray energy would produce an image of a bone next to a muscle with the best contrast.
parts.solutionMd:
The energy that would produce the best contrast is:

- 50 keV; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- Contrast depends on the difference in attenuation; **[1 mark]**
- The difference between *µ* of bone and muscle is greatest with 50 keV X-rays (hence best contrast); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
For X-ray energies around 30 keV and below, the attenuation coefficient *μ* is approximately proportional to the cube of the proton number *Z* of the absorbing material.

The proton numbers of muscle, bone and some contract media are shown in Table 1.2

**Table 1.2**

| **substance** | **main elements** | ** ** |
|---|---|---|
| muscle | `H _ 1`,  `C _ 6`,  `O _ 8` |   |
| bone | `H _ 1`,  `C _ 6`,  `O _ 8`,  `P _ 15`,  `Ca _ 20` |   |
| contrast media | `I _ 53`,  `Ba _ 56` |   |

Using the information in Table 1.2

(i) Show that bone absorbs X-rays about eight times more strongly than muscle.

[3]

(ii) Explain why contrast media are made from elements with high values of atomic number *Z*.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that bone absorbs X-rays about eight times more strongly than muscle:

Determine the average values of Z

| **substance** | **main elements** | **Final answer:** **average ****Z** |
|---|---|---|
| muscle | `H _ 1`,  `C _ 6`,  `O _ 8` | **Final answer:** **5** |
| bone | `H _ 1`,  `C _ 6`,  `O _ 8`,  `P _ 15`,  `Ca _ 20` | **Final answer:** **10** |
| contrast media | `I _ 53`,  `Ba _ 56` | **Final answer:** **55** |

- Average values of *Z* calculated; **[1 mark]**

Determine the ratio of the average values of *Z*:

- Ratio:  $\frac{Z_{bone}}{Z_{muscle}}\approx\frac{10}{5}\approx2$ **[1 mark]**

Use the relationship between µ and Z

- Attenuation coefficient:   $μ\proptoZ^{3}$
- Therefore $\frac{μ_{bone}}{μ_{muscle}}=2^{3}=8$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Contrast media are made from elements with high values of *Z* because:

- A contrast medium is a substance which absorbs X-rays strongly; **[1 mark]**
- As X-rays pass through a medium, they interact with electrons and/or nuclei (of atoms); **[1 mark]**
- Hence, substances with higher numbers of nuclei / electrons will interact with X-rays more, making them more absorbing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows how the attenuation coefficient *μ* of muscle varies with photon energy *E*.

![24-1-2c-h-24-1-h-attenuation-xray-energy-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-2-production-and-use-of-x-rays/assets/004-24-1-2c-h-24-1-h-attenuation-xray-energy-cie-ial.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Using Fig. 1.1, explain why X-rays with energies less than 20 keV are usually filtered out of the beam.
parts.solutionMd:
X-rays with energies less than 20 keV are usually filtered out of the beam because:

- (At energies less than 20 keV) there is more attenuation **OR** (at energies greater than 20 keV) there is less attenuation; **[1 mark]**
- The lower energy photons will be mostly absorbed (by muscles); **[1 mark]**
- Hence these (low energy) photons will not contribute to the imaging process; **[1 mark]**
- Only the higher energy photons will leave the body and be detected by the sensor; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It's important to realise that almost **all **of the low-energy X-rays would be attenuated inside the body, therefore, these X-rays would*

- *Never even reach the sensor*
- *Unnecessarily expose the patient to a higher dose of harmful radiation*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

For X-ray energies around 30 keV and below, the attenuation coefficient μ is approximately proportional to the cube of the proton number Z of the absorbing material. Using the information in Table 1.2: (i) Show that bone absorbs X-rays about eight times more strongly than muscle. [Mark scheme: Average Z of muscle = 5, bone = 10; ratio Z_bone/Z_muscle ≈ 10/5 ≈ 2; since μ ∝ Z³, μ_bone/μ_muscle = 2³ = 8.]

The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows how the attenuation coefficient μ of muscle varies with photon energy E. (From graph, when E = 20 keV, μ_muscle = 1.0 cm⁻¹.)

An X-ray beam of energy 20 keV and intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on a sample of muscle and bone as shown in Fig. 1.2. The emergent beam intensities from the muscle and bone are $I_{m}$ and $I_{b}$ respectively.

![24-1-2d-h-24-1-h-muscle-bone-xray-comparison-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-2-production-and-use-of-x-rays/assets/005-24-1-2d-h-24-1-h-muscle-bone-xray-comparison-cie.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Using the graph in Fig. 1.1, calculate the ratio of intensities to compare the attenuation produced by 1 cm of bone and 1 cm of muscle.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the ratio of intensities to compare the attenuation produced by 1 cm of bone and 1 cm of muscle:

List the known quantities:

- Thickness of muscle/bone, $x$ = 1 cm

Determine µ for muscle and bone at 20 keV:

![24-1-2c-h-24-1-h-attenuation-xra-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-2-production-and-use-of-x-rays/assets/006-24-1-2c-h-24-1-h-attenuation-xra-ma.png)

- (From graph) when *E* = 20 keV, $μ_{muscle}$ = 1.0 cm<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Since $μ\proptoZ^{3}$ and $\frac{μ_{bone}}{μ_{muscle}}\approx8$ (from **(b)**)
- Therefore $μ_{bone}=8\times1.0=8.0\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the attenuation equation to determine the ratio of intensities:

- X-ray attenuation:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- Ratio of intensities:  $\frac{I_{b}}{I_{m}}=\frac{e^{-μx}}{e^{-μx}}$
- Ratio of intensities: $\frac{I_{b}}{I_{m}}=\frac{e^{-8.0\times1}}{e^{-1.0\times1}}=9.1\times10^{-4}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
An ultrasound investigation was used to identify a small volume of an unknown substance in a patient. It is suspected that this substance is either a cyst or a tumour.

During the ultrasound investigation, an ultrasound pulse of frequency 5 MHz is passed through soft tissue and then into the small volume of the unknown substance.

The ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity for the ultrasound pulse reflected at the boundary was found to be 7.54 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

Table 1.1 shows some information about the density and speed of ultrasound in soft tissue, cysts and tumours.

**Table 1.1**

| **material** | **density / kg m**<sup>**−3**</sup> | **ultrasound velocity / m s**<sup>**−1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| soft tissue | 1065 | 1530 |
| cyst | 1020 | 1570 |
| tumour | 990 | 1565 |

(i) Use the information in Table 1.1 to show that the unknown medium is a cyst.

[4]

(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later.

Determine the length of the cyst, in cm.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the percentage of energy from the ultrasonic transducer that is reflected:

- Acoustic impedance:  $Z=ρc$
- Acoustic impedance of soft tissue:  $Z_{st}=1065\times1530=1.629\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of cyst:  $Z_{c}=1020\times1570=1.601\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of tumour:  $Z_{t}=990\times1565=1.549\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$ **1 mark for all Z values correct**

Use the intensity reflection coefficient equation:

- Intensity reflection coefficient:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- Cyst:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 7.5 x 10 ^ negative 5` **[1 mark]**
- Tumour:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 6.3 x 10 ^ negative 4` **[1 mark]**

Compare the ratios to the ratio given in the question to identify the medium:

- `I _ R / I _ 0 = 7.54 x 10 ^ negative 5 = 7.5 x 10 ^ negative 5 ( 2 s. f. )` **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the unknown medium is a cyst

(ii) Determine the length of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Time detected from front of cyst = 27.5 µs
- Time detected from rear of cyst = 43.2 µs
- Speed of ultrasound in cyst, *c* = 1570 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the length of the cyst:

- Distance travelled by ultrasound:  $d=\frac{1}{2}c\Deltat$
- $d = \frac{1}{2} \times 1570 \times ( 43.2 - 27.5 ) \times 10^{ - } 6$ **[1 mark]**
- $d=0.01232m=1.2\mathrm{cm}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later. Determine the length of the cyst, in cm.

Calculate the length of the cyst: d = 1/2 × 1570 × (43.2 − 27.5) × 10^−6 = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm

Fig. 1.1 shows a beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst.

The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue.

![24-1-3b-h-24-1-h-x-ray-intensity-cyst-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-2-production-and-use-of-x-rays/assets/001-24-1-3b-h-24-1-h-x-ray-intensity-cyst-cie-ial-sq.png)

**Fig. 1.1 **(not to scale)

The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>.

The X-ray beam is switched on for a time *t*.

Determine the energy of the X-ray beam incident on the front surface of the cyst each second. State any assumptions you make.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the X-ray energy incident on the cyst each second:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation constant of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance travelled through the tissue, $x$ = 2.1 cm

Calculate the intensity of the X-ray beam at the cyst:

- Intensity of a beam in tissue:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- $I = ( 4.6 \times 10 ^{3} ) e^{ - } ( 0.85 \times 2.1 ) = 771.9 \mathrm{W} \mathrm{m} ^{ - } 2$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the cross-sectional area of the front surface of the cyst:

- Cross-sectional area of the cyst:  $A = \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } \\times ( \frac{0.012}{2} )^{2}$ = 1.13 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> **AND**
- Assumption: the front surface is circular; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the power and energy incident on the cyst:

- Intensity of a wave:  $I=\frac{P}{A}\RightarrowP=IA$
- Incident power:  $P = 771.9 \times ( 1.13 \times 10^{ - } 4 ) = 0.087 \mathrm{W}$
- Energy transferred each second:  $E=Pt=0.087J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An ultrasound investigation was used to identify a small volume of an unknown substance in a patient. It is suspected that this substance is either a cyst or a tumour.

Table 1.1 shows some information about the density and speed of ultrasound in soft tissue, cysts and tumours: soft tissue density 1065 kg m^-3, ultrasound velocity 1530 m s^-1; cyst density 1020 kg m^-3, ultrasound velocity 1570 m s^-1; tumour density 990 kg m^-3, ultrasound velocity 1565 m s^-1.

The length of the cyst was determined to be d = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm.

A beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst. The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue. The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm^-1. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10^3 W m^-2.

The ratio of the intensities of the emergent X-ray beams X and Y is determined to be

$\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$

(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst.

[3]

(ii) Compare the quality of the images that would be obtained from the ultrasound and the X-ray scans of the cyst.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation coefficient of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance between the tissue and cyst = 2.1 cm
- Total distance = 4.8 cm

Use the attenuation equation:

- X-ray attenuation:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- Final intensity of beam X:  $I_{X} = ( 4.6 \\times 10^{3} ) e^{- 0.85 \\times 4.8}$
- Final intensity of beam Y:  $I_{Y} = ( 4.6 \\times 10^{3} ) [ ( e^{- 0.85 \\times 2.1} ) ( e^{- 1.2 \mu } ) ( e^{- 0.85 \\times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 )} ) ]$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute into the ratio given in the question:

- Ratio of the emergent intensities:  $\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$
- Substitute:  $\frac{ ( 4.6 \times 10 ^{3} ) [ ( e^{ - } 0.85 \times 2.1 ) ( e^{ - } 1.2 mu ) ( e^{ - } 0.85 \times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 ) ) ] }{ ( 4.6 \times 10 ^{3} ) e^{ - } 0.85 \times 4.8} = 0.94$ **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $e^{0.85 ( 4.8 - 2.1 - 1.5 ) - 1.2 \mu } = 0.94 \Leftrightarrow e^{1.02 - 1.2 \mu } = 0.94$
- Takes natural logs:  $1.02-1.2μ=\mathrm{ln}0.94\Rightarrowμ=\frac{1.02-\mathrm{ln}0.94}{1.2}$
- Attenuation coefficient of cyst:  $μ$ = 0.90 cm<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Compare the quality of the images that would be obtained from the ultrasound and the X-ray scans:

For the X-ray image...

- The attenuation coefficients (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are too similar / have approximately the same value **AND**

Show that each gamma photon produced has an energy of 512 keV:

List the known quantities:

- Speed of light, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Annihilation of an electron and a positron results in two gamma photons travelling in opposite directions. Therefore, the energy of one photon is equal to the rest mass energy of a single electron **[1 mark]**

Convert the rest mass of an electron into rest energy:

- Mass-energy equivalence:  $E = m c^{2}$
- $E$ = (9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup>) × (3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup>)<sup>2</sup>
- $E$ = 8.199 × 10<sup>−14</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Convert the energy in J to keV:

- $E = \frac{8.199\times10^{-14}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}$ = 512 438 eV = 512 keV **[1 mark]**

> `m = \frac{E}{c^{2}} = \frac{8 . 2 \times 10^{- 14}}{\left(3 . 00 \times 10^{8}\right)^{2}}`* = 9.11 × 10*<sup>*−31*</sup>* kg*
